sections.title: Theoretical Mechanisms: Ensemble Approximation and Regularization
sections.text:
Dropout functions as a regularization method that randomly switches off some neurons in the hidden layers during training with a predefined drop probability [1]. This process can be viewed as bagging with exponentially many neural networks, effectively training and evaluating a large number of different subnetworks within the model [2][1]. By shutting off neurons at random, dropout increases network robustness by providing a solution even if some internal connections are unavailable or highly noisy [2]. This ensemble-like behavior is distinct from simple noise injection, as it involves the systematic deactivation of units rather than just adding stochastic perturbations to weights or inputs [3][4].

The theoretical link between dropout and Bayesian inference is established through the approximation of a latent variable model, which provides a clean view of parameter sharing [5]. In this framework, dropout is formulated as a tractable approximation that enables further theoretical analysis of the gap between training and inference phases [5]. Monte Carlo Dropout is specifically utilized for uncertainty estimation, although it requires manual hyperparameter adjustment [6]. Alternatively, source model uncertainty can be quantified using a Laplace approximation to address the need for manual tuning associated with Monte Carlo methods [6]. The connection to Bayesian neural networks is further exploited in deep contextual multi-armed bandits, where inference-time dropout is used for Thompson sampling by leveraging its connection to sampling from the posterior over weights [7]. In this application, the dropout rate is learned rather than treated as a fixed hyperparameter to adjust exploration levels automatically [7]. Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) is another sampling method for performing Bayesian inference, which is contrasted with dropout in the context of estimating predictive uncertainty for computer vision tasks [8].

Dropout exhibits distinct theoretical properties that differentiate it from traditional regularizers like weight decay. Analysis of dropout in deep networks with rectified linear units and quadratic loss reveals that dropout training can produce negative weights even when the output is the sum of the inputs, which counters the suggestion that dropout primarily discourages co-adaptation of weights [9]. Furthermore, the dropout penalty can grow exponentially in the depth of the network, whereas the weight-decay penalty remains essentially linear [9]. Dropout is also insensitive to various re-scalings of input features, outputs, and network weights, a property that implies there are no isolated local minima of the dropout training criterion [9]. In contrast, weight decay is often implemented as an L2 penalty multiplier, with specific values such as $5 \cdot 10^{-4}$ used in very deep convolutional networks [10]. Other studies set weight decay to $10^{-4}$ or $5 \times 10^{-4}$ depending on the training objective, such as mixup versus empirical risk minimization [11]. An adaptive weight decay has also been proposed to allow the regularization strength for each weight to be dynamically adjusted [1].

The interaction between dropout and other regularization techniques, such as mixup, demonstrates compatibility and complementary effects. Mixup training requires a significantly lower weight decay on CIFAR-10, indicating that mix-based data augmentation has cross-cutting and complementary effects with regularization [12]. Interestingly, the combination of mixup and dropout performs the best among tested methods, showing that the two methods are compatible [11]. In such combinations, specific hyperparameters are selected, such as dropout probabilities $p \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9\}$ and mixup parameters $\alpha \in \{1, 2, 4, 8\}$ [11]. While dropout is widely used for regularization, model compression, and measuring uncertainty, the gap between its training and inference phases has largely remained under-appreciated until recent theoretical formulations [13][5]. These formulations allow for the formal characterization of the inference gap and the use of this measure to regularize the standard dropout training objective, providing explicit control over the gap [5]. Simulation results suggest that these theoretical approximations are good for different prominent models and datasets [14].

sections.title: Impact on Generalization and Decision Boundaries
sections.text:
Dropout functions as a regularization method that randomly deactivates neurons in hidden layers during training with a predefined probability, effectively training and evaluating a large number of different subnetworks within the model [1]. This mechanism can be viewed as bagging with exponentially many neural networks, where the process of combining neglected hidden units with the learned network is analyzed as a form of ensemble learning [2][3]. By training these diverse subnetworks, dropout influences the generalization error, with studies showing that it improves generalization capabilities alongside other methods like L2 regularization and data augmentation in deep reinforcement learning benchmarks [4]. In the context of generalization error bounds, new complexity measures have been proposed that provably bound the generalization error under mild assumptions, providing a theoretical framework for understanding how such regularization affects model performance [5].

The interaction between dropout and other regularization techniques reveals specific effects on decision boundaries and generalization. Mixup, a technique that interpolates between training examples, has been found to be compatible with dropout, with the combination of mixup and dropout performing the best among tested methods [6]. However, mixup with a large alpha parameter outperforms dropout on both best and last epoch test errors while achieving lower training error on real labels and remaining resistant to noisy labels [6]. This suggests that while dropout contributes to robustness, other methods like mixup may offer superior generalization in certain regimes, particularly regarding resistance to label noise [6]. The compatibility of these methods indicates that dropout does not inherently conflict with other strategies aimed at smoothing the decision boundary or improving generalization [6].

Regarding the shape and robustness of decision boundaries, dropout’s effect is linked to the stability of the training process. Research into the Benevolent Training Hypothesis indicates that steady training with dropout implies a training- and data-dependent bound on the complexity of the function being learned [7]. This stability is related to the Lipschitz constant of the network, where more complex networks exhibit longer parameter trajectories and greater variance, whereas steady training helps maintain bounded complexity even in regions far from training points [7]. In contrast, uncertainty-aware domain adaptation methods explicitly model uncertainty to smooth the classifier's decision boundary, thereby improving generalization capabilities in unsupervised settings [8]. While dropout contributes to generalization through ensemble-like effects and training stability, other approaches directly target the smoothing of the decision boundary to address domain gaps and improve classification reliability [8].

The choice of dropout rate significantly impacts the model's behavior, with original authors suggesting a rate between 0.5 and 0.8 [1]. In specific applications, such as the mixup experiments, dropout probabilities were selected from the set {0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} [6]. In other contexts, such as text-to-text transformers, a lower dropout probability of 0.1 is used for regularization [9]. These varying rates reflect the trade-off between the strength of the regularization effect and the preservation of network capacity, which in turn affects the smoothness and robustness of the resulting decision boundaries [6][1][9]. Furthermore, dropout has been identified as a bias mitigation technique in multilingual large language models, indicating that its effects extend beyond simple overfitting prevention to influencing the fairness and robustness of the learned decision boundaries [10].

In self-training scenarios, where reliable classification boundaries are difficult to establish due to limited labeled data, dropout is employed to help manage the error amplification that can occur when confidently labeled examples are added to the training set [11]. The use of dropout in such semi-supervised settings helps in finding reliable classification boundaries by regularizing the model during the iterative labeling process [11]. Additionally, in the context of adversarial robustness, decision-based attacks aim to estimate and cross the decision boundary to obtain misclassification, highlighting the importance of the boundary's shape and robustness [12]. While dropout contributes to generalization and training stability, the specific geometric properties of the decision boundary, such as its smoothness relative to other regularizers like L1 or L2 norms, remain an area where different methods offer distinct advantages [12][4]. L1 and L2 regularization reduce the value of weights, which also affects the decision boundary, but dropout achieves this through the stochastic deactivation of neurons rather than direct weight penalty [12][1].

In this paper, we investigate the problem of overfitting in deep
reinforcement learning. Among the most common benchmarks in RL, it is customary
to use the same environments for both training and testing. This practice
offers relatively little insight into an agent's ability to generalize. We
address this issue by using procedurally generated environments to construct
distinct training and test sets. Most notably, we introduce a new environment
called CoinRun, designed as a benchmark for generalization in RL. Using
CoinRun, we find that agents overfit to surprisingly large training sets. We
then show that deeper convolutional architectures improve generalization, as do
methods traditionally found in supervised learning, including L2
regularization, dropout, data augmentation and batch normalization.

sections.title: Effects on Training Dynamics and Convergence
sections.text:
The application of dropout in deep neural networks fundamentally alters the optimization landscape by effectively training and evaluating a large number of different subnetworks within the model [1]. This mechanism can be viewed as bagging with exponentially many neural networks, where the stochastic nature of the process impacts the trajectory of learning [2]. In the context of non-convex optimization, dropout has been shown to help avoid arbitrarily poor local minima by ensuring that the training objective function decreases by a multiplicative factor, up to a certain approximation error [3]. For convex empirical risk minimizers, dropout acts as a stabilizer or regularizer, rendering the gradient descent method stable in the face of arbitrary changes to any single training point [3].

The stability of the training trajectory is further characterized by the interaction between dropout and momentum-based optimizers. Mean-field analysis of the stochastic heavy ball method (SGD with Polyak's momentum) indicates that dropout contributes to the stability of the network after dropping out part of the neurons [4]. This stability is linked to connectivity along a low-loss path and convergence to the global optimum in the limit of large network widths [4]. By providing a less noisy gradient, the approach strikes a balance that results in a more stable training process [1]. However, the specific impact on convergence speed can vary depending on the implementation; for instance, in distributed resource-aware learning, a dropout mechanism that dynamically adjusts computational complexity by randomly dropping filters can increase convergence speed by allowing devices to select dropout vectors that fit their available resources [5].

Regarding learning rate requirements and the selection of the dropout rate, there is significant variation in recommended values across different studies. The original authors of dropout suggested a rate between 0.5 and 0.8 [1], while other researchers have recommended a lower dropout rate between 0.1 and 0.3 [1]. In specific experimental settings, such as the mixup paper, dropout probabilities were chosen from the set {0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} [6]. In the context of Very Deep Convolutional Networks, a dropout ratio of 0.5 was set for the first two fully-connected layers [7]. For transfer learning applications in pepper quality detection, a dropout rate of 0.3 was used in conjunction with a learning rate of 0.000001 to improve training speed and precision [8]. The choice of dropout rate also interacts with other regularization techniques; for example, in the combination of mixup and dropout, the mixup parameter $\alpha$ was chosen from {1, 2, 4, 8} [6], and this combination performed the best of all methods tested, showing compatibility between the two [6].

The stochastic nature of dropout introduces randomness that can affect model behavior and interpretability. A very high dropout rate, such as 0.8, has been observed to decrease the success rates of certain attacks due to underfitting and increased randomness in the model, which disrupts the linearity between inputs and outputs [9]. This randomness is inherent to the technique, where neurons are randomly switched off during training with a predefined drop probability [1]. In hardware and software optimizations, dropout is noted as a technique that gives good results by randomly selecting and removing neurons at each iteration [10]. While dropout is primarily known for combating over-fitting by shutting off neurons at random to increase network robustness [2], its side effects on the optimization process include the need to balance the drop probability to maintain effective gradient flow and convergence properties [1][3].

sections.title: Architectural and Task-Specific Side Effects
sections.text:
The application of dropout in convolutional neural networks (CNNs) extends beyond standard regularization by introducing noise to the output feature maps of each layer, which yields robustness to variations in images [1]. While dropout is traditionally applied to fully connected layers, as seen in the configuration of very deep convolutional networks where a ratio of 0.5 was set for the first two fully-connected layers, its effect in convolutional layers has been analyzed as a powerful generalization method [2][1]. This mechanism prevents complex co-adaptations, ensuring that each neuron learns to detect a feature that is generally helpful across a combinatorially large variety of internal contexts rather than relying on specific feature detector combinations [3]. In the context of image synthesis, such as in diffusion models, dropout rates are often set to low values, such as 0.1, indicating that the optimal application may vary by architecture and task [4].

In recurrent neural networks (RNNs), the primary challenge is the vanishing gradient problem, which arises from the difficulty of propagating gradients over long sequences of data [5][6]. This issue is particularly common when using sigmoid activations, whereas exploding gradients are more frequent with rectified linear unit activations [7]. The vanishing of gradients occurs because they are attenuated by transition operators and dropped by activation functions as sequence length increases [8]. To address these architectural limitations, specialized versions of RNNs such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) have been proposed to alleviate the problem by allowing gradients to flow backward more easily through memory mechanisms or gates [9][10][11]. Alternative architectures like the Non-saturating Recurrent Unit (NRU) further alleviate vanishing gradients by forgoing saturating activation functions and gates, while IndRNN offers a faster alternative that relies on weight regularization to resolve gradient issues [11][8].

The interaction between dropout and recurrent architectures is complex, as RNNs naturally capture path-dependent features with flexibility, yet they remain susceptible to chaos-based failure modes traced to the spectrum of the Jacobian [12][13]. In specific applications such as recurrent recommender systems, techniques like recency dropout have been explored to address the difficulty of learning long-term dependencies [6]. The theoretical underpinnings of these architectures are further complicated by the hardness of learning under symmetries, where lower bounds for convolutional networks and other architectures scale superpolynomially or exponentially with input dimension [14]. Consequently, hybrid deep learning architectures, such as conformer and MaxViT, have been developed to combine transformers and convolutional neural networks to capture both local and global features, potentially mitigating some of the isolated limitations of single-architecture approaches [5].

Beyond specific architectural constraints, dropout is conceptually viewed as a form of bagging with exponentially many neural networks, effectively training and evaluating a large number of different subnetworks within the model [15][5]. This perspective aligns with the observation that at each iteration, some neurons are randomly selected and removed from the model, a technique that gives good results in various contexts [16]. In tasks involving regional information, such as training strong classifiers with localizable features, methods for regional dropout remove informative pixels on training images by overlaying patches of black pixels or random noise [17]. The choice of dropout probability is a critical hyperparameter, with studies selecting values from sets such as {0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9} in the context of mixup regularization [18]. These architectural and task-specific considerations highlight that the side effects of dropout are not uniform but are deeply intertwined with the specific network topology and the nature of the data being processed [1][3].

sections.title: Inference Costs and Model Interpretability
sections.text:
The application of dropout in deep neural networks introduces specific considerations for the inference phase, primarily concerning the stochastic nature of the model and the computational requirements for maintaining consistent outputs. Dropout is defined as a regularization method that randomly switches off some neurons in the hidden layers during training with a predefined drop probability [1]. This process effectively trains and evaluates a large number of different subnetworks within the model [1]. Consequently, the model can be viewed as performing bagging with exponentially many neural networks [2]. Because the training process involves randomly removing neurons at each iteration [3], the resulting model parameters represent an ensemble of these subnetworks rather than a single deterministic function.

To address the stochasticity inherent in this ensemble view, weight scaling is often required during inference to ensure that the expected output of the full network matches the average output of the subnetworks trained with dropout. While the provided evidence does not explicitly detail the mathematical formula for inverted dropout, it establishes the theoretical framework that dropout training corresponds to approximate Bayesian inference in deep Gaussian processes [4]. This theoretical connection allows for the extraction of information from existing models to represent uncertainty without sacrificing computational complexity or test accuracy [4]. The ability to model uncertainty is a distinct side effect of dropout, providing a mathematically grounded framework to reason about model confidence, which is otherwise difficult to achieve with standard deep learning tools [4].

The stochastic nature of dropout also impacts model interpretability and the linearity between inputs and outputs. Interpretability is defined as a passive characteristic of a model referring to the level at which a given model makes sense for a human observer [5]. High dropout rates can disrupt the linearity between inputs and outputs, thereby affecting the success rates of certain attacks or analyses that rely on such linear relationships [6]. Specifically, a very high dropout rate (0.8) has been shown to decrease the success rates of one attack due to underfitting and increased randomness in the model [6]. This increased randomness complicates the formulation of highly reliable systems, as interpretability is an important part of such formulations even if it does not directly improve performance [7]. Furthermore, the usage of dropout has been identified as detrimental to the privacy of a client's local dataset in federated learning contexts, where it may facilitate the reconstruction of private training samples from weight updates [8].

Regarding computational overhead, the inference phase of dropout-based models does not inherently incur the same high costs as training, but the theoretical framework of dropout as Bayesian approximation offers tools to model uncertainty without prohibitive computational costs [4]. In contrast, other methods for analyzing model influence or training multiple models, such as Leave-One-Out (LOO) or downsampling, come at the price of huge upfront computational costs that are impractical for large datasets [9]. Dropout provides a more efficient alternative for capturing model uncertainty compared to these exhaustive methods. Additionally, the integration of dropout with other techniques, such as mixup, has been shown to be compatible and can result in the best performance among tested methods [10]. The choice of dropout probability, such as values in the range of 0.5 to 0.9, is a critical hyperparameter that balances the degree of stochasticity and the resulting model behavior [10].

In some architectures, the need for dropout may be mitigated by other normalization techniques. For instance, Batch Normalization addresses internal covariate shift by normalizing layer inputs, which allows for higher learning rates and can, in some cases, eliminate the need for Dropout [11]. This suggests that the side effects of dropout, such as the need for weight scaling and the introduction of stochasticity, are not universal requirements for all deep learning models but are specific to architectures that rely on dropout for regularization. The interplay between dropout and other architectural components, such as the use of ReLU activations, further influences the model's properties, including its privacy risks [8]. Ultimately, while dropout facilitates the training of robust models by simulating the removal of connections [2], its inference phase requires careful handling of weights and an understanding of the trade-offs between uncertainty quantification, interpretability, and computational efficiency [4][6][7].

snippets: Training Deep Neural Networks is complicated by the fact that the distribution of each layer's inputs changes during training, as the parameters of the previous layers change. This slows down the training by requiring lower learning rates and careful parameter initialization, and makes it notoriously hard to train models with saturating nonlinearities. We refer to this phenomenon as internal covariate shift, and address the problem by normalizing layer inputs. Our method draws its strength from making normalization a part of the model architecture and performing the normalization for each training mini-batch. Batch Normalization allows us to use much higher learning rates and be less careful about initialization, and in some cases eliminates the need for Dropout. Applied to a state-of-the-art image classification model, Batch Normalization achieves the same accuracy with 14 times fewer training steps, and beats the original model by a significant margin. Using an ensemble of batch-normalized networks, we improve upon the best published result on ImageNet classification: reaching 4.82% top-5 test error, exceeding the accuracy of human raters.

reinforcement learning. Among the most common benchmarks in RL, it is customary

evidence.snippet:
When a large feedforward neural network is trained on a small training set,
it typically performs poorly on held-out test data. This "overfitting" is
greatly reduced by randomly omitting half of the feature detectors on each
training case. This prevents complex co-adaptations in which a feature detector
is only helpful in the context of several other specific feature detectors.
Instead, each neuron learns to detect a feature that is generally helpful for
producing the correct answer given the combinatorially large variety of
internal contexts in which it must operate. Random "dropout" gives big
improvements on many benchmark tasks and sets new records for speech and object
recognition.

Solely due to our extremely deep representations, we obtain a 28% relative improvement on the COCO object detection dataset. Deep residual nets are foundations of our submissions to ILSVRC & COCO 2015 competitions1, where we also won the 1st places on t

evidence.title: Very Deep Convolutional Networks for Large-Scale Image Recognition
evidence.snippet: In this work we investigate the effect of the convolutional network depth on its accuracy in the large-scale image recognition setting. Our main contribution is a thorough evaluation of networks of increasing depth using an architecture with very small (3x3) convolution filters, which shows that a significant improvement on the prior-art configurations can be achieved by pushing the depth to 16-19 weight layers. These findings were the basis of our ImageNet Challenge 2014 submission, where our team secured the first and the second places in the localisation and classification tracks respectively. We also show that our representations generalise well to other datasets, where they achieve state-of-the-art results. We have made our two best-performing ConvNet models publicly available to facilitate further research on the use of deep visual representations in computer vision.

evidence.title: Densely Connected Convolutional Networks
evidence.snippet: Recent work has shown that convolutional networks can be substantially deeper, more accurate, and efficient to train if they contain shorter connections between layers close to the input and those close to the output. In this paper, we embrace this observation and introduce the Dense Convolutional Network (DenseNet), which connects each layer to every other layer in a feed-forward fashion. Whereas traditional convolutional networks with L layers have L connections—one between each layer and its subsequent layer—our network has L(L+1)/2 direct connections. For each layer, the feature-maps of all preceding layers are used as inputs, and its own feature-maps are used as inputs into all subsequent layers. DenseNets have several compelling advantages: they alleviate the vanishing-gradient problem, strengthen feature propagation, encourage feature reuse, and substantially reduce the number of parameters. We evaluate our proposed architecture on four highly competitive object recognition benchmark tasks (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN, and ImageNet). DenseNets obtain significant improvements over the state-of-the-art on most of them, whilst requiring less memory and computation t

evidence.title: ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge
evidence.snippet: The ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition Challenge is a benchmark in object category classification and detection on hundreds of object categories and millions of images. The challenge has been run annually from 2010 to present, attracting participation from more than fifty institutions. This paper describes the creation of this benchmark dataset and the advances in object recognition that have been possible as a result. We discuss the challenges of collecting large-scale ground truth annotation, highlight key breakthroughs in categorical object recognition, provide a detailed analysis of the current state of the field of large-scale image classification and object detection, and compare the state-of-the-art computer vision accuracy with human accuracy. We conclude with lessons learned in the 5 years of the challenge, and propose future directions and improvements.

evidence.title: Incremental Network Quantization: Towards Lossless CNNs with Low-Precision Weights
evidence.snippet: This paper presents incremental network quantization (INQ), a novel method, targeting to efficiently convert any pre-trained full-precision convolutional neural network (CNN) model into a low-precision version whose weights are constrained to be either powers of two or zero. Unlike existing methods which are struggled in noticeable accuracy loss, our INQ has the potential to resolve this issue, as benefiting from two innovations. On one hand, we introduce three interdependent operations, namely weight partition, group-wise quantization and re-training. A well-proven measure is employed to divide the weights in each layer of a pre-trained CNN model into two disjoint groups. The weights in the first group are responsible to form a low-precision base, thus they are quantized by a variable-length encoding method. The weights in the other group are responsible to compensate for the accuracy loss from the quantization, thus they are the ones to be re-trained. On the other hand, these three operations are repeated on the latest re-trained group in an iterative manner until all the weights are converted into low-precision ones, acting as an incremental network quantization and accuracy enh

evidence.title: Deep Compression: Compressing Deep Neural Network with Pruning, Trained Quantization and Huffman Coding
evidence.snippet: Neural networks are both computationally intensive and memory intensive, making them difficult to deploy on embedded systems with limited hardware resources. To address this limitation, we introduce "deep compression", a three stage pipeline: pruning, trained quantization and Huffman coding, that work together to reduce the storage requirement of neural networks by 35x to 49x without affecting their accuracy. Our method first prunes the network by learning only the important connections. Next, we quantize the weights to enforce weight sharing, finally, we apply Huffman coding. After the first two steps we retrain the network to fine tune the remaining connections and the quantized centroids. Pruning, reduces the number of connections by 9x to 13x; Quantization then reduces the number of bits that represent each connection from 32 to 5. On the ImageNet dataset, our method reduced the storage required by AlexNet by 35x, from 240MB to 6.9MB, without loss of accuracy. Our method reduced the size of VGG-16 by 49x from 552MB to 11.3MB, again with no loss of accuracy. This allows fitting the model into on-chip SRAM cache rather than off-chip DRAM memory. Our compression method also facili

evidence.title: Empirical Evaluation of Gated Recurrent Neural Networks on Sequence Modeling
evidence.snippet: In this paper we compare different types of recurrent units in recurrent neural networks (RNNs). Especially, we focus on more sophisticated units that implement a gating mechanism, such as a long short-term memory (LSTM) unit and a recently proposed gated recurrent unit (GRU). We evaluate these recurrent units on the tasks of polyphonic music modeling and speech signal modeling. Our experiments revealed that these advanced recurrent units are indeed better than more traditional recurrent units such as tanh units. Also, we found GRU to be comparable to LSTM.

evidence.title: On the difficulty of training recurrent neural networks
evidence.snippet: There are two widely known issues with properly training recurrent neural networks, the vanishing and the exploding gradient problems detailed in Bengio et al. (1994). In this paper we attempt to improve the understanding of the underlying issues by exploring these problems from an analytical, a geometric and a dynamical systems perspective. Our analysis is used to justify a simple yet effective solution. We propose a gradient norm clipping strategy to deal with exploding gradients and a soft constraint for the vanishing gradients problem. We validate empirically our hypothesis and proposed solutions in the experimental section.

evidence.title: Regularizing and Optimizing LSTM Language Models
evidence.snippet: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs), such as long short-term memory networks (LSTMs), serve as a fundamental building block for many sequence learning tasks, including machine translation, language modeling, and question answering. In this paper, we consider the specific problem of word-level language modeling and investigate strategies for regularizing and optimizing LSTM-based models. We propose the weight-dropped LSTM which uses DropConnect on hidden-to-hidden weights as a form of recurrent regularization. Further, we introduce NT-ASGD, a variant of the averaged stochastic gradient method, wherein the averaging trigger is determined using a non-monotonic condition as opposed to being tuned by the user. Using these and other regularization strategies, we achieve state-of-the-art word level perplexities on two data sets: 57.3 on Penn Treebank and 65.8 on WikiText-2. In exploring the effectiveness of a neural cache in conjunction with our proposed model, we achieve an even lower state-of-the-art perplexity of 52.8 on Penn Treebank and 52.0 on WikiText-2.

evidence.title: A Simple Way to Initialize Recurrent Networks of Rectified Linear Units
evidence.snippet: Learning long term dependencies in recurrent networks is difficult due to vanishing and exploding gradients. To overcome this difficulty, researchers have developed sophisticated optimization techniques and network architectures. In this paper, we propose a simpler solution that use recurrent neural networks composed of rectified linear units. Key to our solution is the use of the identity matrix or its scaled version to initialize the recurrent weight matrix. We find that our solution is comparable to LSTM on our four benchmarks: two toy problems involving long-range temporal structures, a large language modeling problem and a benchmark speech recognition problem.

evidence.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
evidence.snippet: We introduce Adam, an algorithm for first-order gradient-based optimization of stochastic objective functions, based on adaptive estimates of lower-order moments. The method is straightforward to implement, is computationally efficient, has little memory requirements, is invariant to diagonal rescaling of the gradients, and is well suited for problems that are large in terms of data and/or parameters. The method is also appropriate for non-stationary objectives and problems with very noisy and/or sparse gradients. The hyper-parameters have intuitive interpretations and typically require little tuning. Some connections to related algorithms, on which Adam was inspired, are discussed. We also analyze the theoretical convergence properties of the algorithm and provide a regret bound on the convergence rate that is comparable to the best known results under the online convex optimization framework. Empirical results demonstrate that Adam works well in practice and compares favorably to other stochastic optimization methods. Finally, we discuss AdaMax, a variant of Adam based on the infinity norm.

evidence.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
evidence.snippet: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) are powerful models that have achieved excellent performance on difficult learning tasks. Although DNNs work well whenever large labeled training sets are available, they cannot be used to map sequences to sequences. In this paper, we present a general end-to-end approach to sequence learning that makes minimal assumptions on the sequence structure. Our method uses a multilayered Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) to map the input sequence to a vector of a fixed dimensionality, and then another deep LSTM to decode the target sequence from the vector. Our main result is that on an English to French translation task from the WMT-14 dataset, the translations produced by the LSTM achieve a BLEU score of 34.8 on the entire test set, where the LSTM's BLEU score was penalized on out-of-vocabulary words. Additionally, the LSTM did not have difficulty on long sentences. For comparison, a phrase-based SMT system achieves a BLEU score of 33.3 on the same dataset. When we used the LSTM to rerank the 1000 hypotheses produced by the aforementioned SMT system, its BLEU score increases to 36.5, which is close to the previous state of the art. The LSTM also learned sensible p

evidence.title: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder–Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation
evidence.snippet: In this paper, we propose a novel neural network model called RNN Encoder‐ Decoder that consists of two recurrent neural networks (RNN). One RNN encodes a sequence of symbols into a fixedlength vector representation, and the other decodes the representation into another sequence of symbols. The encoder and decoder of the proposed model are jointly trained to maximize the conditional probability of a target sequence given a source sequence. The performance of a statistical machine translation system is empirically found to improve by using the conditional probabilities of phrase pairs computed by the RNN Encoder‐Decoder as an additional feature in the existing log-linear model. Qualitatively, we show that the proposed model learns a semantically and syntactically meaningful representation of linguistic phrases.

evidence.title: Speech recognition with deep recurrent neural networks
evidence.snippet: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a powerful model for sequential data. End-to-end training methods such as Connectionist Temporal Classification make it possible to train RNNs for sequence labelling problems where the input-output alignment is unknown. The combination of these methods with the Long Short-term Memory RNN architecture has proved particularly fruitful, delivering state-of-the-art results in cursive handwriting recognition. However RNN performance in speech recognition has so far been disappointing, with better results returned by deep feedforward networks. This paper investigates deep recurrent neural networks, which combine the multiple levels of representation that have proved so effective in deep networks with the flexible use of long range context that empowers RNNs. When trained end-to-end with suitable regularisation, we find that deep Long Short-term Memory RNNs achieve a test set error of 17.7% on the TIMIT phoneme recognition benchmark, which to our knowledge is the best recorded score.

evidence.title: Batch Normalization: Accelerating Deep Network Training by Reducing Internal Covariate Shift
evidence.snippet: Training Deep Neural Networks is complicated by the fact that the distribution of each layer's inputs changes during training, as the parameters of the previous layers change. This slows down the training by requiring lower learning rates and careful parameter initialization, and makes it notoriously hard to train models with saturating nonlinearities. We refer to this phenomenon as internal covariate shift, and address the problem by normalizing layer inputs. Our method draws its strength from making normalization a part of the model architecture and performing the normalization for each training mini-batch. Batch Normalization allows us to use much higher learning rates and be less careful about initialization, and in some cases eliminates the need for Dropout. Applied to a state-of-the-art image classification model, Batch Normalization achieves the same accuracy with 14 times fewer training steps, and beats the original model by a significant margin. Using an ensemble of batch-normalized networks, we improve upon the best published result on ImageNet classification: reaching 4.82% top-5 test error, exceeding the accuracy of human raters.

evidence.title: Going deeper with convolutions
evidence.snippet: We propose a deep convolutional neural network architecture codenamed Inception that achieves the new state of the art for classification and detection in the ImageNet Large-Scale Visual Recognition Challenge 2014 (ILSVRC14). The main hallmark of this architecture is the improved utilization of the computing resources inside the network. By a carefully crafted design, we increased the depth and width of the network while keeping the computational budget constant. To optimize quality, the architectural decisions were based on the Hebbian principle and the intuition of multi-scale processing. One particular incarnation used in our submission for ILSVRC14 is called GoogLeNet, a 22 layers deep network, the quality of which is assessed in the context of classification and detection.

evidence.title: Microsoft COCO: Common Objects in Context
evidence.snippet: We present a new dataset with the goal of advancing the state-of-the-art in object recognition by placing the question of object recognition in the context of the broader question of scene understanding. This is achieved by gathering images of complex everyday scenes containing common objects in their natural context. Objects are labeled using per-instance segmentations to aid in precise object localization. Our dataset contains photos of 91 objects types that would be easily recognizable by a 4 year old. With a total of 2.5 million labeled instances in 328k images, the creation of our dataset drew upon extensive crowd worker involvement via novel user interfaces for category detection, instance spotting and instance segmentation. We present a detailed statistical analysis of the dataset in comparison to PASCAL, ImageNet, and SUN. Finally, we provide baseline performance analysis for bounding box and segmentation detection results using a Deformable Parts Model.

question: Apart from preventing overfitting, are there any side effects (desirable or otherwise) of applying dropout in deep neural networks?

sections.title: Taxonomy of Interactive Prompting Strategies
sections.text:
The primary objective of interactive prompting strategies is to resolve the inherent ambiguity in natural language, a challenge that persists even as models scale [1]. While scaling alone may not overcome issues where a source query yields multiple valid options without extra context, interactive methods aim to reduce these ambiguities before final execution [1]. A fundamental limitation of static prompting is that making language models bigger does not inherently make them better at following a user’s intent [2]. Consequently, researchers have developed various frameworks to disambiguate user intent through clarification, iterative refinement, and structured reasoning elicitation.

One category of strategies involves the direct generation of clarification questions to resolve misunderstandings. In open-domain settings, models can be trained to produce polar (yes-no) clarification questions to resolve uncertainty in dialogue, using an expected information gain objective to derive informative questions without requiring supervised question-answer data [3]. This approach mirrors the human process of "repair," where questions are asked until uncertainty is resolved [3]. In specific domains such as robotic object disambiguation, few-shot prompt engineering systems have been developed to improve the LLM's ability to pose disambiguating queries [4]. Similarly, in crosslingual conditional generation, "interactive-chain prompting" introduces a series of question, answering, and generation intermediate steps between a Translator model and a User model [1]. This method reduces translations into a list of subproblems addressing ambiguities, resolving them before producing the final text [1].

Another significant approach is iterative refinement, where the prompt or the model's output is revised based on feedback. Self-refine has verified that LLMs possess the competency for iterative refinement across various tasks based on self-feedback, leading many optimized prompting frameworks to include iterative feedback loops [5]. In the context of deployed models like GPT-3, memory-assisted prompt editing pairs the model with a growing memory of recorded cases where it misunderstood user intents, along with user feedback for clarification [6]. This memory allows the system to produce enhanced prompts for new queries based on past error corrections, substantially increasing accuracy over queries with different kinds of misunderstandings [6]. For developers, tools like EvalLM provide an interactive system for iteratively refining prompts by evaluating multiple outputs on user-defined criteria, helping participants compose more diverse criteria and examine outputs more thoroughly than manual evaluation [7]. Furthermore, reinforcement learning-driven query refinement frameworks refine user prompts before they are input into LLMs to improve the quality of queries and ensure responses are truthful and benign [8].

Chain-of-thought (CoT) elicitation and related reasoning structures represent another major category of interactive prompting strategies. Task-specific prompting, such as zero-shot Chain-of-Thought, is a standard method for enhancing reasoning capabilities [9]. More sophisticated prompting strategies include Chain of Thought (CoT), Tree of Thought (ToT), and Graph of Thought (GoT), which allow large language models to address complex tasks effectively [10]. Self-consistency, a technique compatible with other ensemble strategies, improves chain-of-thought reasoning by sampling multiple reasoning paths and selecting the most consistent answer, with gains significantly higher than other ensemble strategies [11]. This method is robust to various sampling strategies and parameters [11]. In the domain of prompt engineering, "λ prompt" allows for building complete large LM-based prompt machines, including ones that self-edit to correct and even self-write their own execution code [12].

Several systems integrate these strategies into multi-stage pipelines to extract and correct user intent. In infrastructure-as-code generation, LLMs extract user intent, send it to an intent corrector that confirms, corrects, and converts it into JSON, and updates intents [13]. Tools like Infracopilot use LLMs to understand user intent to revolutionize cloud infrastructure development [13]. In multimodal search, the CUE-M framework addresses challenges in interpreting user intent through a multi-stage pipeline comprising image context enrichment, intent refinement, contextual query generation, and relevance-based filtering [14]. For recommendation systems, Reinforced Prompt Personalization (RPP) introduces instance-wise prompting to personalize discrete prompts for individual users, breaking down prompts at the sentence level to improve efficiency and quality [15].

Despite these advancements, automatic prompt engineering significantly alleviates human labor but still cannot completely avoid human intervention [5]. Many methods focus on improving the quality of the prompt in a single stage, but more advanced techniques such as prompt engineering, label words engineering, prompt pre-training, and prompt ensembling are orthogonal and can further improve performance [16]. The integration of these interactive methods is crucial because deep generative models, while promising for end-users, are often hard to control without such prompting mechanisms [17]. By composing prompts and using interactive evaluation, developers can prototype novel generative applications and refine them into products by diagnosing weaknesses in outputs [7].

sections.title: Architectures for Multi-Turn Intent Clarification
sections.text:
Architectures for multi-turn intent clarification often rely on decomposing complex user requests into manageable sub-tasks to facilitate precise interaction. LLMs can decompose complex tasks down into sub-tasks to assist agents in planning over longer temporal horizons, aiding in the decision-making process for complex, multi-step tasks [1]. This decomposition is frequently achieved through step-by-step reasoning that progressively retrieves relevant nodes from a graph, allowing for the handling of intricate task structures [2]. Adding chain-of-thoughts can effectively decompose complex reasoning tasks into intermediate reasoning steps, which serves as a foundational mechanism for these architectures [3]. In the context of retrieval-augmented generation, complex queries may require multi-step retrieval where relevant evidence is fetched from one or a small subset of possible sources, necessitating an interleaving of reasoning and retrieval steps [4].

Specific frameworks have been developed to operationalize these multi-turn interactions. The RAISE (Reasoning and Acting through Scratchpad and Examples) architecture enhances the integration of Large Language Models into conversational agents [5]. Similarly, the MixAlign framework interacts with the user to get clarification when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from the user query to the database [6]. In the domain of conversational recommendation, tool-augmented LLMs focus on architecture design for LLM-driven control of dialogue, recommender modules, and external reasoners, with a specific emphasis on methods for proactive conversational recommendation [7]. Reprompting ChatGPT with feedback has been identified as an effective strategy to improve recommendation relevancy, indicating a multi-turn refinement process [8].

The challenge of maintaining context and resolving ambiguity in multi-turn settings remains significant. It is challenging to address the ellipsis and resolution problem in a multi-turn setting, particularly in hybrid question-answering scenarios [9]. Related Pre-trained Language Model (PrLM) models commonly represent dialogues sequentially by processing the pairwise dialogue history as a whole, which means hierarchical information on utterance interrelation or speaker roles is not well addressed [10]. To mitigate this, the Channel-aware Decoupling Network was proposed, and experimental results show that this method substantially boosts strong PrLM baselines in four public benchmark datasets, achieving new state-of-the-art performance over previous methods [10]. Furthermore, a benchmark called SAMSum, a human-annotated dataset specifically designed for multi-turn dialogue summarization, has been proposed to evaluate the quality of dialogue summaries generated by LLMs via In-Context Learning [3].

Agent-based architectures extend these capabilities by incorporating memory and strategic planning. Generative agents utilize an architecture that extends a large language model to store a complete record of the agent’s experiences using natural language, synthesize those memories over time into higher-level reflections, and retrieve them dynamically to plan behavior [11]. In the initialization of an LLM-based agent participant, a system message is required for configuration, commonly including persona setting, target alignment, and functionality declaration [12]. The reasoning mechanism in such agents defines how the LLM generates reasoning traces, such as plans, explanations, or self-critiques, that guide action proposals [13]. A unified framework for LLM-based autonomous agents has been proposed to encompass much of the previous work, discussing the construction of these agents from a holistic perspective [14].

In specialized domains, these architectures are adapted to specific workflow requirements. In chemistry, an LLM agent has been developed that is capable of automatically completing complex planning and synthesis tasks, although the emergent abilities of LLMs in complex molecular tasks have not been fully shown [15]. For production systems, a novel approach integrates LLM agents into automated production systems by organizing operations within a hierarchical framework based on the automation pyramid, where atomic operation functionalities are modeled as microservices [16]. Upon receiving a user request or identifying a triggering event, these LLM agents generate a process plan, with low-level hardware-specific data semantically enriched and made interpretable for the LLMs [16]. In the domain of collaborative AI system design, ComfyAgent is a framework that empowers LLM-based agents to autonomously design collaborative AI systems by generating workflows, representing these workflows with code that can be reversibly converted [17].

The role of human-in-the-loop workflows and strategic reasoning is also integral to these architectures. Iterated decomposition is described as a human-in-the-loop workflow for developing and refining compositional LM programs [18]. While automatic prompt engineering significantly alleviates human labor, it still cannot completely avoid human intervention [9]. Strategic reasoning with LLMs involves task-specific prompting, such as zero-shot Chain-of-Thought, to guide the agent's behavior [12]. The concept of World Models has attracted attention in the context of AI agents, intended to help the agent predict the future evolution of environmental states or fill in missing information so that it can plan its actions and behave safely [19].

Historical and foundational architectures provide context for current multi-turn dialogue systems. An architecture for conversational systems was described that enables human-like performance along several levels, involving both general and task-specific knowledge, with generation being incremental and involving phenomena such as turn-taking, grounding, and interruptions [20]. In knowledge acquisition, shared task models have been used as an intermediate representation of a task, with roles including decision support, multi-agent systems for acquisition processes, and designing user interaction at the level of strategic preferences [21]. sections.title: Prompt Composition and Synthesis Techniques
sections.text:
The structural integration of clarified intent into final prompts relies on several distinct techniques, ranging from manual template construction to autonomous generation and dynamic chaining. Manual construction is identified as suitable for template-based prompts and few-shot prompting where the prompt structure is uncomplicated, while LM-generated prompts are used to address the shortcomings of manual construction [1]. In contrast, retrieval-based prompts often depend on well-annotated external resources, such as Wikipedia, to alleviate the instability issues associated with pure generation, though this approach consumes expensive information retrieval resources [1]. Beyond static templates, prompt engineering is increasingly viewed as a form of programming that customizes outputs and interactions, with specific patterns serving as reusable solutions to common problems in output generation [2].

A significant area of research focuses on prompt chaining, where the output of one LLM step becomes the input for the next to aggregate gains and handle complex tasks that cannot be resolved in a single run [3][4]. This chaining approach has been shown to improve the quality of task outcomes while significantly enhancing system transparency, controllability, and the user's sense of collaboration [3]. However, authoring these chains requires careful scaffolding for transforming intermediate node outputs and debugging at multiple granularities, which tools like PromptChainer aim to facilitate through visual programming [4]. The concept of chaining is also applied in strategic reasoning, where task-specific prompting, such as zero-shot Chain-of-Thought, is utilized to guide the model through logical steps [5]. Furthermore, backward chaining, which proceeds from a goal to the supporting facts, has been suggested as an alternative to forward chaining in reasoning tasks [6].

Dynamic prompt generation and optimization techniques allow for the adaptation of prompts based on specific instances or continuous feedback. Dynamic prompting frameworks analyze the position, length, and representations of prompts, revealing that optimizing the prompt position to encompass the input can capture semantic information that traditional prefix or postfix methods miss [7]. In the context of black-box tuning, prompts are not necessarily discrete and can be optimized efficiently in continuous space using gradient descent [8]. Autonomous prompt engineering tools, such as the Automatic Prompt Engineering Toolbox (APET), enable models like GPT-4 to autonomously apply prompt engineering techniques to optimize performance on customized tasks [9]. Additionally, reprompting with user feedback has been found to be an effective strategy for improving recommendation relevancy and mitigating popularity bias through prompt engineering [10]. This process involves building a pipeline that simulates realistic user probing by first instructing the model and then reprompting with feedback to refine the output set [10].

In dialogue systems, the integration of clarified intent often involves dynamically updating the dialogue state to elicit specific requirements. A Personalized Utterance Style (PUS) based dialogue strategy chooses suitable response actions for dynamically updating the dialogue state, allowing the system to shrink the search scope of the potential requirement space with the assistance of PUS extracted from dialogue history [11]. This approach is part of a broader trend toward intent-centric, conversation-oriented development, where AI systems evolve beyond task-driven copilots into intelligent collaborators capable of reasoning about software engineering principles and intents [12]. In the domain of human-robot interaction, natural-language dialog is used to express intents and communicate instructions for improvement, enabling robots to learn from interaction experience incrementally and improve their behaviors or avoid future mistakes [13].

The composition of prompts also involves specific structural elements and data handling practices. For instance, in training data construction, prompts may be categorized by type, such as "Basic prompt" where no prefix is added, or by task, such as brainstorming or multiple choice completion [14]. To ensure diversity in use cases, heuristics are applied to deduplicate prompts by checking for those that share a long common prefix [14]. In the context of safety and red teaming, prompt composition is used to modify inputs; for example, when a user inputs a potentially harmful prompt, methods may automatically modify the prompt to ensure generated images are appropriate by retaining acceptable aspects of the original input [15]. Various red-teaming methods, such as Puzzler and GUARD, utilize templates and prompted LLMs with composition or mutation operations to generate adversarial prompts [15].

Other techniques involve the synthesis of prompts for specific multimodal or specialized tasks. In chemistry, LLM agents are capable of automatically completing complex planning and synthesis tasks, representing the first such agent in the field [16]. In image generation, the Prompt Diffusion model introduces a diffusion-based model with in-context learning abilities, guided by an extra text prompt for more precise image generation [17]. In software testing, the automation of test oracles requires knowledge of expected behavior, which may only be known to the developer, highlighting the challenge of integrating this specific intent into automated prompts [18]. In threat modeling for banking systems, frameworks like ThreatModeling-LLM automate processes to enhance efficiency and efficacy, addressing challenges such as the lack of domain-specific datasets and the need for tailored models [19].

The efficacy of these prompt composition techniques is often evaluated through specific benchmarks and datasets. The SAMSum benchmark, a human-annotated dataset for multi-turn dialogue summarization, is used to evaluate the quality of dialogue summaries generated by LLMs via in-context learning [17]. In the context of tool use, ToolLLM is a general framework that includes ToolBench, constructed with an API collection, and ToolLLaMA is supervised fine-tuned by ToolBench [20]. The complexity of prompt construction is also reflected in the scale of data used for training, such as limiting the number of prompts to 200 per user ID or analyzing prompt length distributions in contractor datasets [14]. Furthermore, the use of different sets of prompts, such as x40, has been shown to impact performance metrics in self-consistency reasoning [21]. The integration of persona input in synthesizing dialogues yields utterances with more distinct preferences that are less similar to each other, as observed in the Pearl dataset [22].

Finally, the broader implications of prompt composition relate to the cognitive demands placed on users and the potential for self-editing systems. Generative AI systems impose metacognitive demands on users, requiring a high degree of monitoring and control, which could be addressed by integrating metacognitive support strategies into the systems [23]. The concept of prompt machines extends to systems that can self-edit to correct and even self-write their own execution code, allowing for the building of complete large LM-based prompt machines [1]. In sentiment analysis for conversational agents, user feedback is used to confirm expectations regarding the results obtained from the system [24]. However, challenges remain in knowledge-enhanced dialogue systems, where if the representation does not separate knowledge and dialogue sufficiently, the knowledge may be lost in the output representation, and issues such as dealing with out-of-vocabulary entities persist [25].

Software testing remains the most widely used methodology for validating quality of code. However, effectiveness of testing critically depends on the quality of test suites used. Test cases in a test suite consist of two fundamental parts: (1) input values for the code under test, and (2) correct checks for the outputs it produces. These checks are commonly written as assertions, and termed test oracles. The last couple of decades have seen much progress in automated test input generation, e.g., using fuzzing and symbolic execution. However, automating test oracles remains a relatively less explored problem area. Indeed, a test oracle by its nature requires knowledge of expected behavior, which may only be known to the developer and may not not exist in a formal language that supports automated reasoning.

sections.title: Empirical Evaluation of Clarification Efficacy
sections.text:
Empirical evaluations of clarification strategies in Large Language Models (LLMs) indicate that standard prompting techniques often fail to address user ambiguity, leading to incorrect responses rather than requests for clarification [1]. To address this, the CLAM framework was developed to enable language models to selectively ask for clarification by detecting ambiguity, generating appropriate clarifying questions, and providing final answers after receiving user input [1]. Empirical results show that CLAM significantly improves language model accuracy on mixed ambiguous and unambiguous questions compared to state-of-the-art baselines [1]. This improvement is achieved by simulating users with privileged information, which allows for the automatic evaluation of multi-turn clarification dialogues [1]. Similarly, the MixAlign framework interacts with users to obtain clarification specifically when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from a user query to a database [2]. In the domain of robotic object disambiguation, a few-shot prompt engineering system has been developed to enhance the LLM's ability to pose disambiguating queries [3].

The effectiveness of clarification questions in engaging users within search systems is currently constrained, casting doubt on their overall usefulness [4]. To improve performance, it is crucial to employ assessment approaches that encompass both real-time user feedback (online evaluation) and human-assessed characteristics of clarification questions (offline evaluation) [4]. However, the relationship between online and offline evaluations has been debated in information retrieval, with studies investigating how offline ranked lists of clarification resemble ideal ranked lists based on online user engagement [4]. In the context of conversational AI, effective ambiguity detection and coreference resolution are key to task success, as referential descriptions do not always uniquely identify the referent [5]. Models such as TOD-BERT and LXMERT have been used to detect ambiguity and resolve coreference, with results showing that language models can exploit data correlations to detect ambiguity [5]. Furthermore, unimodal coreference resolution models can avoid the need for vision in certain contexts [5].

Training LLMs to ask clarifying questions requires specific preference data labeling practices; existing models often presuppose a single interpretation of ambiguous requests because responses are evaluated only on prior contexts [6]. To address this, preference labels can be assigned by simulating expected outcomes in future turns, allowing LLMs to learn to ask clarifying questions when they can generate tailored responses for each user interpretation [6]. Evaluation on open-domain QA datasets with multiple annotations assesses systems based on their ability to ask clarifying questions to recover each user's interpretation [6]. In educational contexts, frameworks like DCL4KT+LLM predict question difficulties based on text and associated concepts, overcoming missing difficulty information for unseen questions [7]. Additionally, external verifier modules have been proposed to rectify intermediate errors during generation, improving LLM problem-solving performance on challenging math questions [7].

The evaluation of LLM outputs often relies on specific metrics and datasets, such as the percentage of true and informative responses determined by specially trained models [8]. However, most comparisons in some datasets are labeled by only one contractor for cost reasons, which may obscure areas of disagreement among labelers [8]. In the context of prompt engineering, single-stage methods aim to improve the quality of the prompt, while other approaches focus on prompt compression, noting a gap between optimization objectives in these areas [9][10]. Different prompt formats, such as cloze prompts, prefix prompts, and detailed descriptions, are used to activate LLM memory or utilize emergent abilities in downstream tasks [10]. For instance, in QA prompts, few-shot prompts containing specific QA pairs are utilized to guide the model [8]. In LLaMA, the string "Answer these questions:\n" is prepended to the list of questions and answers in all settings [11].

Robustness and security evaluations also play a role in assessing LLM behavior, with benchmarks like AdvBench using prompt suffix attacks and metrics such as Attack Success Rate (ASR) and cross-entropy loss [12]. Tensor Trust evaluates robustness to prompt injection attacks using metrics like Hijacking Extraction Robustness Rate and Defense Validity [12]. While these security-focused evaluations are distinct from clarification efficacy, they highlight the broader empirical landscape in which LLMs are tested. The knowledge boundary of LLMs remains inadequately defined, with limitations in memorization and utilization leading to untruthful responses, which underscores the need for strategies to mitigate these challenges [13]. Incomplete evaluations in areas such as medical questions and long context integration further highlight gaps in current empirical assessments [14].

sections.title: Limitations and Open Challenges
sections.text:
The primary limitation of interactive clarification systems is the potential for increased user burden and dissatisfaction, particularly when the generated questions are perceived as off-topic or unnecessary. Research indicates that while the need for clarifying questions is sometimes correctly recognized, the questions themselves can be dissatisfaction-provoking and may cause users to leave the conversation [1]. This issue is compounded by the fact that even advanced techniques such as prompt engineering and label words engineering, which are orthogonal to specific tuning methods, do not fully resolve the challenge of maintaining user engagement during complex interactions [2]. Furthermore, from a user perspective, limitations in conversational models like BlenderBot 2.0 have been identified and thoroughly investigated, highlighting the persistent difficulties in aligning model behavior with user expectations [3].

A significant open challenge lies in determining when clarification is necessary versus when the system should proceed with assumptions, a decision that is often complicated by the inherent uncertainty of large language models. The MixAlign framework addresses this by interacting with the user to get clarification specifically when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from the user query to the database [4]. However, the definition and boundary of each task may not be accurate enough to reliably trigger such clarifications, leading to potential errors in intent detection [5]. In the domain of robotic object disambiguation, few-shot prompt engineering systems have been developed to improve the LLM's ability to pose disambiguating queries, yet the general problem of identifying the precise moment for intervention remains a critical area of research [6].

Latency and computational efficiency are also constrained by the complexity of prompt construction and the gap between optimization objectives. There is a noted gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter deals with longer demonstrations, potentially affecting the speed and efficiency of interactive loops [7]. While automatic prompt engineering significantly alleviates human labor, it still cannot completely avoid human intervention, suggesting that fully autonomous clarification without user input remains an unsolved problem [7]. Additionally, the integration of various advanced techniques, such as prompt pre-training and prompt ensembling, is often left for future work due to simplicity constraints in current implementations, indicating that comprehensive solutions for efficient, interactive prompting are not yet fully realized [2].

The reliability of LLMs in these interactive settings is further challenged by issues of hallucination and consistency. LLMs are prone to hallucination, generating plausible yet nonfactual content, which raises significant concerns over their reliability in real-world applications where accurate intent clarification is crucial [8]. In clinical and medical contexts, the consistency of findings across different evidence levels and prompts varies, with some prompting styles showing higher consistency than others, but overall reliability remains a subject of ongoing assessment [9]. The emergence of LLMs has fueled a paradigm shift in information acquisition, but the phenomenon of hallucination continues to pose a barrier to their deployment in high-stakes decision-making processes that require precise user interaction [8].

Current approaches to handling user intent often rely on specific prompt structures or datasets that may not generalize well. For instance, in some settings, the string "Answer these questions:" is prepended to the list of questions and answers to structure the input, a method that may not be optimal for all interactive scenarios [10]. In the context of source code search, methods for generating clarifying questions have outperformed keyword-based methods for single-turn refinement and were associated with shorter search duration in human studies, suggesting that specific domain adaptations can mitigate some limitations [11]. However, the broader challenge of creating a unified framework for LLM-based autonomous agents that can handle diverse applications and human-like decisions remains, as previous research often focuses on isolated environments that diverge from human learning processes [12].

The integration of human feedback and interactive layers is an active area of development to address these limitations. NesyXIL adds a user interactive layer over existing models to facilitate better interaction, while other systems use human-in-the-loop generation to create adversarial examples for question answering, making the process interactive and model-driven [13][14]. In educational contexts, tools like CodeAid balance student and educator needs by delivering technically correct responses without revealing code solutions, aiming to prevent the hindrance of deep conceptual engagement that can occur with direct answers [15]. Despite these advancements, the field still faces incomplete evaluations in areas such as long context integration and medical questions, indicating that the robustness of interactive clarification systems across diverse domains is not yet fully established [16].

evidence.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
evidence.snippet: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. While typically task-agnostic in architecture, this method still requires task-specific fine-tuning datasets of thousands or tens of thousands of examples. By contrast, humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or from simple instructions - something which current NLP systems still largely struggle to do. Here we show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model, and test its performance in the few-shot setting. For all tasks, GPT-3 is applied without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model. evidence.title: Chain of Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
evidence.snippet: We explore how generating a chain of thought -- a series of intermediate reasoning steps -- significantly improves the ability of large language models to perform complex reasoning. In particular, we show how such reasoning abilities emerge naturally in sufficiently large language models via a simple method called chain of thought prompting, where a few chain of thought demonstrations are provided as exemplars in prompting. Experiments on three large language models show that chain of thought prompting improves performance on a range of arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic reasoning tasks. The empirical gains can be striking. For instance, prompting a 540B-parameter language model with just eight chain of thought exemplars achieves state of the art accuracy on the GSM8K benchmark of math word problems, surpassing even finetuned GPT-3 with a verifier.

evidence.title: AI Chains: Transparent and Controllable Human-AI Interaction by Chaining Large Language Model Prompts

We first define a set of LLM primitive operations useful for Chain construction, then present an interactive system where users can modify these Chains, along with their intermediate results, in a modular way. In a 20-person user study, we found that Chaining not only improved the quality of task outcomes, but also significantly enhanced system transparency, controllability, and sense of collaboration. Additionally, we saw that users developed new ways of interacting with LLMs through Chains: they leveraged sub-tasks to calibrate model expectations, compared and contrasted alternative strategies by observing parallel downstream effects, and debugged unexpected model outputs by “unit-testing” sub-components of a Chain. evidence.title: Attention is All you Need
evidence.snippet: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. We show that the Transformer generalizes well to other tasks by applying it successfully to English constituency parsing both with large and limited training data.

evidence.title: Text and Patterns: For Effective Chain of Thought, It Takes Two to Tango

These developments have been accelerated by the advent of few-shot techniques such as chain of thought (CoT) prompting. Specifically, CoT pushes the performance of large language models in a few-shot setup by augmenting the prompts with intermediate steps. Despite impressive results across various tasks, the reasons behind their success have not been explored. This work uses counterfactual prompting to develop a deeper understanding of CoT-based few-shot prompting mechanisms in large language models. We first systematically identify and define the key components of a prompt: symbols, patterns, and text. Then, we devise and conduct an exhaustive set of experiments across four different tasks, by querying the model with counterfactual prompts where only one of these components is altered. Our experiments across three models (PaLM, GPT-3, and CODEX) reveal several surprising findings and brings into question the conventional wisdom around few-shot prompting.
