evidence.title: Pre-train, Prompt, and Predict: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Methods in Natural Language Processing
evidence.snippet: This article surveys and organizes research works in a new paradigm in natural language processing, which we dub “prompt-based learning.” Unlike traditional supervised learning, which trains a model to take in an input x and predict an output y as P(y|x), prompt-based learning is based on language models that model the probability of text directly. To use these models to perform prediction tasks, the original input x is modified using a template into a textual string prompt x′ that has some unfilled slots, and then the language model is used to probabilistically fill the unfilled information to obtain a final string x̂, from which the final output y can be derived. This framework is powerful and attractive for a number of reasons: It allows the language model to be pre-trained on massive amounts of raw text, and by defining a new prompting function the model is able to perform few-shot or even zero-shot learning, adapting to new scenarios with few or no labeled data. evidence.title: Prefix-Tuning: Optimizing Continuous Prompts for Generation
evidence.snippet: Fine-tuning is the de facto way of leveraging large pretrained language models for downstream tasks. However, fine-tuning modifies all the language model parameters and therefore necessitates storing a full copy for each task. In this paper, we propose prefix-tuning, a lightweight alternative to fine-tuning for natural language generation tasks, which keeps language model parameters frozen and instead optimizes a sequence of continuous task-specific vectors, which we call the prefix. Prefix-tuning draws inspiration from prompting for language models, allowing subsequent tokens to attend to this prefix as if it were “virtual tokens”. We apply prefix-tuning to GPT-2 for table-to-text generation and to BART for summarization. We show that by learning only 0.1% of the parameters, prefix-tuning obtains comparable performance in the full data setting, outperforms fine-tuning in low-data settings, and extrapolates better to examples with topics that are unseen during training.

We then collect a dataset of rankings of model outputs, which we use to further fine-tune this supervised model using reinforcement learning from human feedback. We call the resulting models InstructGPT. In human evaluations on our prompt distribution, outputs from the 1.3B parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the 175B GPT-3, despite having 100x fewer parameters. evidence.title: Large Language Models as Simulated Economic Agents: What Can We Learn from Homo Silicus?
evidence.snippet: Large language models---because of how they are trained and designed---are implicit computational models of humans---a homo silicus. Social scientists can use LLMs like economists use homo economicus: LLMs can be given endowments, information, preferences, and so on, and then their behavior can be explored in scenarios via simulation. We replicate four experiments using this approach and find qualitatively similar results to the original. Benefits of this approach include trying new variations for fresh insights, piloting studies via simulation, and searching for novel social science insights to test in the real world. The full version of the paper can be accessed at https://apostolos-filippas.com/papers/hs.pdf.

evidence.title: Socially situated artificial intelligence enables learning from human interaction
evidence.snippet: Significance Humans have long demonstrated an ability to learn from interactions with others. However, artificial intelligence (AI) agents learn in social isolation. To create intelligent systems that understand more than a fixed slice of the world, our article formalizes socially situated AI—a framework that enables agents to interact with people as they simultaneously learn new concepts about the world around them. Using our framework, we deploy a field experiment on a photo-sharing social network where our agent interacts with hundreds of thousands of people to learn concepts about the visual world. We combine advances in deep learning, computer vision, natural language processing, and human–computer Interaction to deliver a human-centered AI that learns from interactions with people in social environments.

evidence.title: Out of One, Many: Using Language Models to Simulate Human Samples
evidence.snippet: Abstract We propose and explore the possibility that language models can be studied as effective proxies for specific human subpopulations in social science research. Practical and research applications of artificial intelligence tools have sometimes been limited by problematic biases (such as racism or sexism), which are often treated as uniform properties of the models. We show that the “algorithmic bias” within one such tool—the GPT-3 language model—is instead both fine-grained and demographically correlated, meaning that proper conditioning will cause it to accurately emulate response distributions from a wide variety of human subgroups. We term this property algorithmic fidelity and explore its extent in GPT-3. We create “silicon samples” by conditioning the model on thousands of sociodemographic backstories from real human participants in multiple large surveys conducted in the United States. We then compare the silicon and human samples to demonstrate that the information contained in GPT-3 goes far beyond surface similarity. It is nuanced, multifaceted, and reflects the complex interplay between ideas, attitudes, and sociocultural context that characterize human attitudes.

evidence.title: Social Simulacra: Creating Populated Prototypes for Social Computing Systems
evidence.snippet: Social computing prototypes probe the social behaviors that may arise in an envisioned system design. We demonstrate that social simulacra shift the behaviors that they generate appropriately in response to design changes, and that they enable exploration of “what if?” scenarios where community members or moderators intervene. evidence.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
evidence.snippet: An important paradigm of natural language processing consists of large-scale pre-training on general domain data and adaptation to particular tasks or domains. As we pre-train larger models, full fine-tuning, which retrains all model parameters, becomes less feasible. evidence.title: On the Opportunities and Risks of Foundation Models
evidence.snippet: AI is undergoing a paradigm shift with the rise of models (e.g., BERT, DALL-E, GPT-3) that are trained on broad data at scale and are adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks. evidence.title: Prompt Programming for Large Language Models: Beyond the Few-Shot Paradigm
evidence.snippet: Prevailing methods for mapping large generative language models to supervised tasks may fail to sufficiently probe models’ novel capabilities. Using GPT-3 as a case study, we show that 0-shot prompts can significantly outperform few-shot prompts. We suggest that the function of few-shot examples in these cases is better described as locating an already learned task rather than meta-learning. This analysis motivates rethinking the role of prompts in controlling and evaluating powerful language models. We discuss methods of prompt programming, emphasizing the usefulness of considering prompts through the lens of natural language. We explore techniques for exploiting the capacity of narratives and cultural anchors to encode nuanced intentions and techniques for encouraging deconstruction of a problem into components before producing a verdict. Informed by this more encompassing theory of prompt programming, we also introduce the idea of a metaprompt that seeds the model to generate its own natural language prompts for a range of tasks. evidence.title: Natural Questions: A Benchmark for Question Answering Research
evidence.snippet: We present the Natural Questions corpus, a question answering data set. Questions consist of real anonymized, aggregated queries issued to the Google search engine. An annotator is presented with a question along with a Wikipedia page from the top 5 search results, and annotates a long answer (typically a paragraph) and a short answer (one or more entities) if present on the page, or marks null if no long/short answer is present. The public release consists of 307,373 training examples with single annotations; 7,830 examples with 5-way annotations for development data; and a further 7,842 examples with 5-way annotated sequestered as test data. We present experiments validating quality of the data. We also describe analysis of 25-way annotations on 302 examples, giving insights into human variability on the annotation task. We introduce robust metrics for the purposes of evaluating question answering systems; demonstrate high human upper bounds on these metrics; and establish baseline results using competitive methods drawn from related literature.

evidence.title: ConvAI3: Generating Clarifying Questions for Open-Domain Dialogue Systems (ClariQ)
evidence.snippet: This document presents a detailed description of the challenge on clarifying questions for dialogue systems (ClariQ). The challenge is organized as part of the Conversational AI challenge series (ConvAI3) at Search Oriented Conversational AI (SCAI) EMNLP workshop in 2020. The main aim of the conversational systems is to return an appropriate answer in response to the user requests. However, some user requests might be ambiguous. In IR settings such a situation is handled mainly thought the diversification of the search result page. It is however much more challenging in dialogue settings with limited bandwidth. Therefore, in this challenge, we provide a common evaluation framework to evaluate mixed-initiative conversations. Participants are asked to rank clarifying questions in an information-seeking conversations. The challenge is organized in two stages where in Stage 1 we evaluate the submissions in an offline setting and single-turn conversations. Top participants of Stage 1 get the chance to have their model tested by human annotators.

evidence.title: AmbigQA: Answering Ambiguous Open-domain Questions
evidence.snippet: Ambiguity is inherent to open-domain question answering; especially when exploring new topics, it can be difficult to ask questions that have a single, unambiguous answer. In this paper, we introduce AmbigQA, a new open-domain question answering task which involves predicting a set of question-answer pairs, where every plausible answer is paired with a disambiguated rewrite of the original question. To study this task, we construct AmbigNQ, a dataset covering 14,042 questions from NQ-open, an existing open-domain QA benchmark. We find that over half of the questions in NQ-open are ambiguous, exhibiting diverse types of ambiguity. We also present strong baseline models for AmbigQA which we show benefit from weakly supervised learning that incorporates NQ-open, strongly suggesting our new task and data will support significant future research effort. Our data is available at this https URL.

evidence.title: Answer-based Adversarial Training for Generating Clarification Questions
evidence.snippet: We present an approach for generating clarification questions with the goal of eliciting new information that would make the given textual context more complete. We propose that modeling hypothetical answers (to clarification questions) as latent variables can guide our approach into generating more useful clarification questions. We develop a Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) where the generator is a sequence-to-sequence model and the discriminator is a utility function that models the value of updating the context with the answer to the clarification question. We evaluate on two datasets, using both automatic metrics and human judgments of usefulness, specificity and relevance, showing that our approach outperforms both a retrieval-based model and ablations that exclude the utility model and the adversarial training.

evidence.title: TriviaQA: A Large Scale Distantly Supervised Challenge Dataset for Reading Comprehension
evidence.snippet: We present TriviaQA, a challenging reading comprehension dataset containing over 650K question-answer-evidence triples. TriviaQA includes 95K question-answer pairs authored by trivia enthusiasts and independently gathered evidence documents, six per question on average, that provide high quality distant supervision for answering the questions. We show that, in comparison to other recently introduced large-scale datasets, TriviaQA (1) has relatively complex, compositional questions, (2) has considerable syntactic and lexical variability between questions and corresponding answer-evidence sentences, and (3) requires more cross sentence reasoning to find answers. We also present two baseline algorithms: a feature-based classifier and a state-of-the-art neural network, that performs well on SQuAD reading comprehension. Neither approach comes close to human performance (23% and 40% vs. 80%), suggesting that TriviaQA is a challenging testbed that is worth significant future study.

evidence.title: STaR-GATE: Teaching Language Models to Ask Clarifying Questions
evidence.snippet: When prompting language models to complete a task, users often leave important aspects unsaid. While asking questions could resolve this ambiguity (GATE; Li et al., 2023), models often struggle to ask good questions. We explore a language model's ability to self-improve (STaR; Zelikman et al., 2022) by rewarding the model for generating useful questions-a simple method we dub STaR-GATE. We generate a synthetic dataset of 25,500 unique persona-task prompts to simulate conversations between a pretrained language model-the Questioner-and a Roleplayer whose preferences are unknown to the Questioner. By asking questions, the Questioner elicits preferences from the Roleplayer. The Questioner is iteratively finetuned on questions that increase the probability of high-quality responses to the task, which are generated by an Oracle with access to the Roleplayer's latent preferences. After two iterations of self-improvement, the Questioner asks better questions, allowing it to generate responses that are preferred over responses from the initial model on 72% of tasks. Our results indicate that teaching a language model to ask better questions leads to better personalized responses.

evidence.title: Relying on the Unreliable: The Impact of Language Models' Reluctance to Express Uncertainty
evidence.snippet: As natural language becomes the default interface for human-AI interaction, there is a need for LMs to appropriately communicate uncertainties in downstream applications. In this work, we investigate how LMs incorporate confidence in responses via natural language and how downstream users behave in response to LM-articulated uncertainties. We examine publicly deployed models and find that LMs are reluctant to express uncertainties when answering questions even when they produce incorrect responses. LMs can be explicitly prompted to express confidences, but tend to be overconfident, resulting in high error rates (an average of 47%) among confident responses. We test the risks of LM overconfidence by conducting human experiments and show that users rely heavily on LM generations, whether or not they are marked by certainty. Lastly, we investigate the preference-annotated datasets used in post training alignment and find that humans are biased against texts with uncertainty. Our work highlights new safety harms facing human-LM interactions and proposes design recommendations and mitigating strategies moving forward.

evidence.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
evidence.snippet: Language models are increasingly being deployed for general problem solving across a wide range of tasks, but are still confined to token-level, left-to-right decision-making processes during inference. This means they can fall short in tasks that require exploration, strategic lookahead, or where initial decisions play a pivotal role. To surmount these challenges, we introduce a new framework for language model inference, Tree of Thoughts (ToT), which generalizes over the popular Chain of Thought approach to prompting language models, and enables exploration over coherent units of text (thoughts) that serve as intermediate steps toward problem solving. ToT allows LMs to perform deliberate decision making by considering multiple different reasoning paths and self-evaluating choices to decide the next course of action, as well as looking ahead or backtracking when necessary to make global choices. Our experiments show that ToT significantly enhances language models' problem-solving abilities on three novel tasks requiring non-trivial planning or search: Game of 24, Creative Writing, and Mini Crosswords. evidence.title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
evidence.snippet: Chain-of-thought prompting combined with pre-trained large language models has achieved encouraging results on complex reasoning tasks. In this paper, we propose a new decoding strategy, self-consistency, to replace the naive greedy decoding used in chain-of-thought prompting. It first samples a diverse set of reasoning paths instead of only taking the greedy one, and then selects the most consistent answer by marginalizing out the sampled reasoning paths. Self-consistency leverages the intuition that a complex reasoning problem typically admits multiple different ways of thinking leading to its unique correct answer. Our extensive empirical evaluation shows that self-consistency boosts the performance of chain-of-thought prompting with a striking margin on a range of popular arithmetic and commonsense reasoning benchmarks, including GSM8K (+17.9%), SVAMP (+11.0%), AQuA (+12.2%), StrategyQA (+6.4%) and ARC-challenge (+3.9%).

evidence.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
evidence.snippet: While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across tasks in language understanding and interactive decision making, their abilities for reasoning (e.g. chain-of-thought prompting) and acting (e.g. action plan generation) have primarily been studied as separate topics. In this paper, we explore the use of LLMs to generate both reasoning traces and task-specific actions in an interleaved manner, allowing for greater synergy between the two: reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans as well as handle exceptions, while actions allow it to interface with external sources, such as knowledge bases or environments, to gather additional information. We apply our approach, named ReAct, to a diverse set of language and decision making tasks and demonstrate its effectiveness over state-of-the-art baselines, as well as improved human interpretability and trustworthiness over methods without reasoning or acting components. Concretely, on question answering (HotpotQA) and fact verification (Fever), ReAct overcomes issues of hallucination and error propagation prevalent in chain-of-thought reasoning by interacting with a simple Wikipedi

evidence.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
evidence.snippet: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models (Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018), BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications. BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5 (7.7 point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).

sections.title: Theoretical Foundations of Technology Adoption in Organizations
sections.text:
The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) serves as a foundational framework for understanding user acceptance in the context of Robotic Process Automation (RPA), where poor user acceptance is identified as a critical barrier to initiative success [1]. To address the lack of systematic investigation into variables influencing RPA user acceptance, researchers have derived models by extending TAM with RPA-specific variables, identifying facilitating conditions, result demonstrability, innovation joy, and social influence as significant predictors of perceived usefulness and ease of use [1]. In the specific context of small accounting firms in Taiwan, the success factors of RPA introduction have been measured using constructs from both TAM and the Information System Success Model (ISS) [2]. Empirical findings from this sector indicate that male gender, higher familiarity with the system, and high CEO support are significantly positively correlated with RPA system success, highlighting the challenges small and medium-sized firms face in digital transformation compared to larger entities [2].

While TAM focuses on individual user perceptions, the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework provides a broader lens for analyzing technology adoption at the organizational level, particularly within the Industry 4.0 context [3]. This framework has been applied to examine how technological, organizational, and environmental factors influence the use and development of Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems to support business agility [3]. Similarly, the TOE framework serves as the theoretical basis for investigating implementation challenges and success factors for industrial augmented reality (AR), a technology integral to Industry 4.0 concepts that enables workers to overlay digital information with the physical world [4]. The application of TOE in these contexts allows for the categorization of Industry 4.0 technologies and the assessment of organizational agility, providing a structured approach to understanding the determinants of technology implementation [3][4].

The Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and its extension, UTAUT2, offer additional perspectives on adoption drivers, particularly when adapted for specific industries or developing economies. In a study of Senegalese small and medium enterprises (SMEs) adopting renewable energy technologies, qualitative interviews revealed that the UTAUT2 model serves as a guiding framework, although effort expectancy was generally underestimated and social influence did not significantly affect adoption in that specific context [5]. Conversely, in the healthcare sector, a modified UTAUT2 model integrating perceived security and perceived product advantage was used to analyze telemedicine adoption, finding significant positive effects of performance expectancy, hedonic motivation, and the added variables on behavioral intention [6]. In the financial sector, a modified UTAUT2 model applied to small food businesses identified knowledge, safety perceptions, performance expectations, social influence, facilitation conditions, and price values as key factors affecting FinTech adoption [7].

Beyond individual and organizational acceptance models, the implementation of automation technologies is often characterized by a hybrid state where human and machine roles coexist. Digital Twin (DT) technology, for instance, is described as far from being comprehensive and mature, resulting in piecemeal implementations where some functions are automated while others remain performed by humans [8]. To conceptualize this hybrid nature, a two-dimensional framework called Levels of Digital Twin (LoDT) has been proposed, integrating the types of roles a DT can play (Observer, Analyst, Decision Maker, Action Executor) with the extent of automation for each role [8]. This perspective aligns with the definition of RPA as the rule-based automation of business processes by software bots that mimic human interactions to relieve employees from tedious work, emphasizing the collaborative or substitutive nature of the technology [1].

The adoption of robotic and automated technologies is further influenced by environmental pressures and organizational determinants, particularly in labor-intensive industries. In the construction industry, which suffers from low productivity and labor shortages, the integration of intelligent robots and human-robot collaboration (HRC) is viewed as an evolutionary reforming potential, though major challenges and future research directions remain to be examined [9]. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) adopting intelligent robots, process innovation is driven by technology benefits (direct and indirect usefulness) and environmental pressures from industry and government, with organizational supports acting as moderators [10]. In the hospitality sector, a global study of hotel managers found that perceived competitive advantage and environmental factors significantly influence intentions to adopt robotic technologies, with top management support and competitive pressure playing key roles [11].

Sustainability and user requirements are increasingly recognized as critical components in the implementation of RPA and other automated systems. A multi-objective mathematical model for sustainable RPA implementation has been developed to evaluate efficiency by integrating user requirements and stakeholder perspectives, demonstrating that such integration enhances the assessment of implementation feasibility [12]. The choice of implementation model, such as using external RPA services (insourcing) or creating an internal center of excellence (CoE), is influenced by various determinants including benefits and threats, which vary depending on the specific model chosen [13]. Furthermore, the broader adoption of AI and automation in everyday decision-making, such as for farmers, is challenged by a complex interplay of personal, social, cultural, and economic factors [14].

Explainability and trust remain significant barriers to the practical implementation of AI and automated systems, which can impact user acceptance. Explainability is identified as one of the main barriers AI faces in practical implementation, and it is advocated for as a means to ease the elucidation of model boundaries, thereby facilitating better understanding and implementation [15]. The concept of Responsible Artificial Intelligence emphasizes the need for fairness, model explainability, and accountability in the large-scale implementation of AI methods in real organizations [15]. While these concepts are primarily discussed in the context of AI, they are relevant to RPA as RPA systems increasingly incorporate intelligent features, and the lack of robust evaluation benchmarks or clear boundaries can hinder adoption [16].

The literature also highlights the importance of specific technical and methodological considerations in the development and evaluation of automated systems, which indirectly influence their adoptability. For instance, in the context of automated user acceptance testing (UAT), systems like XUAT-Copilot propose LLM-powered multi-agent collaboration to address the human-labor-intensive stage of test script generation [17]. In other domains, such as marine debris tracking, the application of deep learning methods to automation is noted as an underexplored area, suggesting a gap in the technological maturity that may affect adoption [18]. Similarly, in system log parsing, existing solutions often neglect certain levels of automation, which hinders their adoption in real systems [19]. These technical limitations and the need for specific evaluation metrics, such as the n@k metric for program acceptance or the use of simulators for goal checking, underscore the complexity of implementing reliable automated solutions [20][21].

In summary, the applicability of theoretical lenses to RPA depends on the level of analysis required. TAM and its extensions are well-suited for investigating individual user acceptance and specific RPA variables like innovation joy and result demonstrability [1]. The TOE framework is appropriate for analyzing organizational and environmental determinants, such as CEO support and industry pressures, particularly in the context of Industry 4.0 [2][3][4]. UTAUT2 offers a comprehensive view of behavioral intention, with modifications for specific contexts like security and price value [5][6][7]. However, given the hybrid nature of RPA implementations where human and automated roles coexist, frameworks that account for levels of automation and human-machine collaboration, such as LoDT, provide additional conceptual depth [8]. The integration of sustainability, explainability, and specific technical determinants further refines the understanding of successful RPA adoption [12][15][14].

sections.title: Socio-Technical Systems and Human-Robot Interaction
sections.text:
Socio-technical systems (STS) theory provides a foundational lens for examining the interplay between human workers and automated systems, particularly in the context of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) implementations [1]. In the professional services sector, such as auditing, RPA failure rates remain high despite the technology's potential benefits, a phenomenon attributed to a lack of fit between the technical requirements of the RPA tool and the skills and knowledge of the auditors and clients [1]. This misalignment between the technical subsystem and the social subsystem creates specific challenges that must be addressed during various phases of the work process [1]. To mitigate these issues, researchers have developed evaluation frameworks grounded in STS theory to assist practitioners in deciding which activities to automate [2]. By applying STS theory through design science methodology, such frameworks help explain the mixed findings in prior research regarding the effectiveness and adoption of emerging technologies in audit [2]. The validation of these frameworks through interviews, surveys, and case studies offers practical implications for managing the integration of automation into existing workflows [2].

Beyond specific industry applications, STS approaches are utilized to identify the multiplicity of factors influencing the use of automated tools in diverse contexts [3]. For instance, in the deployment of mobile health technologies among community health workers in rural Rwanda, a combination of user-centric approaches and socio-technical systems theory allowed researchers to identify factors contributing to the relative success of the tool [3]. This approach highlights that user, program, and technical characteristics are all influential in determining the utilization of such systems [3]. Similarly, in New Product Development (NPD) project teams, socio-technical risk factors are empirically linked to project risks and performance [4]. Studies indicate a positive relationship between environmental turbulence and social-related risks, as well as between social-related risks and technical-related risks [4]. Consequently, socio-technical related risks are positively associated with project risks, which in turn have a strong negative relationship with project performance [4]. While communication may moderate the relationship between project risk and performance, this effect was found to be statistically insignificant in some telecommunications contexts [4].

The integration of human-robot interaction (HRI) principles further refines the understanding of social dynamics in automated environments. HRI research has historically been dominated by laboratory studies examining single human-robot interactions, which contrasts with the complex social contexts in which robots are increasingly deployed [5]. As robots enter work contexts and closer proximity to people, the field must address how humans perceive and interact with these agents in realistic settings [5]. Human perceptions and behavior in HRI settings are determined in part by expectations, which can be highly variable and shaped by sources other than direct experience with social robots [6]. Understanding these expectations is critical because they affect interactions with the robot over time [6]. Furthermore, the reduction of cognitive tasks brought about by service robots collaborating with humans in working environments has raised safety challenges related to decreased cognitive activity [7]. Insights from sociology, cognitive sciences, and biology suggest that integrating behavioral patterns into robotic systems can help prevent the problem of reduced cognition in human-robot interaction [7].

In the realm of Human-AI teaming, particularly with large pre-trained models, the focus shifts to mixed-initiative collaboration and job redesign. Future systems require interfaces that expose the agent’s plan, show intermediate progress, and allow users to pause or redirect execution [8]. These interfaces must also place approval gates before irreversible or high-risk actions to manage the potential for harm resulting from a chain of small intermediate choices [8]. Conversational and multimodal interfaces provide a communication surface for this mixed-initiative collaboration, where either the human or the AI can propose, clarify, revise, or redirect the task [8]. This pattern, where both humans and AI can propose, critique, revise, or redirect the task, often yields outcomes superior to individual capabilities by combining human cognitive skills with AI’s computational power [8]. The shift towards AI-interactive jobs indicates a broader preference for technologically engaging roles, which impacts job satisfaction and autonomy [8]. However, this dual effect of LLM-driven automation fosters more creative roles and autonomy while simultaneously raising concerns about job security and the obsolescence of certain jobs [8].

Technical architectures and explainability play a supporting role in these socio-technical dynamics. Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) concepts are crucial for responsible AI, with Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) providing methodological guidelines to consider wider societal contexts such as ethics, public engagement, and governance [9]. XAI systems perform better than classic rule systems in contexts with certain degrees of uncertainty, enhancing their utility in complex decision-making [9]. The use of knowledge bases formalized by ontologies allows data to be processed directly in a qualitative way, which aligns with qualitative research approaches [9]. In the context of human-robot conversation and collaboration, modular system architectures are proposed to integrate Large Language Model (LLM) models [10]. LLM-enhanced reinforcement learning can improve the efficiency of human-robot interaction, help robots understand human needs and behavioral logic, and enhance decision-making and planning capabilities [11]. Additionally, vision models enable robots to perform actions in the real-world by identifying objects within the scene [10].

The physical embodiment of robots also influences social interaction, although most socially interactive robots do not require physical interaction with their environments to perform their tasks [12]. The role of physical embodiment is reviewed to determine when and why embodied robots should be used instead of simpler virtual agents [12]. Socially interactive robots, which provide entertainment, information, or assistance, rely primarily on their social capabilities to achieve their functions [12]. The relationship between appearance and behavior is significant, as more human-like devices are better positioned to elicit responses that people direct toward each other [13]. Research into the human likeness of androids aims to discover principles underlying natural communication to develop expressive humanoid robots [13]. User engagement in HRI is documented through datasets that focus on facial expressions and postural details related to engagement, such as the UE-HRI dataset [14]. While influencing human learning remains an open problem, results demonstrate that this influence is possible and can be helpful in real human-robot interaction [15].

Formal methods and optimization techniques underpin the technical subsystems that interact with these social dynamics. Temporal-logic-based techniques, especially those using Linear Temporal Logic (LTL), employ automata theory and reactive synthesis to generate discrete decision sequences [16]. Spiking neural P systems (SNPS) are considered a branch of Spiking Neural Networks (SNN) based on the principles of formal automata and membrane computing theory [17]. These systems are partly inspired by formal language and automata theory [17]. In the domain of task and motion planning, how physical Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC) can be achieved efficiently via Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) remains an active area of research [16]. Optimization-based approaches handle multidimensional systems, and partial order theory allows for the handling of ordinal data without variable aggregation into composite indicators [18]. By leveraging the theory of signatures, non-linear problems in learning the dynamics of sparsely observed interacting systems can be cast as high-dimensional linear regression [19].

Qualitative research designs are essential for expanding explanations in these complex systems. Qualitative research approaches are adopted to expand explanations and perform macro simulations based on the results [20]. Similarly, qualitative research approaches are followed for fairness certification in Natural Language Processing (NLP) [21]. The flexibility of statistical methods is sometimes lacking, requiring the re-design of selection algorithms if the underlying measurement model changes [22]. In the context of neural code intelligence, virtual software companies like ChatDev function through an array of intelligent agents assuming roles such as programmer, code reviewer, tester, and designer [23]. These agent-based systems illustrate the division of labor and social dynamics within automated software development environments. The integration of these technical and social perspectives is necessary to address the challenges of RPA and broader automation implementations, ensuring that the fit between technical capabilities and human skills is maintained [1][2].

sections.title: Organizational Change and Process Reengineering
sections.text:
Organizational change management is predicated on the necessity for organizations to adapt to a changing environment driven by globalization, new technologies, intense competition, and internal factors [1]. In the context of digital transformation, Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is spreading across industries, enabling the automation of business processes by replacing human work with advanced software robots [2]. This technological shift requires balancing major cultural and organizational changes needed to enforce new principles over processes with the feasibility and compliance of these changes with existing IT assets, policies, and resources [3]. The implementation of such changes is often complicated by the fact that ontologies and knowledge graphs cannot automatically evolve to reflect updates in their respective domains and suffer from quality limitations that require extensive refinement [4]. Furthermore, models trained on suboptimal data may perpetuate errors and overlook organizational or cultural nuances, creating solutions suitable for one context but not another [5].

Business Process Reengineering (BPR) provides a theoretical framework for understanding these structural shifts, utilizing goal decomposition and scenario analysis to refine business process descriptions [6]. In BPR, deriving full scenarios from an organization's prescriptive goals is difficult, whereas explanatory scenarios that justify descriptive goals are easier to obtain but remain fragmentary, indicating that both types of analysis are necessary for effective reengineering [6]. The application of reengineering concepts has been used to provide government agencies with standard operating procedures for assessing core public infrastructure projects, aiming to minimize risks of ineffective execution [7]. Similarly, in high-tech manufacturing, a modified reengineering algorithm has been applied to technology departments, involving functional modeling of business processes in the IDEF0 rotation to improve efficiency and product quality [8].

The specific implementation of RPA involves identifying and automating mundane, repetitive tasks that can be programmed into robots to perform more efficiently than humans [9]. A primary challenge in this process is effectively determining which business tasks are suitable for automation, as RPA tools allow mimicking human tasks through virtual workforces to free human workers for more difficult duties [10]. To address this, a candidate digital tasks selection methodology has been developed to identify suitable tasks for RPA automation [10]. In the Human Resources function, a structured four-step approach involving validation is suggested to identify processes that can be automated to enhance service, compliance, and productivity [11]. The selection of an RPA solution is difficult because standardized evaluation items and indicators have not been widely defined, leading to the development of evaluation breakdown structures derived from prior studies and feasibility studies [12].

Roadmaps for RPA implementation in enterprises clarify the benefits and impacts of automating processes, prioritizing actions that generate new RPA management models and leading organizations toward digitalization [13]. These roadmaps, derived from experimental exercises in industries, show that RPA implementation results in significant efficiencies, freed time for workers, speed in task execution, and availability of information for advanced analysis [13]. RPA positioning in enterprises can be classified into conservative, efficiency improving, and strategic approaches, a classification verified through empirical research using multidimensional correspondence analysis [2]. The broader context of digital transformation, accelerated by events such as the pandemic, is causing profound changes across industries, with RPA serving as a key tool for increasing organizational resilience [2].

While RPA focuses on process automation, the integration of AI methods into real organizations requires a methodology for large-scale implementation that prioritizes fairness, model explainability, and accountability [3]. The implementation of Responsible AI principles must balance the need for major cultural and organizational changes with the constraints of existing IT assets and policies [3]. Organizational structures, such as those defined by role assignments and coordination pathways, reduce coordination complexity and prevent uncontrolled interaction among agents, a principle applicable to both human and automated systems [14]. However, the application of deep learning methods to automation remains an underexplored area, and existing solutions often neglect levels of automation that hinder their adoption in real systems [15][16]. The change of model parameters upon a change of training example is calculated with approximation, highlighting the technical complexities underlying these organizational shifts [17].

sections.title: Empirical Evidence and Theoretical Fit in Qualitative Studies
sections.text:
The existing qualitative literature on Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is limited but provides foundational insights into implementation drivers, organizational impacts, and methodological approaches. A systematic literature review of 63 publications identified thematic clusters that advise further investigations to develop a more detailed structural research approach for RPA [1]. In the context of purchasing and supply management, RPA adoption is described as being in its infancy and hardly explored, particularly in the public sector, despite the technology's promise of high potentials within digital transformation [2]. One case study on electricity billing document management at BYD positioned RPA tools as a component of smart city digital transformation, noting that these tools enable the automation of tasks previously carried out by humans [3].

Several studies have successfully applied specific theoretical lenses to analyze RPA implementations. A study on Nordic companies utilized a blended qualitative approach, combining surveys with interpretative interviews and narrative analysis, to identify key drivers such as financials, employee impact, and risks [4]. The findings from this study highlighted a focus on operational benefits, including releasing employees from monotonous, non-value-adding assignments and strengthening enterprise efficiency, compliance, and quality [4]. Another case study in Sweden employed four value positions—Professionalism, Efficiency, Service, and Engagement—as an analytical framework to examine automated decision-making in social services, revealing that the new technology increased accountability, decreased costs, and enhanced efficiency [5]. This study used interviews with politicians and professionals, complemented by government documents, to provide the empirical data for its analysis [5].

Research into the human impact of RPA has also applied theoretical perspectives to understand employee transformation. A case study investigating the retraining of non-technical employees, specifically accountants, to work as entry-level RPA software developers, used observations blended with interviews to show how retraining transforms employees’ identity, addresses anxiety and skepticism, and impacts the organization [6]. This research highlighted the relevance of domain knowledge in the context of intelligent information systems gradually taking over employees' work efforts [6]. While these studies provide concrete examples of theoretical application, the broader qualitative methodology in related fields often relies on techniques such as interviews and grounded theory to construct causal influence path models [7]. For instance, a study on information behavior adopted a qualitative research design to expand explanations and macro simulation based on qualitative research results [7], and another study used interviews with authors followed by macro simulation according to deductive and qualitative content analysis results [7].

Despite these specific applications, significant gaps remain in the theoretical grounding of RPA research. The systematic review noted that the discovered thematic clusters advise further investigations to develop an even more detailed structural research approach for RPA [1]. Current literature often lacks a unified theoretical framework that systematically analyzes, assesses, and compares existing as well as upcoming RPA works, although a framework for this purpose has been derived from SLR findings [1]. Furthermore, while qualitative methods like interviews are common, the integration of these methods with broader theoretical models specific to RPA implementation remains underdeveloped compared to other areas of digital transformation. For example, in consumer response studies, the Reflexive Participant Approach (RPA) is used to examine how preferences may be influenced by the approach, recognizing that participants may be ignorant of the benefits of novel technologies [8]. However, this specific approach is distinct from the Robotic Process Automation context and highlights the need for clear theoretical differentiation in the literature.

The use of qualitative data in RPA research is often supported by complementary methods or frameworks from adjacent fields. In the context of risk perception, the Risk Perception Attitude (RPA) framework classifies people according to their perceptions of disease risk and self-efficacy beliefs to predict preventive behaviors, a model applied to diabetes prevention among American Indians [9]. Similarly, in emergency contexts, mixed-method approaches using surveys and in-depth key informant interviews have been used to understand the relationship between risk perception and information-seeking behavior [10]. These examples illustrate how qualitative designs are employed to understand complex human behaviors in response to technological or environmental changes, a parallel that can be drawn to RPA implementation studies. However, the specific application of such risk or behavioral theories to RPA adoption is not explicitly detailed in the provided RPA-specific excerpts, indicating a gap in theoretical transfer.

Methodological challenges in qualitative research on technology adoption are also evident in related literature. For subjective features such as semantic connotation, online workers tend to deteriorate in the quality of their responses as they work longer, which poses challenges for crowdsourced qualitative analysis [11]. In the domain of fairness certification for natural language processing, semi-structured expert interviews with a wide range of experts have been conducted to review a large body of literature on algorithmic fairness [12]. These methodological considerations are relevant to RPA research, where expert interviews are frequently used to gather insights on implementation drivers and barriers [4][6]. The reliance on expert knowledge and narrative analysis in RPA studies [4] aligns with broader qualitative practices in technology research, but the lack of a dominant, widely accepted theoretical lens specific to RPA implementation remains a notable gap in the current empirical evidence.

sections.title: Recommendations for Selecting a Theoretical Lens
sections.text:
Selecting a theoretical lens for qualitative research on Robotic Process Automation (RPA) requires aligning the analytical framework with the specific level of analysis, whether focusing on individual adoption, organizational impact, or broader societal implications. For studies examining the organizational and strategic dimensions of RPA implementation, a multilevel framework is recommended to address the gap in existing literature regarding systematic reviews of AI applications in management disciplines [1]. This approach allows researchers to connect AI-augmented functional areas to domain-level and organizational outcomes, which is essential for understanding how RPA contributes to sustainable competitive advantage [1]. Similarly, research into the distinct effects of AI technologies in organizations should utilize frameworks that explore the tensions and opportunities these technologies present for information systems research, as AI poses new significant challenges that set it apart from other digital technologies [2].

When the research focus is on the drivers and barriers of RPA adoption within specific business functions, such as purchasing and supply management, a multiple case study design is appropriate to explore potentials and implementation challenges in contexts where adoption is still in its infancy [3]. In such exploratory empirical studies, a blended qualitative approach that combines surveys with interpretative interviews and narrative analysis can effectively identify key drivers, including financial benefits, employee impact, and risks [4]. This methodological alignment ensures that the theoretical lens captures the operational benefits of RPA, such as releasing employees from non-value-adding assignments and strengthening enterprise efficiency and compliance [4].

For qualitative research aimed at understanding the causal mechanisms and information behavior surrounding technology adoption, methods such as interviews and grounded theory are suitable for constructing causal influence path models [5]. This qualitative research design allows for the expansion of explanations and the development of macro simulations based on the results of the qualitative analysis [5]. Furthermore, when the research involves the processing of data in a qualitative manner, the use of a knowledge base formalized by an ontology can facilitate direct qualitative processing of data [6].

If the research lens extends to the public sector or social services, where automated decision-making and robot technology are expected to make dramatic changes, a value positions framework is recommended [7]. In this context, analytical frameworks based on value positions such as Professionalism, Efficiency, Service, and Engagement can be used to analyze the goals, policies, and responses to changes in service delivery [7]. This approach is supported by empirical data from interviews with politicians and professionals, as well as government documents, which reveal how new technology impacts accountability, costs, and efficiency in association with citizen centricity [7].

For broader considerations of responsible AI and the wider context of scientific research, the Responsible Research and Innovation (RRI) framework provides methodological guidelines and recommendations [6]. RRI considers perspectives ranging from the lab to global societal challenges, including sustainability, public engagement, ethics, science education, gender equality, open access, and governance [6]. This lens is particularly relevant when addressing the misuse of AI in scientific contexts, where safety and harmlessness scores are critical evaluation metrics [8].

In the context of evaluating the effectiveness of theoretical frameworks or models, it is important to note that comparisons between models with different variables can be problematic due to unobserved heterogeneity, which may invalidate the comparison [6]. Therefore, when selecting a theoretical lens, researchers must ensure that the framework allows for valid comparisons and robust theoretical foundations, such as those found in statistical learning theory and information theory used to quantify and detect information leakage [9]. Additionally, spatial statistics can provide a theoretical framework for exploratory analysis and inference on spatial data, which may be relevant if the RPA implementation has geographic or spatial dimensions [10].

Ultimately, the choice of theoretical lens should be guided by the need to address specific gaps in the literature, such as the lack of cumulative building of knowledge in AI research within information systems [11]. By selecting a framework that aligns with the research focus—whether it be a multilevel framework for organizational outcomes [1], a value positions framework for public sector impacts [7], or a grounded theory approach for causal modeling [5]—researchers can ensure that their qualitative study on RPA implementations is both theoretically grounded and empirically robust.

snippets: AI has received increased attention from the information systems (IS) research community in recent years. There is, however, a growing concern that research on AI could experience a lack of cumulative building of knowledge, which has overshadowed IS research previously. This study addresses this concern, by conducting a systematic literature review of AI research in IS between 2005 and 2020. The search strategy resulted in 1877 studies, of which 98 were identified as primary studies and a synthesise of key themes that are pertinent to this study is presented. In doing so, this study makes important contributions, namely (i) an identification of the current reported business value and contributions of AI, (ii) research and practical implications on the use of AI and (iii) opportunities for future AI research in the form of a research agenda.

evidence.title: challenges of using rpa in auditing: a socio‐technical systems approach
evidence.snippet: Summary: The use of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is rapidly growing in the professional services sector such as auditing. Despite the great benefits RPA can offer, RPA failure rates are still high. In this research, we draw on socio‐technical systems theory to examine the challenges of using RPA in the various phases of auditing and how auditors address these challenges. By interviewing experienced partners and auditors in auditing firms and technology companies, we show that challenges arise when there is a lack of fit between the technical requirements of the RPA tool (technical subsystem) and the skills and knowledge of the auditors and clients (social subsystem). We discuss our findings and provide valuable practical implications and opportunities for future research.

evidence.title: robotic process automation -- a systematic literature review and assessment framework
evidence.snippet:
Robotic Process Automation (RPA) is the automation of rule-based routine
processes to increase efficiency and to reduce costs. Due to the utmost
importance of process automation in industry, RPA attracts increasing attention
in the scientific field as well. This paper presents the state-of-the-art in
the RPA field by means of a Systematic Literature Review (SLR). In this SLR, 63
publications are identified, categorised, and analysed along well-defined
research questions. From the SLR findings, moreover, a framework for
systematically analysing, assessing, and comparing existing as well as upcoming
RPA works is derived. The discovered thematic clusters advise further
investigations in order to develop an even more detailed structural research
approach for RPA.

evidence.title: Artificial intelligence in information systems research: A systematic literature review and research agenda
evidence.snippet: AI has received increased attention from the information systems (IS) research community in recent years. There is, however, a growing concern that research on AI could experience a lack of cumulative building of knowledge, which has overshadowed IS research previously. This study addresses this concern, by conducting a systematic literature review of AI research in IS between 2005 and 2020. The search strategy resulted in 1877 studies, of which 98 were identified as primary studies and a synthesise of key themes that are pertinent to this study is presented. In doing so, this study makes important contributions, namely (i) an identification of the current reported business value and contributions of AI, (ii) research and practical implications on the use of AI and (iii) opportunities for future AI research in the form of a research agenda.

evidence.title: Applying robotic process automation (RPA) in auditing: A framework
evidence.snippet: Robotic process automation (RPA) has been widely adopted in many industries, including the accounting industry, to automate well-defined and repetitive tasks; however, its application to auditing has lagged behind because of the unique nature of this industry. This study applies RPA in the auditing area. An RPA framework is proposed that frees auditors from doing repetitive and low-judgment audit tasks and enables them to focus on tasks that require professional judgment. This paper also demonstrates the feasibility of RPA by implementing a pilot project that applies RPA to the confirmation process.

evidence.title: Impacts of Robotic Process Automation on Global Accounting Services
evidence.snippet: The aim of this study is to understand the impact of Robotic Process Automation (RPA) on Global Accounting Services (GAS) using the institutional logic lens. This study uses an in-depth case study approach in one of the largest global business services firm that provides global accounting services. The result of the study showed that RPA technology has significant impacts on individual and organization resulted in the change and reduction of work, thus reducing the number of employees. Nevertheless, the introduction of new technology in the organization creates unnecessary competition between humans and robots. Although the RPA technology could solve issues involving humans such as disciplinary problems, employee productivity, and human resource shortages, high level of works such as analytical aspect could not be completely replaced by robots and can only be done by humans.

evidence.snippet: Summary: One of the distinguishing features of digital transformation is the large scale business process automation, and, in particular, robotic process automation – with the use of software from the currently growing RPA (Robotic Process Automation) category. This is such a new field that a commonly accepted conceptual apparatus (terminology) has not been developed yet, also methodical tools for effective robotic process automation management are missing. Based on the above observations it was deemed justified to conduct research aimed at: (G1): developing a ”robotic process automation” definition proposal, (G2): identifying the key ”robotic process automation” management aspects in Polish medium and large enterprises; (G3): developing a robotic process automation management model structure and completing its initial verification. The outcome of the research conducted is the development of a proprietary robotic process automation management model structure that was initially verified at one of companies.

evidence.title: Towards a Framework of Implementing Software Robots: Transforming Human-executed Routines into Machines
evidence.snippet: Software robots tend to increasingly take over organizational processes. However, little is known about principles of building and implementing as opposed to using robotic systems, such as bots for process automation (RPA) and chatbots. Therefore, based on an empirically illustrated theoretical conceptualization of routine automation and affordance actualization, this paper develops a framework that guides how different types of software robots can be built and implemented through transforming a human-executed routine into a robot-automated routine by applying specific implementation guidelines.

evidence.title: Let the robots do it! – Taking a look at Robotic Process Automation and its potential application in digital forensics
evidence.snippet: Abstract The challenges of tackling increasing caseloads, large volumes of digital data and maintaining examination efficiency in order to adhere to tight criminal justice system deadlines persist. As the field looks towards techniques for improving efficiency, forms of automation are both simultaneously touted as a potential solution, whilst also attracting criticism. The potential for techniques which mechanise parts of the digital forensic examination process, and do it reliably, is great, however developing the capability to do this remains a challenge. This work provides an introductory discussion to Robotic Process Automation, a form of service task automation. It's potential application is debated and two case studies are offered demonstrating potential areas of applicability. An objective evaluation is offered, debating whether technology has a place in improving efficiency in this field.

evidence.title: Are Robots Taking Our Jobs? A RoboPlatform at a Bank
evidence.snippet: Automation has been replacing manual activities in workplace for decades. Robots had been most active in blue-collar industrial manufacturing. Now that they are entering white-collar jobs, in the form of software taking over administrative work, it is time to ask the following questions.

question: Can you recommend a suitable theoretical lens for qualitative research concerning robotics process automation (RPA) implementations?

sections.title: Taxonomy of Tree Compression Algorithms
sections.text:
Tree compression algorithms can be broadly categorized into grammar-based methods, succinct data structures, and wavelet or entropy-based approaches, each offering distinct trade-offs between space efficiency and query performance [1][2][3]. Grammar-based compression represents a primary family of techniques that exploit structural redundancy by transforming trees into context-free grammars or Straight-Line Programs (SLPs) [3][4]. In this approach, a binary tree is first transformed into a context-free grammar from which the original tree can be reconstructed, and the grammar is subsequently encoded into a binary codeword [3]. This method is shown to be a universal code for families of probabilistic binary tree source models satisfying specific weak restrictions [3]. Similarly, SLPs, a general kind of context-free grammar, are utilized in self-indexed grammar-based compression to exploit repetitiveness in data [4]. For an SLP with $n$ rules representing a text, the compressed representation requires $2n \log_2 n$ bits, while a self-indexed version allows for substring extraction and pattern searching with specific time complexities dependent on the grammar's height [4].

Succinct data structures constitute another major category, focusing on minimizing space occupancy while retaining the ability to perform operations efficiently on the data [5]. This approach distinguishes between data compression, which stores data for later retrieval, and data optimization, which compresses data while maintaining efficient operation support [5]. Jacobson’s seminal work introduced succinct data structures for unlabeled trees, achieving $2t + o(t)$ bits of space for $t$ nodes while supporting navigational operations in $O(1)$ time [6]. This space usage is asymptotically optimal with respect to the information-theoretic lower bound averaged over all trees [6]. Subsequent research has extended these concepts to labeled trees, where the goal is to support operations such as finding the parent or $i$-th child of a node with specific labels [6]. The range min-max tree was proposed as a simple and flexible data structure that reduces complex tree operations to a few primitives carried out in constant time on polylog-sized trees, achieving $2n + O(n/\text{polylog}(n))$ bits of space for static trees [7]. This space is optimal for a core subset of operations and is significantly lower than previous proposals [7]. Furthermore, static unlabeled trees and planar graphs can be represented with structures that are asymptotically optimal, using fewer bits per node than conventional pointer-based representations while maintaining comparable time efficiency for traversal [2].

Entropy-based and opportunistic data structures represent a third family, where space occupancy is a function of the entropy of the underlying data set [1]. These structures are termed "opportunistic" because their space occupancy decreases when the input is compressible, achieving this reduction without significant slowdown in query performance [1]. Specifically, such a data structure stores text using $O(H_k(T)) + o(1)$ bits per input symbol in the worst case, where $H_k(T)$ is the $k$-th order empirical entropy [1]. This approach allows for searching occurrences of a pattern in $O(p + \text{occ} \log^\epsilon u)$ time [1]. In the context of optimal alphabet selection for single text compression, the choice of codebook representation is critical, as switching from a naive to a compact representation significantly improves performance for alphabets with a large number of symbols, such as words [8]. The compression performance in such scenarios must be evaluated by the full code length, which includes both the length of the encoded text and the length of the codebook [8].

While the primary focus is on structural compression, related fields utilize tree transformations and hierarchical structures for data organization and classification. Tree transformations are employed to organize document content into logical tree structures to aid in categorization and extraction [9]. In the domain of system log parsing, log entries are encoded with tailor-made data structures, including trees, and matched or grouped based on predefined similarity metrics [10]. Decision trees, which are hierarchical structures for decision making, are used to support regression and classification problems by learning a tree structure containing nodes, branches, and leaves from training data [11][12]. Tree ensembles aggregate predictions from multiple trees learned on different subsets of training data to overcome poor performance [12]. In the context of isomorphism testing, the problem can be reduced to a sequence of structured tree comparisons rather than an explicit search over permutations [13]. Additionally, in deep graph generation, data structures inspired by Fenwick trees, such as the row-binary forest, are proposed to encode edge-binary trees [14].

The evaluation of these compression and representation methods often involves comparing compression ratios and computational efficiency. For instance, in medical document summarization, a compression ratio of 10 was observed for specific tokens compared to a ratio of 45 for all tokens [15]. In the context of prompt compression for large language models, methods are divided into Text-to-Vector (T2V) compression in continuous space and Text-to-Text (T2T) compression in discrete space [16]. T2V compression considers the language model as a compressor that compresses essential text information into more compact vector representations [16]. Pruning is defined as an extractive compression method, while summarization is an abstractive compression method [16]. In image compression, most frameworks contain static compression and decompression models which are fixed after training, limiting efficient rate-distortion optimization [17]. Sparse representation methods, which can be categorized by different norm minimizations used in sparsity constraints, provide another perspective on data reduction, with categories including $l_0$-norm, $l_p$-norm, and $l_{2,1}$-norm minimization [18]. The efficiency of certain algorithms, such as LeafRefit, derives from the simplifying assumption that instance deletions do not affect the trees’ structure [19]. In metagenomics, the Kaiju classifier uses the Burrows-Wheeler transform to find maximum exact matches on the protein level, achieving higher sensitivity and classifying up to 10 times more reads compared to k-mer-based classifiers [20].

sections.title: Space Complexity and Compression Ratios
sections.text:
The asymptotic space efficiency of static tree representations is a foundational concern in data structure design, where conventional pointer-based representations are often less efficient than specialized structures [1]. For static unlabeled trees, specific data structures have been developed that are asymptotically optimal, meaning no other structure can encode $n$-node trees with fewer bits per node as $n$ grows without bound [1]. While these optimal structures maintain time efficiency for traversal operations comparable to conventional methods, they achieve superior space utilization [1]. In the context of planar graphs and graphs of bounded page number, similar linear space data structures are within a constant factor of the most succinct representation [1].

When evaluating compression performance for tree-based data, such as XML documents, it is critical to account for the full code length, which includes both the length of the encoded text and the length of the codebook [2]. The representation of the codebook itself is significant; switching from a naive representation to a compact one significantly improves compression matters, particularly for alphabets with a large number of symbols such as words [2]. For instance, XBZIPINDEX utilizes succinct tree representations to maintain XML documents in a highly compressed format, allowing for navigation and searching without decompressing the entire data set [3]. This approach addresses the challenge that XML representations are significantly larger than their native state and that search involves complex path and content operations on labeled tree structures [3].

In the domain of prompt compression for large language models, algorithms are categorized into Text-to-Vector (T2V) compression in continuous space and Text-to-Text (T2T) compression in discrete space [4]. T2V compression treats the language model as a compressor that condenses essential text information into more compact vector representations [4]. The choice between coarse-to-fine and fine-grained compression strategies depends on the task, with coarse-to-fine being more beneficial for complex reasoning and fine-grained compression suitable for long context tasks [4]. Practical compression ratios vary widely; for example, 500xCompressor achieves compression ratios ranging from 6x to 480x while maintaining the ability to answer various types of questions [4]. In contrast, other summarization approaches may yield lower ratios, such as a compression ratio of only 10 compared to 45 for all tokens in specific medical document summarization contexts [5].

For sequential universal data compression of binary tree sources, the context-tree weighting method achieves computational and storage complexity that is linear in the source sequence length [6]. This method weights coding distributions corresponding to all bounded memory tree sources in an efficient recursive way, achieving a desirable coding distribution for tree sources with unknown models and parameters [6]. The cumulative redundancy of this method is bounded by terms identified as coding, parameter, and model redundancy, with the bound holding for all source sequence lengths [6]. Similarly, in the compression of deep neural networks, which can be viewed as structured data, a three-stage pipeline of pruning, trained quantization, and Huffman coding reduces storage requirements by 35x to 49x [7]. Pruning reduces the number of connections by 9x to 13x, while quantization reduces the bits per connection from 32 to 5 [7].

Huffman coding is noted as the most efficient method to encode scattered data due to its optimal compression rate, although its complexity makes it difficult to employ in hardware due to the need for computation-hungry compressor and decompressor schemes [8]. In the context of geometric compression for 3-D models, which often rely on triangulated structures, vertex positions are quantized within desired accuracy to reduce memory and disk space requirements [9]. Multi-dimensional trees are also used for controlled volume rendering and compression, where each node contains a model of the data, a measure of error, and a measure of importance [10]. A divide-and-conquer algorithm permits efficient computation of these quantities, and trees over large datasets can be pruned to provide data representations of reduced size [10].

In machine learning applications involving tree structures, such as decision trees, the structure contains nodes, branches, and leaves learned from training data [11]. However, certain tree-based search structures, like K-D trees, can degenerate into linear search in higher dimensions due to sparse data distribution [12]. For scalable tree boosting systems like XGBoost, insights into cache access patterns, data compression, and sharding are utilized to build a system that scales beyond billions of examples using fewer resources [13]. The sparsity-aware algorithm and weighted quantile sketch in XGBoost contribute to this efficiency in approximate tree learning [13].

Path compression algorithms on balanced trees offer fast computation for functions defined on paths, with running times of $O((m + n)\alpha(m + n, n))$, where $\alpha$ is a functional reverse of Ackermann's function [14]. These algorithms improve upon previous bounds for problems such as verifying minimum spanning trees and finding dominators in flow graphs [14]. Self-adjusting binary search trees, such as splay trees, provide an amortized time bound of $O(\log n)$ per operation for standard search tree operations, making them as efficient as balanced trees when total running time is the measure of interest [15].

In the realm of neural representation learning, models such as VAE, VQ-VAE, and VIMCO obtain specific bit rates per dimension, such as 4.51, 4.67, and 5.14 bits/dim respectively [16]. A reduction in bits can be calculated based on the dimensions and channels of the data, with one example showing a reduction of approximately 42.6 in bits [16]. For biological sequence compression, which is essential for addressing the data deluge from high-throughput sequencing, methods are compared in terms of compression ratio, memory usage, and compression/decompression speed [17]. The challenge to store and process sequencing data is addressed by specialized compression algorithms that reduce storage space and processing costs [18].

Estimation methods without data compression provide an upper bound of the real scenario, highlighting the potential for further reduction through compression techniques [19]. Pointwise influence analysis always has a space complexity of at least $O(n)$, indicating a lower bound for certain analytical tasks [20]. In the context of tree transformations for document analysis, organizing content into a logical tree structure aids in categorization and extraction [21]. Sentence compression methods may consider every node in a constituent parse tree to decide whether to remove or retain it, using integer linear programming to solve the problem [22]. Simplifying inessential parts of a parse tree, such as parentheses, by implying information in its hierarchy is another technique used in natural language processing for programming [23].

Tree structures are also employed in optimization-based task and motion planning, where a tree structure for STL formulas results in a more efficient encoding that uses fewer binary variables [24]. In sparse graphical models, tree-based node aggregation leverages side information in the form of a tree that encodes node similarity to facilitate interpretation [25]. For protein alignments at the tree-of-life scale, improved versions of tools like DIAMOND harness supercomputing to perform alignments in hours while matching the sensitivity of standard methods [26]. In neural graphics primitives, a multiresolution hash encoding reduces the cost of training and evaluation by permitting the use of a smaller network, significantly reducing floating point and memory access operations [27]. The use of float types for representation, such as 4 bytes per value, is a standard approach in these computational contexts [19].
