sections.title: Time Complexity for Construction and Querying
sections.text:
The construction of compressed tree structures involves varying computational costs depending on the specific algorithm and representation used. For instance, the Top program construction algorithm constructs a correct Top program in polynomial time from a finite number of examples [1]. In contrast, certain parsing algorithms, such as LKE, exhibit $O(n^2)$ time complexity, which renders them incapable of processing large datasets in a reasonable time [2]. The efficiency of some tree-based methods relies on simplifying assumptions; for example, LeafRefit’s efficiency derives from the assumption that instance deletions do not affect the trees’ structure [3]. Additionally, pruning strategies can be introduced during tree construction to eliminate interference from query-irrelevant nodes, as seen in hypothesis tree building for temporal sentence localization [4].

Querying compressed tree structures for standard operations such as level-ancestor, lowest common ancestor (LCA), and depth often achieves constant time complexity under specific models. Succinct representations of static ordinal trees can support a variety of navigation operations, including level-ancestor, in $O(1)$ time on the RAM model while using $2n + o(n)$ bits of space [5]. Similarly, the range min-max tree data structure reduces a large number of relevant tree operations to a few primitives that are carried out in constant time on polylog-sized trees, extending to trees of arbitrary size while retaining constant time [6]. These succinct representations are within $o(n)$ bits of the information-theoretic minimum for representing an $n$-node tree [5]. The underlying indexable dictionaries used in these structures support rank and select operations in $O(1)$ time on the RAM model [7][8].

The trade-offs between space and time in compressed tree representations are significant, particularly when comparing different succinct data structures. The range min-max tree achieves a space complexity of $2n + O(n/\text{polylog}(n))$ bits, which is optimal for a core subset of operations and significantly lower than previous proposals [6]. In the context of suffix trees, which are critical in bioinformatics, recent research has obtained various compressed representations with widely different space-time tradeoffs [9]. The use of range min-max trees in suffix tree representations yields novel practical space/time tradeoffs and allows for the indexing of highly repetitive collections [9]. Conversely, opportunistic data structures achieve space occupancy that is a function of the entropy of the underlying data set, decreasing space when input is compressible at no significant slowdown in query performance [10]. Specifically, such structures allow searching for occurrences of a pattern $P$ in text $T$ in $O(p + \text{occ} \log^\epsilon u)$ time [10].

While many succinct tree structures aim for constant-time queries, other approaches involve higher computational overhead or different complexity profiles. For example, extracting maximal disconnected principal submatrices in poset-related analyses requires $O(n^4)$ time, remaining tractable for specific sizes where backtracking algorithms time out [11]. In the domain of phylogenetic tree construction, algorithms based on Lempel-Ziv complexity construct trees automatically without sequence alignment, though the specific time complexity for the distance measure calculation is not detailed in the provided excerpt [12]. Furthermore, the complexity of encoding and decoding in general data compression models, which include macro schemes based on finding redundant strings, is a subject of discussion regarding trade-offs between compression amount and algorithmic cost [13].

The efficiency of tree-based data structures can also be influenced by the specific application and data characteristics. In deep learning, XGBoost provides insights into cache access patterns and data compression to build a scalable tree boosting system, scaling beyond billions of examples using fewer resources [14]. However, in high-dimensional spaces, K-D trees can degenerate into linear search due to sparse data distribution, impacting query efficiency [15]. For geometric compression, efficient compression and decompression algorithms for triangulated models aim to reduce transmission time and storage space, though the specific time complexity for the topological surgery is not explicitly quantified in the excerpt [16]. In the context of graphical models, the sample complexity of the SGA algorithm for partial recovery of tree-structured models is significantly better than that of the algorithm by Katiyar et al. [17].

The evaluation of compression performance and complexity often requires considering the full cost of the representation. For text compression, performance should be evaluated by the full code length, which includes the length of the encoded text plus the length of the codebook [18]. Switching from a naive codebook representation to a compact one significantly improves matters for alphabets with a large number of symbols [18]. In the context of medical document summarization, a compression ratio of 10 was observed for specific tokens compared to a ratio of 45 for all tokens, highlighting the variability in compression efficiency [19]. Similarly, in neural network compression, Huffman coding is noted as the most efficient method for encoding scattered data due to its optimal compression rate, but its complexity makes it difficult to employ due to computation-hungry compressor/decompressor schemes [20].

Dynamic tree structures introduce additional complexity compared to static ones. The range min-max tree data structure is extended to the dynamic case, where insertion and deletion operations are supported, although the specific time complexity for these dynamic operations is not fully detailed in the provided excerpt beyond the mention of the extension [6]. In contrast, static succinct trees focus on supporting operations in constant time on the RAM model [5][8]. The choice of data structure, such as the row-binary forest inspired by Fenwick trees, is proposed to encode edge-binary trees, indicating a specific structural approach to managing tree data [21]. Overall, the computational cost of building and querying compressed trees varies from polynomial time for construction in some algorithms to constant time for queries in succinct static representations, with significant trade-offs in space usage and implementation complexity [6][1][5].

sections.title: Trade-offs Between Space and Time
sections.text:
The trade-off between space and time in tree-based data structures is fundamentally characterized by the necessity to balance storage efficiency against query latency and preprocessing overhead. In the context of database indexing, B-trees have become the de facto standard for file organization, with their success attributed to a careful contrast of the relative merits and costs of various implementations, such as the B+-tree [1]. However, this balance is not uniform across all dimensions; for instance, K-D trees, which are effective in lower dimensions, degenerate into linear search in higher dimensions due to sparse data distribution, indicating a significant increase in time complexity as dimensionality grows [2]. Similarly, in high-dimensional feature spaces used for multimedia retrieval, query processing requires navigating complex similarity searches that transform content-based retrieval into point searches, where the efficiency of the underlying structure dictates the overall system performance [3].

Specific compression algorithms for tree structures often involve explicit trade-offs between the compactness of the representation and the computational cost of encoding or decoding. For example, in the domain of parse trees, simplifying inessential parts such as parentheses by implying information through hierarchy reduces the structural complexity, effectively trading explicit storage for implicit structural inference [4]. This approach aligns with broader compression strategies where reducing space impacts the ability to perform efficient lookups; in medical document summarization, a compression ratio of only 10 is observed for specific token types compared to a ratio of 45 for all tokens, highlighting that the granularity of compression directly affects the resulting data size and potentially the retrieval fidelity [5]. The choice of representation is critical, as switching from a naive representation to a compact codebook significantly improves matters for alphabets with a large number of symbols, such as words, thereby optimizing the space-time balance for large-scale text compression [6].

In machine learning contexts, the trade-off often manifests as a choice between model complexity and computational resources during training or inference. XGBoost, a scalable tree boosting system, provides insights on cache access patterns, data compression, and sharding to build a system that scales beyond billions of examples using far fewer resources, demonstrating how specific architectural choices mitigate the time costs associated with large-scale tree operations [7]. Conversely, in federated recommendation systems, the reduction of communication costs through model compression sacrifices the computation resources of the clients, necessitating a careful consideration of the trade-off between computation and communication costs [8]. This dynamic is also evident in image compression, where learned frameworks may use static compression and decompression models fixed after training, which prevents efficient rate-distortion optimization and thus limits the ability to dynamically adjust the space-time trade-off based on real-time requirements [9].

Preprocessing steps often introduce significant time overheads that must be weighed against the benefits of subsequent compression or analysis. For instance, in system log parsing, algorithms such as SLCT, Paddy, Lenma, and LogCluster are sensitive to preprocessing, with variations in this phase affecting up to 10% of the overall performance, indicating that the initial structuring of data into tree-like or clustered formats has a measurable impact on efficiency [10]. Similarly, in the analysis of tree ring data, the use of Random Forest methods yields accurate results with the lowest Root Mean Square Error, but the computational cost of training such ensemble models must be considered against the accuracy gains [11]. In the context of dynamic least-squares regression, sharp separations exist between the amortized update times of fully versus partially dynamic settings, showing that the level of dynamism and accuracy required directly dictates the computational complexity of maintaining the underlying data structures [12].

Structural transformations and canonicalization also play a role in managing these trade-offs. Reducing isomorphism testing to a sequence of structured tree comparisons rather than an explicit search over permutations offers a more efficient pathway, although fast canonicalization remains a natural but currently missing preprocessing step in many workflows [13]. In the domain of graph generation, data structures like the row-binary forest, inspired by Fenwick trees, are proposed to encode edge-binary trees, aiming to optimize the storage and retrieval of generated structures [14]. Furthermore, in temporal sentence localization, pruning strategies are introduced during tree construction to eliminate query-irrelevant nodes, which reduces the search space and thereby improves query execution time at the cost of potential information loss [15].

The impact of compression on query performance is further illustrated by indexing techniques that improve average query execution time. Multi-component key indexes, for example, can improve average query execution time by up to 130 times for high-frequency word queries, demonstrating that specific indexing structures can drastically reduce time complexity for certain query patterns [16]. In contrast, caching policies, such as those used in ATRAPOS for metapath query workloads, select intermediate results to cache and reuse by detecting frequent sub-metapaths using an Overlap Tree, which trades storage space for reduced computation time in real-time evaluation [17]. These examples underscore that the optimal balance between space and time is highly dependent on the specific workload, data distribution, and the nature of the queries being executed.

sections.title: Empirical Performance and Practical Limitations
sections.text:
Empirical evaluations of tree-based and compression algorithms reveal significant disparities in performance metrics, particularly regarding compression ratios and the fidelity of the resulting representations. In the context of medical document summarization, specific compression methods have been observed to achieve a compression ratio of only 10, which stands in stark contrast to the compression ratio of 45 achieved when processing all tokens [1]. This discrepancy highlights that the choice of algorithm and the granularity of the data being compressed directly impact the efficiency of the reduction process. Similarly, in the domain of prompt compression for large language models, empirical distinctions are drawn between Text-to-Vector (T2V) and Text-to-Text (T2T) approaches, where T2V treats the model as a compressor for vector representations, while T2T directly measures token informativeness to remove redundancy [2]. The effectiveness of these methods is often constrained by the underlying representation of the data; for instance, in single text compression, switching from a naive codebook representation to a compact one significantly improves performance, particularly for alphabets with a large number of symbols such as words [3]. Consequently, accurate evaluation of compression performance requires accounting for the full code length, which includes both the length of the encoded text and the length of the codebook itself [3].

Memory overhead and storage requirements constitute a critical practical limitation for many tree-based and neural compression algorithms. Neural networks are characterized as both computationally and memory intensive, making their deployment on embedded systems with limited hardware resources difficult [4]. To mitigate this, the "deep compression" pipeline employs pruning, trained quantization, and Huffman coding to reduce storage requirements by 35x to 49x without affecting accuracy, with pruning alone reducing the number of connections by 9x to 13x [4]. In the realm of 3-D geometric compression, the need to reduce the memory or disk space required to store complex triangulated models has driven the development of schemes that quantize vertex positions and utilize vertex spanning trees [5]. Furthermore, in the context of approximate algorithms for maximum inner product search, systems like Sinnamon offer levers to trade-off memory consumption, latency, and accuracy, making them suitable for constrained applications [6]. The practical aspects of using data compression for prefetching in database systems also involve analyzing the I/O involved in moving objects from slow memory to cache, where prefetchers based on Lempel-Ziv data compressors have been shown to be theoretically optimal in the limit [7].

Scalability issues remain a persistent challenge for tree-based algorithms and related machine learning methods when applied to large-scale datasets. While tree boosting is a highly effective method, systems like XGBoost require specific insights on cache access patterns, data compression, and sharding to scale beyond billions of examples using fewer resources than existing systems [8]. In contrast, many deep graph generation methods, despite their goal of being used on real-world applications such as social network graphs, suffer from scalability issues [9]. This limitation is not unique to graph generation; scalability issues also limit the applicability of manifold learning methods for handling large-scale data [10], and researchers have focused on inductive reasoning models for knowledge graphs due to scalability and expressive ability issues in previous approaches [11]. The computational scalability of methods for large posets, which involve reducing isomorphism testing to structured tree comparisons, remains to be systematically evaluated [12]. Additionally, parameter-centric approaches in recommender systems lack scalability and flexibility, as the capacity is hard to scale and the knowledge is inflexible to utilize [13].

The evaluation of these algorithms is further complicated by inconsistencies in experimental setups and the lack of standardized benchmarks. In time series classification, previous evaluations made comparisons between algorithms difficult due to the use of different programming languages, single train/test splits, and inconsistent data normalization practices [14]. To address this, a common Java framework was implemented to evaluate 18 recently proposed algorithms against standard baselines on an expanded archive of 85 datasets [14]. Similarly, in the field of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, poor reporting of key information has diminished the value of these studies for clinicians and policy makers, leading to the development of guidelines like PRISMA to improve clarity and transparency [15][16]. In the context of privacy-preserving model explanations, greedy algorithms for constructing decision trees select features based on Gini impurity, allowing for the identification and discarding of attribute combinations that do not contribute to an optimal tree [17]. However, the estimation of performance without data compression serves as an upper bound of the real scenario, indicating that empirical results must account for the overhead of compression techniques to be realistic [18].

Real-world data characteristics and the specific nature of the tasks impose additional constraints on algorithmic performance. Tree transformations are used to organize document content into a logical tree structure to aid in categorization and extraction, but the effectiveness of these structures depends on the logical coherence of the source material [19]. In financial applications, market microstructure poses challenges to volatility estimation from high-frequency data, where the "usual" volatility estimator fails when returns are sampled at the highest frequency [20]. For global land data assimilation, systems like GLDAS must ingest satellite and ground-based observational data to generate optimal fields of land surface states, requiring the integration of a huge quantity of observation-based data at high resolution [21]. The rapid evolution of big data has forced the academic press to catch up with industry adoption, highlighting the need for efficient analytic methods for unstructured data, which constitutes 95% of big data [22]. In the domain of explainable AI, tree ensembles aim to overcome poor performance by aggregating predictions from trees learned on different subsets of training data, yet the scalability of such ensemble methods remains a concern [23]. Finally, while gradient-based learning techniques like back-propagation are successful for synthesizing complex decision surfaces, real-life document recognition systems are composed of multiple modules including field extraction, segmentation, and language modeling, indicating that tree-based or compression algorithms must integrate within broader pipelines [24].

evidence.title: A Universal Grammar-Based Code for Lossless Compression of Binary Trees
evidence.snippet: We consider the problem of lossless compression of binary trees, with the aim of reducing the number of code bits needed to store or transmit such trees. A lossless grammar-based code is presented, which encodes each binary tree into a binary codeword in two steps. In the first step, the tree is transformed into a context-free grammar from which the tree can be reconstructed. In the second step, the context-free grammar is encoded into a binary codeword. The decoder of the grammar-based code decodes the original tree from its codeword by reversing the two encoding steps. It is shown that the resulting grammar-based binary tree compression code is a universal code on a family of probabilistic binary tree source models satisfying certain weak restrictions.

evidence.snippet: This paper presents a tree-to-tree transduction method for sentence compression. Our model is based on synchronous tree substitution grammar, a formalism that allows local distortion of the tree topology and can thus naturally capture structural mismatches. We describe an algorithm for decoding in this framework and show how the model can be trained discriminatively within a large margin framework. Experimental results on sentence compression bring significant improvements over a state-of-the-art model.

evidence.snippet: Self-indexes aim at representing text collections in a compressed format that allows extracting arbitrary portions and also offers indexed searching on the collection. sections.title: Definitions and Theoretical Frameworks
sections.text:
In-context learning (ICL) is defined as a paradigm that allows language models to learn tasks given only a few examples in the form of demonstration, operating on the key idea of learning from analogy [1]. This capability eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates, as the model generates responses or performs tasks by inputting cueing examples or related knowledge [2]. ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where the demonstration examples are part of the prompt [1]. However, the performance of ICL is highly sensitive to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. Consequently, in-context learning is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, and which in-context reasoning examples make the most effective prompts remains an unknown problem in the literature [3][4].

Standard supervised overfitting is characterized by models suffering from increasing validation error as training progresses, such as at epoch 150 when learning rates are reduced [5]. In the context of ICL, overfitting is distinct because it involves the model's inability to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context [6]. Relying solely on high-confidence data generated from unsupervised downstream tasks for in-context prompting or prompt optimization may lead to overfitting [7]. Furthermore, traditional fine-tuning methods, which are often used to enhance generation quality, are prone to overfitting, degraded generalization, and unnatural language generation [8]. To address these limitations, approaches like Consistent In-Context Editing (ICE) leverage the model's in-context learning capability to optimize toward a contextual distribution rather than a one-hot target, thereby preventing overfitting and preserving the model's integrity [8].

The role of prompt length and the number of demonstrations significantly impacts the generalization ability of ICL. The scarcity of examples poses a challenge to the generalization ability of ICL [1]. Conventional in-context learning is usually restricted by length constraints, rendering it ineffective to absorb supervision from a large number of examples [9]. Enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains a significant challenge [1]. While few-shot prompting typically outperforms zero-shot prompting [10], the advent of Long Context Language Models (LCLMs) has raised questions about whether ICL performance in a many-shot regime is still sensitive to the method of sample selection [11]. Surprisingly, sophisticated example selection techniques do not yield significant improvements over a simple random sample selection method in the context of LCLMs [11]. Structured prompting has been introduced to break the length limit and scale in-context learning to thousands of examples by encoding demonstration examples separately with well-designed position embeddings [9].

Theoretical frameworks for understanding ICL often distinguish between memorization and generalization. Transformers exhibit ICL, and recent work shows that the transition from memorization to generalization is sharp with increasing task diversity [12]. One interpretation is that a network's limited capacity to memorize favors generalization, but mechanistic examinations show that the relative rates at which sub-circuits for memorization and generalization learn explains this transition, rather than capacity constraints [12]. A memorization scaling law has been uncovered that determines the task diversity required for this transition [12]. In large language models, distinct neuron subsets are responsible for memorization and generalization behaviors, and inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward either [13]. These findings reveal a modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time [13].

Memorization in ICL is closely correlated with performance and the surfacing of training data. ICL significantly surfaces memorization compared to zero-shot learning in most cases [14]. Demonstrations, without their labels, are the most effective element in surfacing memorization [14]. ICL improves performance when the surfaced memorization in few-shot regimes reaches a high level, approximately 40% [14]. There is a very strong correlation between performance and memorization in ICL [14]. However, memorization can also lead to undesirable behaviors, such as the model's output outside the training data [15]. Mixup and CutMix methods reduce the memorization of corrupt labels and facilitate model generalization by averting memorization [15][16]. In the context of pre-training, models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks, suggesting possible memorization [17]. Deduplication methods have been proposed to simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [18].

The sensitivity of ICL to label noise and data quality is evident in its high variance and potential for poor performance. In-context learning performs even worse than manual prompt on some tasks and suffers from high variance [6]. Feature-based methods perform slightly better than manual prompt and in-context learning [6]. ICL methods may be prone to knowledge conflict issues, and their unlearning effectiveness depends on the in-context learning capability of the used LLMs [19]. The debate over whether LLMs genuinely generalize to unseen tasks or predominantly rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data remains active [20]. Out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization in ICL settings, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning, remains an open and underexplored question [21]. Theoretical surveys aim to unveil the underlying mechanisms of foundation models, covering the analysis of generalization performance [22]. Additionally, in-context deep learning via transformer models provides theoretical guarantees for the approximation and convergence of ICL gradient descent, showing that ICL performance matches that of direct training in synthetic settings [23].

snippets: We investigate how Large Language Models (LLMs) distinguish between memorization and generalization at the neuron level. Through carefully designed tasks, we identify distinct neuron subsets responsible for each behavior. Experiments on both a GPT-2 model trained from scratch and a pretrained LLaMA-3.2 model fine-tuned with LoRA show consistent neuron-level specialization. We further demonstrate that inference-time interventions on these neurons can steer the model's behavior toward memorization or generalization. To assess robustness, we evaluate intra-task and inter-task consistency, confirming that these neuron-behavior associations reflect generalizable patterns rather than dataset-specific artifacts. Our findings reveal modular structure in LLMs and enable controlling memorization and generalization behaviors at inference time.

snippets: We investigate the transformer's capability to simulate the training process of deep models via in-context learning (ICL), i.e., in-context deep learning. Our key contribution is providing a positive example of using a transformer to train a deep neural network by gradient descent in an implicit fashion via ICL. Specifically, we provide an explicit construction of a $(2N+4)L$-layer transformer capable of simulating $L$ gradient descent steps of an $N$-layer ReLU network through ICL. We also give the theoretical guarantees for the approximation within any given error and the convergence of the ICL gradient descent. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the more practical setting using Softmax-based transformers. We validate our findings on synthetic datasets for 3-layer, 4-layer, and 6-layer neural networks. The results show that ICL performance matches that of direct training.

sections.title: Mechanisms of Overfitting in ICL
sections.text:
Overfitting in in-context learning (ICL) is characterized by a high sensitivity to specific prompt configurations, including the selection, order, and template of demonstration examples [1][2]. This sensitivity results in high variance in model performance, where ICL can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks [3]. The underlying mechanism involves a failure to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context, leading to performance declines that indicate a need for further investigation into these instabilities [3][2]. In few-shot settings, the objective function to be optimized is deterministic rather than stochastic because all training data can be placed into a single batch, which alters the standard bias-variance dynamics observed in stochastic optimization [3]. While the bias-variance tradeoff is a fundamental concept in learning, its application in few-shot scenarios is complicated by the limited number of examples, which remains a major challenge for current models [4][5].

The transition from induction to memorization is a critical mechanism underlying overfitting, as models may rely on memorizing vast amounts of pretraining data rather than genuinely generalizing to unseen tasks [6]. Memorization leads to undesirable behavior outside the training data, a phenomenon that has been observed when models attain significantly smaller training losses as the size of the pre-training dataset shrinks [7][8]. Recent research has identified distinct neuron subsets responsible for memorization versus generalization in Large Language Models (LLMs), demonstrating that these behaviors can be steered at inference time through interventions on specific neurons [9]. This modular structure suggests that LLMs possess the capacity to distinguish between these modes, yet they may still rely on memorization without truly understanding the underlying problems, as seen in domains like molecular chemistry [10]. The debate over whether LLMs generalize or memorize remains active, with some studies failing to find evidence of memorization in complex outputs, though such findings are limited by the unavailability of training sets and models for inspection [11].

Label noise further exacerbates overfitting mechanisms, as deep neural networks have a high capacity to completely memorize noisy labels given sufficient training time, which leads to performance degradation [12]. In practical scenarios, label noise arises from annotator variability and can degrade recognition performance, necessitating methods to identify wrong labels and minimize their negative impact [13]. Regularization techniques, such as early learning regularization, are used to prevent models from overfitting to label noise [14]. Context-based virtual adversarial training (ConVAT) has been proposed to prevent text classifiers from overfitting to noisy labels by enforcing consistency between inputs and perturbed inputs, thereby encouraging the generalization of clean samples while preventing the learning of noisy ones [12]. In federated learning settings, label noise variations among clients can cause existing centralized approaches to exhibit unsatisfactory performance, highlighting the difficulty of handling noisy labels across decentralized training stages [15].

The impact of label noise is also evident in specific application domains, such as audio tagging, where systems must evaluate performance on large sets of noisy-labeled data alongside smaller manually-labeled sets [16]. Similarly, in medical applications like cardiac abnormalities classification, aggregated datasets from various sources are prone to label noise due to inter- and intra-observer variability, which affects the performance and generalizability of trained models [17]. While techniques like Mixup and CutMix can impair baseline performance under certain noise conditions, other regularization strategies aim to improve robustness by interpolating between inputs, although interpolating only between inputs with equal labels does not yield the same performance gains [18][7]. The challenge of learning from very few examples, such as in few-shot class-incremental learning, requires models to preserve the topology of the feature manifold to mitigate forgetting and improve representation learning for new classes [19].

Induction heads in transformers play a role in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, where models must infer hidden rules behind input prompts without fine-tuning [20]. However, the reliance on memorization can hinder this process, as evidenced by the need for deduplication methods that can simultaneously reduce memorization while improving performance [21]. Metrics such as extraction likelihood and memorization accuracy have been proposed to quantify the extent of memorization by considering overlaps of n-grams and matching of identical token sequences [22]. Despite the potential for overfitting, few-shot learning can achieve cross-lingual capabilities in non-English languages without requiring translation, suggesting that some generalization mechanisms are robust across languages [23]. Furthermore, self-consistency methods can robustly boost performance in few-shot in-context learning for common NLP tasks, offering a reliable way to add rationales and potentially mitigate some instabilities associated with standard prompting [24]. Nevertheless, standard few-shot promptings have not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning, indicating that the mechanisms of overfitting and limited generalization remain significant barriers in complex domains [11].

sections.title: Empirical Evidence and Experimental Findings
sections.text:
Empirical investigations into in-context learning (ICL) reveal that the capability to learn from analogy is not uniform and is significantly constrained by the quality and selection of input examples [1]. While ICL is defined as learning from a few examples in the context without explicit model retraining or gradient updates, studies indicate that this mechanism often fails to effectively utilize the labeled samples included in the context [2][1]. Consequently, in-context learning can perform even worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and is characterized by high variance [3]. This instability is further exacerbated by the sensitivity of ICL performance to specific settings, including the prompt template, the selection and order of demonstration examples, and other factors [1]. For instance, despite improvements brought by Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, ICL remains greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars [4].

The relationship between the number of demonstrations and model performance presents a significant empirical challenge, as enhancing the scalability and efficiency of ICL with more demonstrations remains an open problem [1]. Although ICL can be regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, the ability to rapidly adapt to new tasks and provide human-like responses does not guarantee robustness against overfitting-like behaviors in the context of noisy or poorly selected data [1][5]. Research into noisy label learning provides relevant empirical parallels to these overfitting behaviors, showing that models can suffer from confirmation bias where noisy labels are incorrectly selected as clean, leading to damaged accuracy [6]. In such scenarios, quick convergence to select clean subsets combined with fast overfitting of noisy labels creates an inevitable bias that degrades performance [6].

Comparisons across different learning paradigms and model scales highlight the fragility of ICL compared to other optimization techniques. For example, mixup regularization with a large alpha parameter outperforms dropout on both best and last epoch test errors while remaining resistant to noisy labels, suggesting that standard ICL lacks similar robustness mechanisms [7]. In contrast, ICL’s reliance on input cueing for examples or related knowledge makes it vulnerable to the specific configuration of the prompt rather than the inherent quality of the data distribution [2]. Empirical studies in other domains, such as deep feedforward neural networks for predicting breast cancer metastasis, demonstrate that overfitting tends to negatively correlate with hyperparameters like learning rate, decay, and batch size, indicating that generalization is weakened when models fit too closely to specific training conditions [8]. Similarly, in the context of federated learning, large-scale empirical studies investigating quality from multiple angles of attacks and faults reveal that SOTA techniques face significant quality challenges, mirroring the sensitivity of ICL to environmental and data perturbations [9].

Specific empirical findings on noisy label learning further illustrate the mechanisms of overfitting that parallel ICL's sensitivity to exemplar quality. Methods like Asymmetric Co-teaching (AsyCo) improve over state-of-the-art methods on synthetic and real-world noisy-label datasets by addressing the issue of wrong selection of noisy label samples [6]. However, the underlying problem of overfitting to noisy labels remains a critical factor in model degradation [6]. Furthermore, frameworks like Knockoffs-SPR validate theoretical results through experimental results on benchmark and real-world noisy datasets, demonstrating the effectiveness of clean sample selection in mitigating the negative impacts of label noise [10]. These findings collectively suggest that the "overfitting" observed in ICL is closely tied to the model's inability to generalize from the specific, often noisy or suboptimal, set of in-context demonstrations provided [3][6].

sections.title: Mitigation Strategies and Robustness
sections.text:
Mitigating the overfitting and high variance observed in in-context learning (ICL) involves several strategies, including prompt optimization, ensemble techniques, and careful demonstration selection, though the effectiveness of these methods is often limited by the inherent sensitivity of ICL to exemplar choice [1]. ICL is characterized by a high variance and can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks, indicating a susceptibility to overfitting specific context configurations [1]. This sensitivity is further highlighted by the fact that ICL is greatly sensitive to the selection of exemplars, even when using advanced techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting [2]. Consequently, overcoming strong prior biases and ensuring the model gives equal weight to all contextual information remain significant challenges in mitigating this overfitting behavior [3].

Prompt optimization serves as a primary mitigation strategy, with black-box tuning frameworks proposed to optimize continuous prompts via derivative-free optimization [1]. To address the intractability of optimizing in the original high-dimensional prompt space, methods such as black-box tuning perform optimization in a randomly generated subspace, leveraging the low intrinsic dimensionality of large pre-trained models [1]. However, there is a noted gap between optimization objectives in prompt engineering and prompt compression, where the former tends to optimize shorter instructions while the latter deals with longer demonstrations [4]. Despite these optimization efforts, ICL may still suffer from knowledge conflict issues, and the effectiveness of unlearning or mitigation depends on the underlying in-context learning capability of the large language models used [5]. Furthermore, ICL is regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, linking its overfitting characteristics directly to prompt design [3].

Ensemble techniques and self-consistency methods offer another avenue for improving robustness against overfitting. Self-consistency has been shown to be robust to various sampling strategies and parameters, including variations in temperature sampling [6]. This robustness suggests that aggregating multiple reasoning paths can stabilize performance, although the specific application of ensemble methods like bootstrap aggregation (bagging) and cross-validation to reduce overfitting is primarily documented in other domains such as reservoir policy search [7]. In that context, calibration-validation strategies and ensemble aggregation methods were found to improve out-of-sample tradeoffs, providing a methodological parallel for mitigating overfitting in sequential decision-making [7]. Similarly, in portfolio optimization, high out-of-sample performance scores from hold-out techniques can be a "Fata Morgana" arising from vulnerability to overfitting, necessitating dedicated methodologies like combinatorially symmetric cross-validation [8].

Demonstration selection strategies are critical for mitigating overfitting, as they directly influence the ICL performance [3]. Most existing selection strategies operate at the instance level, but the corpus-level selection strategy is considered more important yet remains underexplored [3]. The inability of ICL to effectively utilize labeled samples included in the context further complicates mitigation efforts, as the model may not leverage the provided data to correct for overfitting tendencies [1]. Advanced techniques for ICL have been organized and discussed to address these limitations, but the fundamental issue of sensitivity to exemplar selection persists [2]. While ICL eliminates the need for explicit model retraining or gradient updates by using input cueing, this very mechanism makes the model prone to overfitting the specific context provided [9].

Data augmentation and feature selection techniques, while primarily developed for other domains, offer insights into mitigating overfitting through diverse training samples. For instance, CutMix regularization shows a steady decrease in validation error, indicating that diverse training samples reduce overfitting in classification tasks [10]. In the context of radio galaxy classification, wavelet analysis is used to pick key features and accentuate niche details, aiming to optimize models for high accuracy with fewer features to prevent overfitting caused by new features from powerful telescopes [11]. Additionally, Bayesian methods for tensor networks have been applied to reduce overfitting and improve the performance of normal tensor network models [12]. Although these methods are not directly applied to ICL in the provided evidence, they illustrate the broader principle that reducing feature complexity and increasing sample diversity can mitigate overfitting [11][12][10].

The robustness of ICL is also a key consideration in emerging applications, such as recommendation systems, where an ideal foundation model should demonstrate robust in-context learning capabilities [13]. However, the current state of ICL is hindered by its sensitivity and the challenges in ensuring equal weighting of contextual information, which limits the generalizability of mitigation strategies [3]. The use of few-shot prompts, such as those containing six QA pairs, is a standard practice, but the specific configuration of these prompts can lead to overfitting if not carefully optimized [14]. Ultimately, while prompt optimization, self-consistency, and demonstration selection provide tools to mitigate overfitting, the high variance and sensitivity of ICL to exemplars remain central challenges that require further exploration, particularly at the corpus level [2][1][3].

sections.title: Open Problems and Future Directions
sections.text:
The fundamental mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) is described as learning from analogy, a process that enables large language models to adapt to new tasks rapidly without explicit model retraining or gradient updates [1][2][3]. However, this capability is not without significant limitations, particularly regarding the effective utilization of labeled samples included in the context, which ICL may fail to leverage effectively [4]. Consequently, the generalization ability of ICL faces challenges due to the scarcity of examples, and the selection of exemplars remains a critical factor, as ICL is greatly sensitive to this choice [5][1]. This sensitivity is further evidenced by observations that ICL can perform worse than manual prompting on certain tasks and suffers from high variance [4].

A major open problem in the literature is determining which in-context reasoning examples constitute the most effective prompts, a question that remains unknown [6]. While standard few-shot prompting provides input–output pairs for test-time examples, this approach has not yet proved sufficient to achieve high performance on challenging tasks such as mathematical reasoning [6]. Similarly, research indicates that models fall short on tasks requiring multiple steps of reasoning, despite their remarkable few-shot performance across other varieties of tasks [7]. The reliance on ICL also introduces risks of knowledge conflict issues, where the effectiveness of unlearning methods depends on the specific ICL capability of the underlying large language models [8].

Theoretical understanding of ICL is currently limited, with explaining ICL through the lens of gradient descent identified as a reasonable, general, and promising direction for future research [1]. ICL is often regarded as a subclass of prompt tuning where demonstration examples are part of the prompt, yet the specific mechanisms driving its success or failure in few-shot settings lack comprehensive theoretical guarantees [1]. To address these gaps, designers are urged to thoroughly explore generalization limitations before integrating models into real-world applications, aiming to maximize transparency of model capabilities [9]. Furthermore, the questions of how emergent abilities arise and whether further scaling will enable additional capabilities remain important future research directions for the field [10].

In summary, while ICL facilitates swift adaptation and human-like responses, the field lacks better metrics to quantify generalization in few-shot settings and robust theoretical frameworks to explain its behavior [3][9]. The high variance and sensitivity to exemplar selection highlight the need for more rigorous analysis of how models process in-context information [5][4]. Future work must continue to address the unknowns regarding optimal prompt construction and the boundaries of ICL's applicability to complex reasoning tasks [6][7].

The results show that ICL performance matches that of direct training.

evidence.title: Rethinking the Role of Demonstrations: What Makes In-Context Learning Work?
evidence.snippet: Large language models (LMs) are able to in-context learn—perform a new task via inference alone by conditioning on a few input-label pairs (demonstrations) and making predictions for new inputs. However, there has been little understanding of how the model learns and which aspects of the demonstrations contribute to end task performance. In this paper, we show that ground truth demonstrations are in fact not required—randomly replacing labels in the demonstrations barely hurts performance on a range of classification and multi-choce tasks, consistently over 12 different models including GPT-3. Instead, we find that other aspects of the demonstrations are the key drivers of endtask performance, including the fact that they provide a few examples of (1) the label space, (2) the distribution of the input text, and (3) the overall format of the sequence. Together, our analysis provides a new way of understanding how and why in-context learning works, while opening up new questions about how much can be learned from large language models through inference alone.

evidence.title: Calibrate Before Use: Improving Few-Shot Performance of Language Models
evidence.snippet: GPT-3 can perform numerous tasks when provided a natural language prompt that contains a few training examples. We show that this type of few-shot learning can be unstable: the choice of prompt format, training examples, and even the order of the training examples can cause accuracy to vary from near chance to near state-of-the-art. We demonstrate that this instability arises from the bias of language models towards predicting certain answers, e.g., those that are placed near the end of the prompt or are common in the pre-training data. To mitigate this, we first estimate the model's bias towards each answer by asking for its prediction when given the training prompt and a content-free test input such as "N/A". We then fit calibration parameters that cause the prediction for this input to be uniform across answers. On a diverse set of tasks, this contextual calibration procedure substantially improves GPT-3 and GPT-2's average accuracy (up to 30.0% absolute) and reduces variance across different choices of the prompt.

evidence.snippet: GPT-3 has attracted lots of attention due to its superior performance across a wide range of NLP tasks, especially with its in-context learning abilities. Despite its success, we found that the empirical results of GPT-3 depend heavily on the choice of in-context examples. Intuitively, the examples selected with such a strategy may serve as more informative inputs to unleash GPT-3’s power of text generation. We evaluate the proposed approach on several natural language understanding and generation benchmarks, where the retrieval-based prompt selection approach consistently outperforms the random selection baseline. Moreover, it is observed that the sentence encoders fine-tuned on task-related datasets yield even more helpful retrieval results. Notably, significan

evidence.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
evidence.snippet: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. While typically task-agnostic in architecture, this method still requires task-specific fine-tuning datasets of thousands or tens of thousands of examples. By contrast, humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or from simple instructions - something which current NLP systems still largely struggle to do. Here we show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model, and test its performance in the few-shot setting. For all tasks, GPT-3 is applied without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model. GPT-3 achieves strong performance on many NLP datasets, including translation, question-answering, and cloze tasks, as well as several tas

evidence.title: A Discourse-Aware Attention Model for Abstractive Summarization of Long Documents
evidence.snippet: Neural abstractive summarization models have led to promising results in summarizing relatively short documents. We propose the first model for abstractive summarization of single, longer-form documents (e.g., research papers). Our approach consists of a new hierarchical encoder that models the discourse structure of a document, and an attentive discourse-aware decoder to generate the summary. Empirical results on two large-scale datasets of scientific papers show that our model significantly outperforms state-of-the-art models.

evidence.title: Learning To Retrieve Prompts for In-Context Learning
evidence.snippet: In-context learning is a recent paradigm in natural language understanding, where a large pre-trained language model (LM) observes a test instance and a few training examples as its input, and directly decodes the output without any update to its parameters. However, performance has been shown to strongly depend on the selected training examples (termed prompts). In this work, we propose an efficient method for retrieving prompts for in-context learning using annotated data and an LM. Given an input-output pair, we estimate the probability of the output given the input and a candidate training example as the prompt, and label training examples as positive or negative based on this probability. We then train an efficient dense retriever from this data, which is used to retrieve training examples as prompts at test time. We evaluate our approach on three sequence-to-sequence tasks where language utterances are mapped to meaning representations, and find that it substantially outperforms prior work and multiple baselines across the board.

evidence.title: Fantastically Ordered Prompts and Where to Find Them: Overcoming Few-Shot Prompt Order Sensitivity
evidence.snippet: When primed with only a handful of training samples, very large, pretrained language models such as GPT-3 have shown competitive results when compared to fully-supervised, fine-tuned, large, pretrained language models. We demonstrate that the order in which the samples are provided can make the difference between near state-of-the-art and random guess performance: essentially some permutations are “fantastic” and some not. We analyse this phenomenon in detail, establishing that: it is present across model sizes (even for the largest current models), it is not related to a specific subset of samples, and that a given good permutation for one model is not transferable to another. While one could use a development set to determine which permutations are performant, this would deviate from the true few-shot setting as it requires additional annotated data. Instead, we use the generative nature of language models to construct an artificial development set and based on entropy statistics of the candidate permutations on this set, we identify performant prompts. Our method yields a 13% relative improvement for GPT-family models across eleven different established text classification tasks

evidence.title: Co-teaching: Robust training of deep neural networks with extremely noisy labels
evidence.snippet: Deep learning with noisy labels is practically challenging, as the capacity of deep models is so high that they can totally memorize these noisy labels sooner or later during training. Nonetheless, recent studies on the memorization effects of deep neural networks show that they would first memorize training data of clean labels and then those of noisy labels. Therefore in this paper, we propose a new deep learning paradigm called Co-teaching for combating with noisy labels. Namely, we train two deep neural networks simultaneously, and let them teach each other given every mini-batch: firstly, each network feeds forward all data and selects some data of possibly clean labels; secondly, two networks communicate with each other what data in this mini-batch should be used for training; finally, each network back propagates the data selected by its peer network and updates itself. Empirical results on noisy versions of MNIST, CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 demonstrate that Co-teaching is much superior to the state-of-the-art methods in the robustness of trained deep models.

evidence.title: MentorNet: Learning Data-Driven Curriculum for Very Deep Neural Networks on Corrupted Labels
evidence.snippet: Recent deep networks are capable of memorizing the entire data even when the labels are completely random. To overcome the overfitting on corrupted labels, we propose a novel technique of learning another neural network, called MentorNet, to supervise the training of the base deep networks, namely, StudentNet. During training, MentorNet provides a curriculum (sample weighting scheme) for StudentNet to focus on the sample the label of which is probably correct. Unlike the existing curriculum that is usually predefined by human experts, MentorNet learns a data-driven curriculum dynamically with StudentNet. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach can significantly improve the generalization performance of deep networks trained on corrupted training data. Notably, to the best of our knowledge, we achieve the best-published result on WebVision, a large benchmark containing 2.2 million images of real-world noisy labels. The code are at this https URL

evidence.title: Decoupling "when to update" from "how to update"
evidence.snippet: Deep learning requires data. A useful approach to obtain data is to be creative and mine data from various sources, that were created for different purposes. Unfortunately, this approach often leads to noisy labels. In this paper, we propose a meta algorithm for tackling the noisy labels problem. The key idea is to decouple "when to update" from "how to update". We demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm by mining data for gender classification by combining the Labeled Faces in the Wild (LFW) face recognition dataset with a textual genderizing service, which leads to a noisy dataset. While our approach is very simple to implement, it leads to state-of-the-art results. We analyze some convergence properties of the proposed algorithm.

evidence.title: Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization
evidence.snippet:
Despite their massive size, successful deep artificial neural networks can exhibit a remarkably small difference between training and test performance. Conventional wisdom attributes small generalization error either to properties of the model family, or to the regularization techniques used during training. 
Through extensive systematic experiments, we show how these traditional approaches fail to explain why large neural networks generalize well in practice. Specifically, our experiments establish that state-of-the-art convolutional networks for image classification trained with stochastic gradient methods easily fit a random labeling of the training data. This phenomenon is qualitatively unaffected by explicit regularization, and occurs even if we replace the true images by completely unstructured random noise. We corroborate these experimental findings with a theoretical construction showing that simple depth two neural networks already have perfect finite sample expressivity as soon as the number of parameters exceeds the number of data points as it usually does in practice. 
We interpret our experimental findings by comparison with traditional models.

evidence.title: Making Deep Neural Networks Robust to Label Noise: A Loss Correction Approach
evidence.snippet: We present a theoretically grounded approach to train deep neural networks, including recurrent networks, subject to class-dependent label noise. We propose two procedures for loss correction that are agnostic to both application domain and network architecture. They simply amount to at most a matrix inversion and multiplication, provided that we know the probability of each class being corrupted into another. We further show how one can estimate these probabilities, adapting a recent technique for noise estimation to the multi-class setting, and thus providing an end-to-end framework. Extensive experiments on MNIST, IMDB, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and a large scale dataset of clothing images employing a diversity of architectures — stacking dense, convolutional, pooling, dropout, batch normalization, word embedding, LSTM and residual layers — demonstrate the noise robustness of our proposals. Incidentally, we also prove that, when ReLU is the only non-linearity, the loss curvature is immune to class-dependent label noise.

sections.title: Methodological Frameworks for AL in LLM Fine-Tuning
sections.text:
Active learning in the context of large language model (LLM) fine-tuning is defined as an iterative process where the model selectively identifies data requiring labeling to optimize system performance with minimal training data [1]. This approach is particularly crucial for fine-tuning large pre-trained foundation models, which typically require substantial labeled data for specific user scenarios [1]. The integration of active learning with transfer learning allows for a framework that starts directly with a pre-trained model to seek "worthy" samples for annotation, thereby reducing annotation costs in domains where labeling is tedious and costly [2]. In this paradigm, the role of humans shifts from mass annotators to targeted teachers during the fine-tuning process, balancing annotation cost against model performance [1].

A primary methodological challenge in LLM fine-tuning is the high-dimensional, non-convex nature of the optimization landscape, which complicates traditional uncertainty estimation. Fine-tuned LLMs often become overconfident under limited adaptation data, necessitating reliable uncertainty quantification to detect hallucinations and erroneous outputs [3]. To address this, uncertainty-aware fine-tuning approaches have been proposed to enhance the model's ability to provide reliable uncertainty estimates without compromising accuracy [4]. One specific framework, Functional-Level Uncertainty Quantification for Calibrated Fine-Tuning (UQ4CT), calibrates uncertainty over the functional space induced by prompt-dependent mixtures of LoRA experts [3]. UQ4CT implements this through a mixture-of-experts fine-tuning framework where a calibration loss aligns functional-level confidence with predictive correctness during training [3]. Alternatively, self-consistency methods can be used to provide an uncertainty estimate of the model in its generated solutions by sampling multiple reasoning paths [5].

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) techniques are central to adapting LLMs for active learning scenarios due to resource constraints. PEFT methods lower training and deployment costs, which is essential for effective adaptation under data scarcity in low-resource languages and specialized domains [6]. Techniques such as LoRA inject learnable modules into the encoder blocks of the transformer, allowing for efficient adaptation while preserving the base model's capabilities [7]. In the context of uncertainty quantification, PEFT-based methods are often post hoc, estimating uncertainty after fine-tuning rather than improving how adapters specialize to task-specific input-output relationships [3]. However, integrating active learning with PEFT allows for the selection of high-value data points that specifically target the model's areas of uncertainty or incomplete pre-trained knowledge [1].

The selection of data for active learning in LLMs often involves strategies that go beyond simple uncertainty sampling. A key open challenge is the design of bias-aware active learning methods that identify not only areas of model uncertainty but also regions where pre-trained knowledge is skewed or incomplete [1]. In recommendation systems, active learning strategies proactively select items to ask users to rate, a concept that translates to selecting specific prompts or queries for LLM fine-tuning [8]. For instance, in the context of instruction tuning, supervised fine-tuning is applied on demonstration datasets to align model behavior, with specific epochs and dataset sizes determining the extent of adaptation [9]. The use of small amounts of instruction fine-tuning has been found to improve performance on benchmarks such as MMLU, indicating that targeted data selection is more effective than indiscriminate scaling [10].

Multifidelity modeling strategies offer another perspective on efficient data utilization, where information fusion from lower-fidelity models can reduce the frequency of calls to high-fidelity models [11]. While primarily applied in nuclear fuel reliability estimation, this principle of leveraging cheaper approximations to guide expensive evaluations is analogous to using smaller proxy models or heuristics to select data for LLM fine-tuning [11]. Similarly, in the selection of pre-trained models for fine-tuning, resource-constrained tasks can be formulated as predicting fine-tuning performance using scaling laws [12]. The fine-tuning scaling curve includes a "pre-power phase" that existing scaling laws fail to capture, necessitating the concept of "pre-learned data size" to better fit experimental results [12]. This suggests that the initial phase of fine-tuning is distinct and may require different active learning strategies than the later convergence phase [12].

In specific application domains, active learning frameworks are adapted to handle the unique constraints of the task. In medical imaging, active learning is integrated with transfer learning to gradually enhance the fine-tuned CNN via continual fine-tuning, starting with a pre-trained model to seek worthy samples [2]. For LLMs applied to mechanics problems, frameworks like MeLM utilize autoregressive attention models to represent large multi-particle systems, where interaction potentials are discovered through graph-forming self-attention mechanisms [13]. While not explicitly an active learning method, the ability to incorporate diverse materials and scales highlights the flexibility required in fine-tuning strategies for complex, non-convex problems [13]. In software engineering, LLM-based agents are used for perception, planning, decision-making, and action, creating production value in fields like bridge operation and maintenance [14][15].

The evaluation of active learning strategies in LLMs often relies on specific benchmarks and metrics. For example, in closed-book question answering, parameter-efficient fine-tuning techniques are used to train models on small amounts of data to reduce hallucinations [16]. The performance of such models can be evaluated using metrics like Expected Calibration Error, which UQ4CT aims to reduce across multiple-choice benchmarks and open-ended generative QA tasks [3]. In the context of code generation, LLMs are used to generate source code from natural language descriptions, a task that benefits from systematic reviews of cutting-edge progress [17]. The integration of retrieval mechanisms, such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), enhances the quality of augmented generations in dialogues, addressing gaps in evaluating LLMs' ability to leverage retrieval for precise responses [18].

Despite the advancements, there are notable limitations and open problems in the methodological frameworks for active learning in LLM fine-tuning. The shift in the human role to that of a targeted teacher requires new methods for data curation that are bias-aware and capable of identifying skewed pre-trained knowledge [1]. Furthermore, the non-identically distributed nature of data and label scarcity in real-world scenarios, such as in federated learning for medical imaging, pose obstacles to generalization [19]. In federated settings, task-agnostic and generalization problems on unseen tasks are addressed by adapting self-supervised frameworks, which may inform how active learning is applied in distributed LLM fine-tuning [19]. The challenge of selecting the most appropriate pre-trained model amidst a sea of options remains, as fine-tuning all models is unrealistic given constrained resources [12].

In summary, the methodological frameworks for active learning in LLM fine-tuning are evolving to address the specific challenges of high-dimensional, non-convex optimization landscapes. Strategies such as uncertainty-aware fine-tuning, parameter-efficient adaptation, and bias-aware data selection are critical for optimizing performance with minimal labeled data [1][4][3][1]. The integration of active learning with transfer learning and PEFT techniques allows for efficient adaptation in data-scarce scenarios, while multifidelity modeling and scaling laws provide theoretical underpinnings for resource-constrained selection tasks [2][6][11][12]. Future research must focus on designing methods that not only identify model uncertainty but also address the inherent biases and incompleteness of pre-trained knowledge [1].

sections.title: Empirical Performance and Data Efficiency Gains
sections.text:
Active learning is defined as an iterative process where a model selectively identifies data requiring labeling to optimize system performance with minimal training data, a strategy particularly crucial for fine-tuning large pre-trained foundation models that typically require substantial labeled data for specific user scenarios [1]. The core objective of this approach is to maximize a model’s performance while annotating as little training data as possible [2]. By prioritizing samples with the most uncertainty, active learning improves labeling efficiency, although it remains limited by the necessity of human labor, which often restricts the amount of ground truth data that can be collected [3]. In the context of large language models (LLMs), fine-tuning with limited data poses a practical challenge in low-resource languages, specialized domains, and constrained deployment settings, necessitating focused and efficient fine-tuning techniques to achieve effective adaptation under data scarcity [4].

Empirical studies indicate that active learning strategies can significantly reduce annotation efforts compared to passive baselines. For instance, in the domain of coreference resolution, active learning mitigates the problem of models not transferring to new, low-resource domains by sampling a small subset of data for annotators to label [5]. Similarly, in the context of action spotting in association football videos, an active learning framework that selects the most informative video samples drastically reduces annotation effort and accelerates the training of models to reach the highest accuracy at a faster pace [6]. In medical applications, a committee-based active learning method has been suggested to reduce the number of clinical experiments required to optimize stimulation variables by exploring the configuration space more efficiently [7]. Furthermore, in the specific case of active learning under malicious mislabeling and poisoning attacks, a proposed active learning method achieved a desired accuracy of 89% using only one-third of the dataset on average, whereas the baseline active learning method based on random sampling performed poorly with about 50% accuracy [8].

However, the generalizability of these gains is not uniform across all models and tasks. While active learning has shown promise in retrospective evaluations, practical obstacles exist, and the benefits of current approaches do not generalize reliably across different models and tasks [9]. This lack of generalization is problematic because in practice, researchers do not have the opportunity to explore and compare alternative active learning strategies [9]. A study on pre-trained language models (PLMs) found that while task adaptation improves active learning, standard short fine-tuning in active learning does not provide improvements over random sampling [10]. Additionally, in realistic annotation scenarios where out-of-distribution data is extensive, advanced active learning algorithms have been found to be "lame," leading to the development of novel frameworks like Bamboo to build high-quality vision datasets with human-machine synergy [11].

Recent work has focused on enhancing the label efficiency of active fine-tuning for PLMs by leveraging unlabeled data. AcTune, a framework for semi-supervised active learning, switches between data annotation and model self-training based on uncertainty, selecting high-uncertainty unlabeled samples for active annotation and low-uncertainty ones for model self-training [12]. This framework includes a region-aware sampling strategy to reduce redundancy when actively querying for annotations and a momentum-based memory bank to suppress label noise [12]. Another approach, Smooth Sailing, addresses practical challenges in active learning for PLMs by leveraging representation smoothness analysis to improve effectiveness [10]. This method develops an early stopping technique that does not require a validation set, which is often unavailable in realistic active learning settings, and observes significant improvements across multiple datasets and active learning methods [10].

In the specific domain of preference learning for LLMs, strategies to select worth-annotating response pairs have been studied to achieve cost-efficient annotation. Research indicates that annotating response pairs with small implicit reward margins is generally better than selecting those with large margins or using random selection, under both single- and multi-iteration scenarios [13]. Furthermore, empirical results suggest that allocating more annotation budgets in the earlier iterations rather than later across multiple iterations yields better performance [13]. In the context of data filtering for LLM pretraining, the SIEVE approach uses active learning to fine-tune lightweight text classification models in the background with a small number of calls to GPT-4o, allowing it to perform up to 500 filtering operations for the cost of one GPT-4o filtering call [14].

Despite these advancements, the integration of active learning with other efficiency techniques presents complex trade-offs. For example, while Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) reduces trainable parameters, it still requires expensive activation memory, and methods like LoRA-FA aim to reduce this memory without performance degradation [15]. In federated learning settings, where privacy concerns arise during data collection, active learning must contend with challenges such as model convergence issues due to heterogeneous data and high communication costs [16]. Moreover, the inherent exploratory nature of reinforcement learning paradigms demands significant samples to learn, and while pre-trained LLMs can enhance data generation or leverage prior knowledge to improve sample efficiency, directly employing pre-trained large-scale LLMs to generate actions still demands huge computational resources and data for fine-tuning [17].

The practical implementation of active learning also faces constraints related to data quality and annotation consistency. In the training of language models to follow instructions with human feedback, most comparisons are often labeled by only one contractor for cost reasons, and having examples labeled multiple times could help identify areas where contractors disagree [18]. Additionally, in the context of black-box tuning for language models as a service, certain sampling strategies, such as those using random embeddings sampled from a uniform distribution instead of normal distributions, may not perform well in specific scenarios [19]. The use of active learning in sequence labeling has also been explored through methods that aim to improve efficiency by expanding the queried data and synthesizing new sequences in each iteration [20].

In summary, while active learning offers significant potential for reducing the number of labeled examples required for fine-tuning LLMs, its effectiveness is contingent on the specific task, model architecture, and realistic annotation constraints. Techniques such as uncertainty sampling, representation smoothness analysis, and iterative preference selection have demonstrated improvements in label efficiency [12][13][10]. However, the benefits are not guaranteed across all domains, with some studies showing no improvement over random sampling in standard fine-tuning scenarios [10], and others highlighting the failure of advanced algorithms in the presence of extensive out-of-distribution data [11]. The field continues to evolve with methods that integrate unlabeled data, optimize annotation budgets across iterations, and address the practical obstacles of deployment and data quality [12][13][9].
