sections.title: Challenges in Uncertainty Estimation and Calibration
sections.text:
Active learning is defined as an iterative process where a model selectively identifies data requiring labeling to optimize system performance with minimal training data, a approach particularly crucial for fine-tuning large pre-trained foundation models that require substantial labeled data for specific user scenarios [1]. The core objective of this methodology is to maximize a model’s performance while annotating as little training data as possible [2]. In many active learning frameworks, the selection process simplifies to maximizing the add-one-in influence, where each unlabeled instance’s marginal influence must be estimated [2]. However, a key open challenge remains to design bias-aware active learning methods that identify not only areas of model uncertainty but also regions where pre-trained knowledge is skewed or incomplete [1].

The reliability of uncertainty metrics in Large Language Models (LLMs) is a significant concern, as BERT-based rankers have been found to be not robustly calibrated, whereas stochastic BERT-based rankers yield better calibration [3]. Uncertainty estimation is beneficial for risk-aware neural ranking, which takes into account the uncertainty when ranking documents, and for predicting unanswerable conversational responses [3]. To address calibration issues, self-consistency has been proposed as a method to provide an uncertainty estimate of the model in its generated solutions [4]. Beyond accuracy gains, self-consistency is useful for collecting rationales when performing reasoning tasks and for providing uncertainty estimates and improved calibration of language model outputs [4]. Additionally, Nucleus Sampling was proposed as a solution that captures the region of confidence of language models effectively [5].

Various approaches have been developed to detect hallucinations and estimate reliability in LLMs. InterrogateLLM is a sampling-based approach that attempts to reconstruct an original query given a possibly hallucinated LLM response and measures the similarity of the two queries [6]. The accuracy of such detection is dependent on the complexity of the LLM itself, as well as the training data of the proxy LLM [6]. A hybrid approach that merges verbalized uncertainty with self-contradiction detection outperforms the individual components alone on expected calibration error, which compares predicted confidence and actual model accuracy [6]. Lin et al. fine-tune the model with data pairs of a question and the empirical accuracy on the task that the question originates from in the calibration dataset, such that the model is expected to similarly output a probability of accuracy at test-time [6]. Another proposed LLM is able to self-estimate if it is able to answer directly or needs to request an external tool [7]. The MixAlign framework interacts with the user to get clarification when the LLM is uncertain about its mapping from the user query to the database [6].

Despite these advancements, theoretical and practical limitations persist. There is theoretical justification for why uncertainty calibration might be difficult to combine with Bayesian Optimization due to the small sample sizes commonly used [8]. In the context of model evaluation, even when a model has a reasonably high accuracy of 80%, developers may have difficulty understanding the failure modes of the model [9]. Error-analysis prompting (EAPrompt) with chain-of-thought reasoning and collaborative detection workflows route annotator attention to likely failure modes, lowering variance and cost [1]. In specific domains, such as physics-informed neural networks, an uncertainty-based adaptive weighting method is employed to balance the multiple learning tasks when training the model [10]. Similarly, in Bayesian deep learning pipelines for state of health estimation, uncertainty quantification cannot be addressed with only point estimation, necessitating uncertainty-aware model development [11].

Other calibration and alignment techniques have been applied to enhance LLM performance in specialized tasks. A novel approach incorporates rule-based alignment within the architecture of an open-source language model, Llama, to enhance its geometric reasoning capabilities by embedding explicit geometric rules into the model's neural network [12]. An adaptive difficulty calibration of Large Language Models using Reinforcement Learning introduces a dynamic difficulty adjustment mechanism that allows models to adapt to varying levels of task difficulty in real-time [13]. In recommender systems, Query-SeqRec includes LLM query embeddings as inputs to a transformer-based recommender [14], while dense retrievers produce a ranked list of documents by evaluating the similarity between encoder-only LLM document embeddings and the query embedding [14]. The SCA module in form understanding functions as a two-way cross-attention mechanism that facilitates interaction between different modes, where one set of model features serves as the query, and another set serves as both the key and value [15].

sections.title: Computational Costs and Practical Feasibility
sections.text:
Active learning is fundamentally an iterative process where a model selectively identifies data requiring labeling to optimize system performance with minimal training data [1]. This approach is particularly crucial for fine-tuning large pre-trained foundation models, which otherwise require substantial labeled data for specific user scenarios [1]. The core objective of active learning is to maximize a model’s performance while annotating as little training data as possible [2]. In this context, the learning algorithm selectively queries the most informative data points for labeling [3]. For instance, in recommender systems, active learning strategies proactively select items and ask users to rate these [4]. However, the differences between various active learning algorithms in such settings are often small [4].

The computational burden of fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) is significant, as directly employing pre-trained large-scale LLMs to generate actions demands huge computational resources and huge data for fine-tuning in specific tasks [5]. Evaluating LLMs also incurs a high cost in computational resources [6]. The integration of LLMs into learning processes, such as reinforcement learning, introduces complexities in terms of computational overhead and inference times, which slow down the learning process [5]. For example, in the training of language models to follow instructions with human feedback, the PPO training phase required specific computational resources, with a training time of 6.01 units and a validation time of 27.96 units for the reward model [7]. The PPO training process involved specific hyperparameters, including 31,144 training steps and 166 validation steps [7]. Additionally, supervised fine-tuning for 2 epochs on the demonstration dataset is a standard component of this pipeline [7].

The iterative nature of active learning introduces additional computational costs associated with model retraining and inference. Active learning often simplifies to maximizing the add-one-in influence, where each unlabeled instance’s marginal influence must be estimated [2]. This estimation process can be computationally intensive, and the amortization of the retraining cost induces an $O(np)$ storage complexity [2]. While active learning aims to reduce labeling costs, it may require additional labeled artificial data generated through techniques like adversarial retraining without increasing the labeling budget [8]. The goal of such methods is often to reduce computational overhead on resource-constrained devices [9]. However, even with optimizations, transformer-based architectures suffer from severe memory and computational overhead [10].

There is a lack of comprehensive cost-benefit analyses to guide practitioners in these scenarios. For example, in machine translation evaluation, there are no cost-benefit analyses that could be used to guide practitioners who plan to collect references [11]. Similarly, while taxonomies like TePIA provide frameworks to evaluate alternatives considering the cost-benefit of information attributes, specific applications to LLM active learning remain underexplored [12]. A key open challenge remains to design bias-aware active learning methods that identify not only areas of model uncertainty but also regions where pre-trained knowledge is skewed or incomplete [1]. Furthermore, zero-shot cost models can be used in a few-shot mode that improves their quality by retraining them with a small number of additional training queries on the unseen database [13]. Despite these tools, the trade-off between labeling cost savings and the increased computational overhead of iterative model retraining and inference remains a critical consideration for the practical feasibility of active learning in LLM fine-tuning [1][5].

sections.title: Limitations and Open Problems
sections.text:
The application of active learning to fine-tune large pre-trained foundation models is characterized by an iterative process where the model selectively identifies data requiring labeling to optimize performance with minimal training data [1]. This approach is considered crucial for scenarios where substantial labeled data is required for specific user applications [1]. However, the literature highlights that directly employing pre-trained large-scale LLMs to generate actions or for fine-tuning in specific tasks demands huge computational resources and large amounts of data [2]. Consequently, scalability remains a significant challenge, particularly when evaluating modern modeling approaches on large datasets [3]. While active learning seeks to maximize model performance while annotating as little training data as possible [4], the scalability and efficiency of related techniques, such as in-context learning with more demonstrations, remain significant challenges [5]. Furthermore, ML-driven approaches in this domain face challenges including lengthy data collection processes and limited scalability [6].

A major gap in the current literature is the lack of standardized benchmarks and the difficulty in generalizing evaluation samples. Robust and effective adversarial testing for large language models is still an open problem space with varied results due to the challenges of generalization in evaluation samples [7]. This issue is compounded by the fact that differences between active learning algorithms are often small, making it difficult to distinguish superior strategies without rigorous, standardized comparisons [8]. For instance, in the context of recommender systems, active learning strategies proactively select items and ask users to rate these, yet the comparative advantages of different algorithms remain subtle [8]. The absence of clear, large-scale benchmarks is further evidenced by the fact that scalability is an issue when evaluating modern modeling approaches on standard datasets like CommonsenseQA [3].

The sensitivity of active learning outcomes to the quality and biases of the initial pre-trained model represents another critical limitation. Since the LLM acts as an instructor to provide expert actions, the bias and limitations inherent in the pre-trained model are also inherited by the agent [2]. A key open challenge remains to design bias-aware active learning methods that identify not only areas of model uncertainty but also regions where pre-trained knowledge is skewed or incomplete [1]. Current methods often focus on selecting the most informative data points for labeling [9], but this does not necessarily address the structural biases present in the foundation model. For example, while integrating structural fairness mechanisms and active learning frameworks into models like Mistral Large aims to promote equitable outcomes, the underlying pre-trained knowledge may still contain skewed regions that standard uncertainty-based selection fails to correct [10][1].

Methodological variations in active learning, such as the choice between batch and sequential strategies, present additional complexities. Active learning involves an iterative process where a model selectively identifies data requiring labeling [1], and strategies may proactively select items for user rating [8]. However, the literature notes that differences between these active learning algorithms are small [8], suggesting that the choice of strategy may be less impactful than the quality of the initial model or the specific task constraints. In the domain of reinforcement learning, directly employing pre-trained large-scale LLMs to generate actions demands huge computational resources [2], which limits the feasibility of extensive active learning loops. Additionally, the use of synthetic reinforcement learning feedback, while offering a scalable approach to bypass human evaluators, still faces challenges in aligning outputs with user needs and ethical standards [11].

Emergent abilities and scaling behaviors further complicate the assessment of active learning efficacy. Other categories with a large fraction of flat scaling curve tasks are non-language, repeated interaction, context length, computer code, and multi-step, all targeting weaknesses of large language models [12]. This implies that simply increasing the amount of data selected by active learning may not yield proportional improvements in these specific areas. The integration of explanations in an Active Learning framework, known as eXplanatory Active Learning (XAL), has been surveyed as a method to improve model understanding, but its impact on mitigating the aforementioned scaling and bias issues remains an area of ongoing investigation [13]. Ultimately, while active learning is designed to optimize system performance with minimal training data [1], the interplay between computational resource demands [2], inherited model biases [2], and the lack of robust generalization in evaluation [7] constitutes the primary open problems in the field.

evidence.snippet: We introduce a new language representation model called BERT, which stands for Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers. Unlike recent language representation models (Peters et al., 2018a; Radford et al., 2018), BERT is designed to pre-train deep bidirectional representations from unlabeled text by jointly conditioning on both left and right context in all layers. As a result, the pre-trained BERT model can be fine-tuned with just one additional output layer to create state-of-the-art models for a wide range of tasks, such as question answering and language inference, without substantial task-specific architecture modifications. BERT is conceptually simple and empirically powerful. It obtains new state-of-the-art results on eleven natural language processing tasks, including pushing the GLUE score to 80.5 (7.7 point absolute improvement), MultiNLI accuracy to 86.7% (4.6% absolute improvement), SQuAD v1.1 question answering Test F1 to 93.2 (1.5 point absolute improvement) and SQuAD v2.0 Test F1 to 83.1 (5.1 point absolute improvement).

evidence.title: Attention is All you Need
evidence.snippet: The dominant sequence transduction models are based on complex recurrent or convolutional neural networks in an encoder-decoder configuration. The best performing models also connect the encoder and decoder through an attention mechanism. We propose a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely. Experiments on two machine translation tasks show these models to be superior in quality while being more parallelizable and requiring significantly less time to train. Our model achieves 28.4 BLEU on the WMT 2014 English-to-German translation task, improving over the existing best results, including ensembles by over 2 BLEU. On the WMT 2014 English-to-French translation task, our model establishes a new single-model state-of-the-art BLEU score of 41.8 after training for 3.5 days on eight GPUs, a small fraction of the training costs of the best models from the literature. sections.title: Theoretical Rationale: Representation Learning vs. Lookup
sections.text:
The Transformer architecture fundamentally distinguishes itself from earlier recurrent models by relying solely on attention networks, where input embeddings are augmented with sinusoid-style position encodings rather than being static features [1]. In this design, word embeddings are defined as numerical vector representations that allow for mathematical operations, such as distance computations and additions, to be applied to words [2]. Unlike CBOW, which employs static word representations, and RNNs, which acquire contextualized word representations, the Transformer treats these embeddings as learnable parameters within a unified framework [3]. This approach aligns with the broader deep learning paradigm where representations are formally defined as functions whose semantics are encoded in the network's operations, optimized via backpropagation [4].

The decision to initialize embeddings randomly rather than using pre-trained fixed vectors is rooted in the need for joint optimization with the rest of the model. First-generation pre-trained language models (PLMs) such as Skip-Gram and GloVe aimed to obtain good word embeddings for downstream tasks directly, treating them as static features [5]. In contrast, modern architectures like BERT and GPT learn word embeddings via next-word prediction or bidirectional context, integrating the embedding layer into the end-to-end training process [3][6]. For instance, in BERT, the purpose of the embedding layer is explicitly to bias the representation towards the actual observed word, a goal achieved through joint training rather than fixed lookup [6]. This contrasts with approaches in tasks like CommonsenseQA, where pre-trained word embeddings such as 300d GloVe or Numberbatch are kept fixed at training time, limiting their adaptability to the specific model's internal representations [7].

Joint optimization allows the model to discover task-specific representations that static embeddings cannot provide. In recommendation systems, training-derived embeddings of sparse features are essential, and techniques like Multi-Layer Embeddings Training (MLET) demonstrate that training embeddings via factorization can produce superior results compared to single-layer embeddings, even when the search space is not larger [8]. Similarly, in sponsored search, deeply supervised architectures jointly learn the semantic embeddings of a query and an ad along with their corresponding click-through-rate (CTR), improving performance over models that rely on fixed similarity metrics [9]. This joint learning capability is critical because static embeddings, such as those from FastText or IndicNLP used in Marathi text classification, may not capture the specific contextual nuances required by a deep neural network trained from scratch [10].

The theoretical basis for this approach is further supported by the ability of transformers to implement learning algorithms implicitly. Neural sequence models, especially transformers, exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning by constructing new predictors from sequences of labeled examples without further parameter updates [11]. Research has proven by construction that transformers can implement learning algorithms for linear models based on gradient descent and closed-form ridge regression, suggesting that the internal representations are dynamically adjusted to encode these algorithms [11]. This dynamic adjustment is facilitated by the architecture's reliance on residual connections and layer normalization to stabilize optimization, ensuring that the gradients flow effectively to update the embedding parameters [1].

Furthermore, the flexibility of the Transformer architecture allows for various modifications that support this learnable embedding paradigm. For example, a modified transformer integrated with convolutional layers instead of fully connected layers has been proposed, indicating that the core attention mechanism can be adapted while maintaining the learnable nature of the inputs [12]. In visual transformers, positional encoding with dimension $d_{model}$ is added to the original input embedding to allow the final input vector of the word to be obtained, reinforcing the idea that the input representation is a composite of learned and positional components [13]. The feed-forward networks in each block, consisting of dense layers with specific output dimensionalities and ReLU nonlinearities, further process these learned representations, highlighting the depth of the optimization process [14].

The use of pre-trained embeddings from existing models is often suboptimal for new pre-training tasks due to domain and dimensionality mismatches. In medical image segmentation, leveraging pre-trained Transformers from 2D natural images for 3D medical imaging is challenging due to the difference in dimensionality, and existing solutions often fail to effectively leverage these pre-trained weights [15]. Similarly, in the context of building language-specific LLMs, adapting monolingual or multilingual models shows that the initial performance of an LLM does not always correlate with the final performance after adaptation, suggesting that starting with a fresh, randomly initialized embedding layer may allow for better alignment with the target language's specific characteristics [16]. This is consistent with findings in cross-lingual phonetic representation learning, where polyglot models trained with shared representations of symbols generalize better to held-out data than monolingual models, implying that the learning process itself, rather than the initial state, drives the quality of the representation [17].

While some approaches utilize frozen pre-trained components, the general trend in large-scale pre-training favors end-to-end learnability. For instance, in reinforcement learning frameworks, frozen pre-trained Language Transformers are used to extract history representation and compression, but this is a specific application of a frozen component rather than the standard pre-training paradigm [18]. In contrast, the standard Transformer pre-training process involves optimizing all parameters, including embeddings, to minimize the prediction loss. This is evident in the architecture of the decoder, which includes an additional self-attention layer that attends to the outputs of the encoder, all of which are trained jointly [2]. The sharing of position embedding parameters across all layers in models like T5 further illustrates the efficiency and interdependence of these learned components [14].

The distinction between lookup-based and representation-learning-based approaches is also evident in how models handle discrete data. Mapping sequences of discrete data to a point in a continuous space makes it difficult to retrieve those sequences via random sampling, a challenge addressed by methods like AriEL that construct volumes in a continuous space [19]. However, the Transformer's approach of learning embeddings as part of the model's parameters allows it to navigate this continuous space effectively through optimization. This is supported by the fact that neural language embedding models can be effectively trained to map dictionary definitions to lexical representations, performing as well as or better than existing commercial systems, which relies on the model's ability to learn these mappings from scratch [20].

In summary, the random initialization of the Transformer embedding layer is a deliberate choice to enable the model to learn task-specific, contextualized representations through joint optimization. This approach contrasts with the use of fixed, pre-trained embeddings, which may not align with the specific optimization landscape of the new model [7][5]. The theoretical underpinnings of this choice are supported by the transformer's ability to implement learning algorithms implicitly [11], the necessity of stabilizing optimization through architectural components like layer normalization [1], and the empirical success of training-derived embeddings in various domains such as recommendation systems [8] and search [9]. By treating embeddings as learnable parameters, the Transformer ensures that the input representation is co-adapted with the attention and feed-forward mechanisms, leading to more robust and generalizable models [4][1].

sections.title: Empirical Evidence: Impact on Convergence and Performance
sections.text:
Experimental investigations into the initialization of transformer embedding layers reveal that while pre-trained vectors can accelerate convergence, they do not necessarily yield superior final performance compared to random initialization in many standard settings. For instance, research on large language models indicates that initializing with other natural language models yields no noticeable gain compared to training from scratch, except for accelerating convergence [1]. This finding aligns with observations in black-box tuning scenarios, where both random projections and pre-trained prompt embeddings can achieve considerable cross-entropy loss on tasks such as SST-2 and AG’s News, though faster convergence is specifically obtained when using uniform distribution random initialization rather than pre-trained vectors [2].

In the context of low-resource or in-domain language modeling, the utility of pre-trained embeddings becomes more pronounced, particularly for handling rare vocabulary. Studies show that initializing and freezing input embeddings using in-domain data can improve language model performance by providing a useful representation of rare words, a pattern that holds across several different domains [3]. However, this approach comes with specific architectural implications; the standard convention of tying input and output embeddings does not improve perplexity when initializing with embeddings trained on in-domain data [3]. Conversely, in general-purpose pre-training frameworks like BERT, the embedding layer is typically initialized randomly or learned from scratch to support the specific objectives of the pre-training task, such as masked language modeling, which forces the model to keep a distributional contextual representation of every input token [4][5]. The BERT paper notes that the purpose of certain initialization or masking strategies is to bias the representation towards the actual observed word, ensuring the encoder does not trivially predict targets [4].

Comparative analyses of different embedding types further highlight the dominance of contextual, learned embeddings over static pre-trained vectors like GloVe or Word2Vec. For example, in polarity and subjectivity detection, models using pre-trained BERT embeddings work better than those based on GloVe embeddings [6]. This superiority is attributed to the fact that second-generation pre-trained language models focus on learning word embeddings in dynamic contexts, whereas static embeddings may suffer from issues such as static token embedding bias [7][8]. Even when static embeddings are used, their dimensionality and specific training data (e.g., 100 dimensions for word embeddings in cross-domain recommendation) may limit their effectiveness compared to the high-dimensional, context-aware representations learned during transformer pre-training [9].

The impact of initialization on convergence and final accuracy is also evident in specialized domains and multi-stage pre-training. In abstractive summarization, multi-stage pretraining with full-network initialization demonstrates improvements of 1.05 ROUGE-L points on the Gigaword benchmark and 1.78 ROUGE-L points on the CNN/DailyMail benchmark compared to a randomly-initialized baseline [10]. Similarly, in multilingual settings, initializing models using existing multilingual models can lead to state-of-the-art results for some downstream tasks [11]. However, the choice of random initialization distribution itself can affect training dynamics; in black-box tuning, sampling from a uniform distribution for random embeddings leads to faster convergence compared to normal distributions [2]. Furthermore, the random initialization choice can significantly impact the final output, as seen in image generation tasks where it affects reconstruction quality [12].

Recent work has also explored the potential of randomly weighted transformers, demonstrating that hidden subnetworks within one-layer randomly weighted neural networks can achieve impressive performance on machine translation tasks without modifying weight initializations [13]. In these experiments, using a fixed pre-trained embedding layer allowed subnetworks to match 98%/92% of the performance of a trained Transformer small/base on IWSLT14/WMT14, suggesting that the interaction between random weights and fixed embeddings can be highly effective [13]. Additionally, in continual learning contexts, methods like ExSSNeT propose exclusive subnetwork weight training to avoid conflicting updates, contrasting with approaches that use randomly initialized, fixed base networks which may suffer from sub-optimal performance due to restricted representational power [14].

Finally, the relationship between scale, initialization, and performance is complex. Emergent abilities in large language models, such as few-shot prompting, are characterized by random performance until a certain scale is reached, after which performance increases significantly [15]. Even when error rates are close to random, cross-entropy loss consistently improves for models trained with more compute, indicating that the training process itself drives performance gains regardless of initial embedding quality [15]. In specific application domains like legal NLP, fine-tuned transformer baselines show promising results, performing well above random on most questions, underscoring the robustness of transformer architectures even when starting from standard initialization procedures [16].

sections.title: Architectural Compatibility and Dimensionality Mismatch
sections.text:
The dimensionality of word embeddings in legacy models often differs significantly from the hidden state dimensions required by modern transformer architectures, creating a structural incompatibility for direct initialization. For instance, the Neural Machine Translation model by Bahdanau et al. utilized a word embedding dimensionality of 620 [1], whereas the Transformer architecture employed in T5 specifies that all other sub-layers and embeddings have a dimensionality of $d_{\text{model}} = 768$ [2]. Similarly, visual transformer architectures may utilize hidden layer dimensionalities such as $d_h = 2048$ [3], further highlighting the variance in required vector sizes across different model families. This discrepancy means that static embeddings from previous systems cannot be directly mapped to the input layer of a transformer without dimensionality adjustment, as the physical quantities and vector spaces are not inherently aligned [4].

Beyond simple size differences, there is a fundamental semantic misalignment between static vector spaces and the contextualized spaces learned by transformers. CBOW employs static word representations, while RNNs and subsequent transformer-based models acquire contextualized word representations [5]. Second-generation pre-trained language models, such as BERT and GPT, focus on learning word embeddings in dynamic contexts rather than relying on fixed static vectors [6]. Static embeddings allow for mathematical operations such as distance computations, additions, and subtractions [7], but these operations do not capture the dynamic, context-dependent nature of transformer outputs. Contextualized models tend to find phonological and lexical analogies, while static models are better at finding relations among geographical proper names, indicating that the two types of embeddings occupy different semantic geometries [8]. Consequently, initializing a transformer with static embeddings would introduce a mismatch between the pre-trained static space and the dynamic contextual space the model is designed to learn [6].

The lack of alignment between static and contextualized embeddings is further evidenced by the need for specific techniques to bridge these spaces. Zheng et al. proposed a spring network to use contextual representations to pull static word embeddings to better positions in a unified space for easy alignment [9]. This necessity for explicit alignment mechanisms underscores that static and contextualized embeddings do not naturally share the same coordinate system. Furthermore, the addition of position vectors to token vectors in transformers is often criticized because token vectors and position vectors are different physical quantities that cannot be directly combined through addition without careful consideration of dimensional reduction and physical meaning [4]. This principle extends to the initialization of the embedding layer itself; if the initial static embeddings do not share the same physical and semantic basis as the transformer's internal representations, their direct use may be as problematic as the naive addition of position encodings [4].

Research into the interpretability and structure of these embeddings reveals further disparities. SensePOLAR extends the POLAR framework to enable word-sense aware interpretability for pre-trained contextual word embeddings, addressing limitations in standard approaches [10]. The resulting interpretable word embeddings achieve performance comparable to original contextual word embeddings across benchmarks like GLUE and SQuAD [10]. However, the process of extracting or aligning these embeddings often requires complex transformations. For example, in few-shot learning, embedding alignment and standardization are used to maximize inter-class dissimilarity, highlighting the complexity of adapting embedding spaces for new tasks [11]. Similarly, in knowledge-enhanced pre-trained language models, KEPLER adds a knowledge embedding pre-training task that shares a Transformer Encoder with the Masked Language Modeling task, obtaining text-enhanced knowledge embeddings simultaneously [6]. This suggests that integrating external or pre-existing embeddings into a transformer framework requires joint training or specific architectural modifications to ensure compatibility, rather than simple random or static initialization.

The challenge of aligning different embedding spaces is also evident in cross-modal and cross-domain applications. In cross-modal alignment, vulnerabilities related to compositional adversarial attacks within the aligned embedding space have been identified [12]. In cross-domain recommendation, researchers have identified drawbacks related to root- and distance-based alignment, which are problematic in preserving tree-like structures within hyperbolic spaces [13]. These findings indicate that aligning embeddings from different sources or domains is a non-trivial task that often requires specific geometric considerations, such as hyperbolic space embedding [13]. Therefore, the direct initialization of a transformer's embedding layer with pre-trained static embeddings is technically constrained by both dimensional mismatches and the lack of inherent semantic alignment between static and contextualized vector spaces [2][1][8].

sections.title: Training Dynamics and Optimization Stability
sections.text:
The stability of optimization in Transformer architectures is fundamentally supported by architectural choices such as residual connections and layer normalization, which are applied in each sub-layer to stabilize the training process [1]. These mechanisms are critical because the model can still be unstable if the learning rate is too big, and the first layer is unlikely to be the essential reason for such instability [2]. In the context of gradient-based optimization, which is a local optimization technique, it is indispensable to restart the optimization several times with random initialization of parameters, keeping only the best optimization result, due to the non-linear nature of the loss function [3]. This reliance on random initialization is further supported by findings in structured learning, where a random initialization of link parameters compares similarly to having good prior knowledge of those parameters [3].

The choice of initialization significantly impacts the final outcome of the model; for instance, in face generation, the random initialization choice can significantly impact the final reconstruction image [4]. Similarly, in optimization-based task and motion planning, optimization results can be dependent on the initialization of decision variables, which might cause the planner to get stuck in local optima [5]. To mitigate these issues, providing good weight initialization is considered important since the training process involves iterative optimization [6]. In specific applications like nurse rostering, semi-random initialization is applied to avoid violation of hard constraints from the beginning, thereby improving the construction solution phase [7].

Regarding the specific handling of embeddings, pre-trained word embeddings such as 300d GloVe and 300d Numberbatch ConceptNet node embeddings are often kept fixed at training time in certain tasks [8]. However, in the Transformer architecture, the model relies solely on attention networks with additional sinusoid-style position encoding added to the input embedding [1]. A positional encoding with dimension $d_{model}$ is added to the original input embedding to allow the final input vector of the word to be obtained [2]. In the T5 model, for efficiency, position embedding parameters are shared across all layers, though within a given layer each attention head uses a different learned position embedding [9].

The flow of gradients and semantic convergence across layers is a key aspect of training dynamics. A mathematical analysis of semantic convergence in transformer-based language models establishes that there exists a monotonically increasing function that provides a lower bound on the rate at which the average cosine similarity between token embeddings at consecutive layers and the final layer increases [10]. This indicates that semantic alignment of token representations consistently increases through the network, exhibiting a pattern of progressive refinement [10]. In other contexts, such as entity alignment decoding, methods like TFP innovatively channel gradient flow through three views: entity-to-entity, entity-to-relation, and relation-to-entity [11].

The structure of the Transformer encoder and decoder further influences these dynamics. The encoder consists of a number of blocks, each one consisting of two subcomponents: a self-attention layer followed by a feed-forward network, with a residual skip connection adding the output of each subcomponent to its input [12]. The decoder is similar in structure but includes an additional self-attention layer that attends to the outputs of the encoder [12]. The feed-forward networks in each block consist of a dense layer with an output dimensionality of $d_{ff} = 3072$ followed by a ReLU nonlinearity and another dense layer [9]. In contrast to RNNs, whose hidden state must be computed sequentially, the Transformer is more efficient because the output of the self-attention layer and the fully connected layers can be computed in parallel and easily accelerated [2].

While random initialization is standard, alternative approaches exist. For example, in Graph Convolutional Networks, random projection forest (rpForest) is used to initialize the GCN by assigning varying weights on edges indicating varying importance, which enhances learning compared to fixed $k$-nearest neighbor graphs [13]. In the domain of black-box tuning for language models, methods solve high-dimensional derivative-free optimization problems via random embedding [14]. Furthermore, techniques like mixup help to combat memorization of corrupt labels, sensitivity to adversarial examples, and instability in adversarial training [15]. ProGAN tackles the training instability of GANs by progressively growing the generator and discriminator [16].

In specialized applications, embedding initialization and structure are tailored to specific data characteristics. In traffic flow forecasting, a multi-granularity temporal embedding Transformer network merges complex temporal embeddings, a temporal encoder, and a spatial encoder to address the heterogeneous and nonlinear nature of the data [17]. Similarly, the STFEformer addresses the challenge of modeling intricate spatial–temporal correlations by using Transformer-based methods to capture dynamic spatial dependencies, which GNN-based methods may limit by focusing statically on spatial correlations [18]. In the context of knowledge-enhanced pre-trained language models, entity embeddings need to be retrained when the knowledge graph is updated, and model parameters have to be retrained if injected in the pre-training phase [19].

The use of pre-trained embeddings is also evident in other domains. For predicting SARS-CoV-2 epitope-specific TCR recognition, self-supervised transfer learning has been demonstrated to be powerful for extracting useful features, although challenges remain due to the enormous diversity of TCRs and lack of available training data [20]. In grammatical error correction, applying BERT as a contextual embedding is more challenging than fine-tuning the model, as machine translation output does not generate annotated data for evaluation [21]. In visual transformers, a modified transformer integrated with a convolutional layer instead of a fully connected layer has been proposed [16]. The BERT model includes embeddings as a component, with specific values noted in its architecture description [22].

Other optimization strategies include alternating minimization and random search based on the annealing method [16]. In the analysis of training data influence, authors specifically use the gradients of only those tokens that appear in both training and test instances [23]. While some approaches require a large amount of labeled training data, others like ELA features suffer from strong correlation between multiple features and limited applicability to multi-objective continuous optimization problems [24]. Random initialization baselines in contrastive learning are trained for 40,000 steps, which is sufficiently long to achieve near-maximal accuracy [25].

sections.title: Modern Practices: When Pre-trained Embeddings Are Used
sections.text:
While random initialization is the standard for from-scratch pre-training, pre-trained embeddings are utilized in specific contexts such as fine-tuning, low-resource scenarios, and multimodal tasks. In the fine-tuning phase of models like BERT, the model is initialized with pre-trained parameters, and all parameters are fine-tuned using labeled data from downstream tasks [1]. This approach allows even low-resource tasks to benefit from deep unidirectional architectures [1], and transfer learning generally enables good performance on low-resource tasks [2]. For instance, in the context of multilingual models, pre-trained multilingual LMs are fine-tuned to extract more useful representations, which are then combined with static and extracted contextual embeddings to achieve high-quality cross-lingual word embeddings [3].

In low-resource language scenarios, pre-trained embeddings are often employed to mitigate data scarcity. Pre-trained Hindi fastText word embeddings from IndicNLP and Facebook are used in conjunction with CNN and LSTM models for hostility detection [4]. Similarly, for low-resource Egyptian Arabic dialects, a semi-supervised neural machine translation approach utilizes word embeddings, where increasing the embedding size from 300 to 512 dimensions improved the BLEU score from 24 to 29.5 [5]. In cross-lingual sentence embedding for low-resource Chinese-Vietnamese pairs, powerful pre-training models are effectively fine-tuned by constructing sentence-level positive and negative samples to avoid catastrophic forgetting [6]. Furthermore, in low-resource NMT, data augmentation methods use paraphrase embedding and POS-tagging to generate fake monolingual corpora by replacing specific POS labels based on word embedding similarity [7].

Beyond standard language modeling, pre-trained embeddings are applied in multimodal and specialized domains. In deep visual semantic embedding, word embedding initialization is used for text encoders based on recurrent neural networks to unify images and texts in the same feature space [8]. In the domain of molecular generation, Adapt-cMolGPT modifies molecular representation and optimizes the fine-tuning process by incorporating an adapter module into a pre-trained base model to address small dataset challenges [9]. Additionally, in reinforcement learning for hybrid electric vehicles, an advanced driver experience model is embedded into deep reinforcement learning to improve training convergence efficiency [10].

However, the use of pre-trained or external embeddings presents certain limitations and complexities. In knowledge-enhanced pre-trained language models, entity embeddings need to be retrained when the knowledge graph is updated, and model parameters must be retrained if injected in the pre-training phase [11]. Similarly, KEPLER adds a knowledge embedding pre-training task that shares a Transformer Encoder with Masked Language Modeling, obtaining text-enhanced knowledge embeddings and knowledge-enhanced PLMs simultaneously [11]. In the context of data augmentation, "Mixing in Embedding Space" tends to slow convergence due to the complexity of selecting appropriate embedding layers for mixing [12], although embedding-level mixing is noted as a consistently effective strategy [12]. For position embeddings, Position Interpolation rescales Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to support longer sequences with minimal fine-tuning [13].

In specific tuning scenarios, such as black-box tuning, random embeddings are sometimes preferred or modified. For example, in Black-Box Tuning, the random embedding matrix is set by sampling from a uniform distribution instead of normal distributions [14]. Alternatively, a prompt embedding can be pre-trained on publicly available NLI tasks, such as the MNLI training set, for better initialization [14]. In the original BERT paper, the embedding layer is listed as a component with a specific parameter count, but the text does not explicitly detail the initialization method in the provided excerpt [1]. Other studies note that updating all of a pre-trained model’s parameters during fine-tuning outperformed methods designed to update fewer parameters, despite being more expensive [2]. Ensembling models fine-tuned from the same base pre-trained model performed worse than pre-training and fine-tuning all models completely separately [2]. The best performing method for BERT fine-tuning concatenates token representations from the top four hidden layers of the pre-trained Transformer [1].

evidence.title: what learning algorithm is in-context learning? investigations with linear models
evidence.snippet: Neural sequence models, especially transformers, exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning. They can construct new predictors from sequences of labeled examples $(x, f(x))$ presented in the input without further parameter updates. We investigate the hypothesis that transformer-based in-context learners implement standard learning algorithms implicitly, by encoding smaller models in their activations, and updating these implicit models as new examples appear in the context. Using linear regression as a prototypical problem, we offer three sources of evidence for this hypothesis. First, we prove by construction that transformers can implement learning algorithms for linear models based on gradient descent and closed-form ridge regression. evidence.snippet:
Modern DNN-based recommendation systems rely on training-derived embeddings of sparse features. Input sparsity makes obtaining high-quality embeddings for rarely-occurring categories harder as their representations are updated infrequently. We demonstrate a training-time technique to produce superior embeddings via effective cross-category learning and theoretically explain its surprising effectiveness. The scheme, termed the multi-layer embeddings training (MLET), trains embeddings using factorization of the embedding layer, with an inner dimension higher than the target embedding dimension. For inference efficiency, MLET converts the trained two-layer embedding into a single-layer one thus keeping inference-time model size unchanged.

evidence.snippet: We investigate an extension of continuous online learning in recurrent neural network language models. The model keeps a separate vector representation of the current unit of text being processed and adaptively adjusts it after each prediction. evidence.title: title:polyglot neural language models: a case study in cross-lingual phonetic representation learning
evidence.snippet: Abstract:We introduce polyglot language models, recurrent neural network models trained to predict symbol sequences in many different languages using shared representations of symbols and conditioning on typological information about the language to be predicted. We apply these to the problem of modeling phone sequences---a domain in which universal symbol inventories and cross-linguistically shared feature representations are a natural fit. Intrinsic evaluation on held-out perplexity, qualitative analysis of the learned representations, and extrinsic evaluation in two downstream applications that make use of phonetic features show (i) that polyglot models better generalize to held-out data than comparable monolingual models and (ii) that polyglot phonetic feature representations are of higher quality than those learned monolingually.

evidence.snippet:

evidence.title: machine learning for refining knowledge graphs: a survey
evidence.snippet: Knowledge graph (KG) refinement refers to the process of filling in missing information, removing redundancies, and resolving inconsistencies in KGs. With the growing popularity of KG in various domains, many techniques involving machine learning have been applied, but there is no survey dedicated to machine learning-based KG refinement yet. Based on a novel framework following the KG refinement process, this article presents a survey of machine learning approaches to KG refinement according to the kind of operations in KG refinement, the training datasets, mode of learning, and process multiplicity. Furthermore, the survey aims to provide broad practical insights into the development of fully automated KG refinement.

evidence.title: title:improving low compute language modeling with in-domain embedding initialisation
evidence.snippet: Abstract:Many NLP applications, such as biomedical data and technical support, have 10-100 million tokens of in-domain data and limited computational resources for learning from it. How should we train a language model in this scenario? Most language modeling research considers either a small dataset with a closed vocabulary (like the standard 1 million token Penn Treebank), or the whole web with byte-pair encoding. We show that for our target setting in English, initialising and freezing input embeddings using in-domain data can improve language model performance by providing a useful representation of rare words, and this pattern holds across several different domains. sections.title: Definition and Calculation of EVM for Digital Modulations
sections.text:
The Error Vector Magnitude (EVM) is a metric used to quantify the fidelity of generated or received waveforms, with reported values in optical arbitrary waveform generation reaching approximately 16.4% [1]. In the context of RF power amplification, EVM serves as a critical performance indicator, where an RMS value of 1.60% and a peak value of 5.87% were achieved for EDGE signals to meet specific power requirements [2]. The measurement of EVM can be performed using low-cost solutions that rely on 1-bit under-sampled acquisition of the RF modulated signal and specific post-processing algorithms [3].

The calculation of EVM involves determining the distance between the received signal points and their ideal reference locations. This process often requires mean centering, which is achieved by subtracting the geometric mean vector of a complex output trace from each sampled signal point [4]. The fundamental operation relies on computing the distance between vectors, a concept analogous to calculating the dot product between normalized vectors or using distance metrics such as the Mahalanobis distance to capture disparities in data structures [5][6]. In some measurement models, a cost minimization technique is employed for the value calculation of these signal parameters [4].

Regarding the applicability of a single general equation across different modulation types, the evidence indicates that EVM is a standard metric applied to both constant-envelope and non-constant-envelope signals. For instance, EVM is explicitly used to evaluate the performance of polar modulated RF power amplifiers, which handle signals with varying amplitude and phase [2]. Conversely, techniques for combining multiple signal components into a constant envelope composite signal, such as those proposed for GNSS signals, address the challenge of maintaining signal integrity in constant-envelope modulation [7]. While the provided excerpts do not explicitly define a distinct mathematical formula for EVM that differs between MPSK and MQAM, they confirm that EVM is a universal metric for assessing modulation fidelity in both optical and RF domains [1][3][2].

The accuracy of EVM measurement and the underlying signal processing are influenced by various factors, including phase noise and non-linear distortions. In millimeter-wave systems, phase noise can cause significant performance losses if not corrected using phase tracking reference signals [8]. Furthermore, non-linear transformations in the continuous-time domain, such as those caused by power amplifiers, can be characterized and compensated for using Volterra series models, which impacts the final EVM measurement [9]. The estimation of Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR), which is closely related to EVM, can be performed for both QAM and PSK modulation signals using blind estimation methods that allow for accurate BER or SER estimation with a small number of symbols [10].

To ensure accurate EVM measurement, normalization and calibration steps are often necessary. Normalization refers to mapping real value ranges of several data structures to a standard scale [4]. In localization and sensing applications, linear transformations of phase values are used as a calibration step to improve stability, a principle that parallels the need for phase calibration in EVM measurements [11]. Additionally, distance correction techniques may scale correlation profiles to account for sample strength fall-off, which is relevant when measuring signal integrity over varying distances or through complex channels [4]. The use of complex channel responses and the agreement of entries in complex vectors are critical for accurate signal reconstruction and, by extension, accurate EVM calculation [11].

In summary, while EVM is calculated by measuring the vector distance between received and ideal signal points, often involving mean centering and normalization [4], the provided evidence does not explicitly state that a single general equation is invalid for both MPSK and MQAM. Instead, it demonstrates that EVM is a standard metric applied across different modulation schemes, including QAM, PSK, and polar modulation [10][1][2]. The precision of this measurement depends on correcting for phase noise, non-linear distortions, and ensuring proper calibration of the measurement system [8][9][11].

sections.title: Theoretical Relationship Between EVM and BER/SER
sections.text:
Error Vector Magnitude (EVM) is defined as the deviation of the in-phase and quadrature components of a received signal from their ideal constellation points, serving as a fundamental metric for assessing signal quality [1]. In the context of heterogeneous wireless overlay systems, EVM has been proposed as a generic Quality of Service (QoS) trigger for vertical handover execution, functioning alongside other metrics such as SNR, bandwidth, jitter, BER, and delay [1]. The utility of EVM as a performance figure of merit is established by deriving relationships among EVM metrics for different performance indicators, demonstrating that EVM can be equivalently useful as signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and bit error rate (BER) [2]. Specifically, for M-ary quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM) formats in optical coherent systems, the relationship between EVM and BER allows for the estimation of bit error ratio from EVM analysis [3]. This estimation capability applies to both data-aided and non-data-aided reception, provided a correction factor is applied for different combined linewidth symbol duration products at the target BER [3].

The accuracy of BER estimation from EVM is critical for monitoring system performance near the target BER, particularly for modulation schemes such as QPSK, 16-QAM, and 64-QAM [3]. Without the appropriate correction factor, the calibrated BER would otherwise be underestimated, leading to unreliable performance monitoring in optical coherent systems employing carrier phase recovery with differential decoding [3]. Similarly, in radio-over-fiber applications utilizing semiconductor optical amplifier Mach-Zehnder interferometers (SOA-MZI), the error vector magnitude is acquired in the repetition rate range to evaluate the conversion gain of simultaneous frequency up-conversion of QPSK signals [4]. For transmitter mask testing of PM-QPSK, time-resolved EVM is used to accept transmitters where individual impairments cause less than a 0.5 dB OSNR penalty, linking EVM directly to hardware performance limits [5].

While EVM serves as a proxy for signal quality, it is distinct from direct error counts, and its relationship with BER is influenced by the specific modulation type and channel conditions. For instance, SNR estimation methods for blind signals in QAM and PSK modulation can be modified to accurately estimate BER or SER with a transaction of a relatively small number of symbols [6]. This highlights that while EVM and SNR are related, the mapping to BER requires specific considerations for the modulation format, such as the compensation of BPSK signal offset using AWGN in the channel [6]. In high-speed optical transmission, such as 32.5 Tbit/s 16QAM Nyquist WDM, the performance is evaluated through spectral efficiency and transmission distance, where EVM implicitly underpins the signal integrity required to maintain these rates without optical dispersion compensation [7]. Furthermore, in systems affected by hardware impairments like amplifier non-linearities, quantization artifacts, and phase noise, the error-rate performance is limited by these transmit-side factors, which are captured by EVM but must be accounted for in data detection algorithms to achieve optimal performance [8].

The theoretical link between EVM and error rates is further contextualized by the need for accurate channel and signal reconstruction. In massive MIMO systems, avoiding bit allocation problems during feedback involves concatenating the complex channel and embedding uplink channel magnitude to the channel reconstruction at the base station [9]. This reconstruction process is essential for accurately assessing the EVM, as the deviation from ideal points is only meaningful relative to the correctly estimated channel state. In the domain of discrete memoryless channels, the cost of channel identification scales quadratically with the alphabet size, and a fundamental lower bound for the required number of channel senses is derived to identify the best channel with a certain confidence [10]. This complexity in channel identification underscores why EVM, as a direct measurement of signal deviation, is a practical metric for real-time QoS assessment compared to the more complex task of full channel identification [10].

In advanced communication systems, the relationship between signal quality metrics and error rates is also influenced by probabilistic shaping and capacity constraints. Optimized PMF models can be used to perform probabilistic shaping of constellations in the peak power-constrained additive white Gaussian noise channel, which affects the distribution of error vectors and thus the EVM [11]. Additionally, in the context of 5G and beyond, the integration of features like scalable numerology and flexible spectrum aims to meet targets for Ultra-Reliable and Low Latency Communication (uRLLC), where precise EVM monitoring is crucial for maintaining the required reliability [12]. The use of EVM as a generic QoS trigger facilitates seamless session transfer between networks with different access standards, ensuring that the Quality of Experience is maintained despite variations in underlying signal quality [1]. Ultimately, while EVM provides a robust measure of signal fidelity, its translation to BER or SER requires careful calibration and consideration of modulation-specific factors, such as those detailed for QAM and PSK signals [6][2][3].

sections.title: Limitations of General EVM Equations and Non-Linear Distortions
sections.text:
The fundamental assumption of linear measurement models often fails when the physical system exhibits non-linear behavior, as the accuracy of techniques based on linear resistive models is compromised when the underlying processes evolve non-linearly [1]. In such scenarios, the reliability of results is contingent upon having modeled the correct non-linear relationship with prior knowledge of the interactions involved [2]. For instance, in optical coherent systems employing carrier phase recovery, the relationship between Error Vector Magnitude (EVM) and Bit Error Ratio (BER) requires a specific correction factor to account for laser phase noise, particularly for QPSK, 16-QAM, and 64-QAM formats [3]. Without this correction factor, the calibrated BER would otherwise be underestimated, demonstrating that a simple linear EVM equation is insufficient for accurate performance monitoring near the target BER [3].

Phase noise specifically degrades overall system performance by affecting ranging accuracy in photonic radar systems, where an analytical laser phase noise model must be derived to analyze its impact [4]. Under the assumption of standard white Gaussian laser phase noise, the monostatic and bistatic responses of the detector are altered, further complicating the direct application of general EVM equations [4]. Similarly, in millimeter-wave sensing, phase tracking introduces an extra dependency on a random variable in addition to phase inputs, which adds complexity to the measurement model [5]. To address stability issues arising from such phase variations, schemes like PhaseFi utilize a linear transformation of the phase value as a calibration step to improve the stability of phase values before constructing fingerprint databases [6].

Non-linear distortions, such as those from power amplifiers, can be analyzed using non-linear analysis techniques for harmonic and intermodulation distortion, which are necessary when linear techniques lack confidence or reliability [1]. The presence of noise and distortion significantly affects the accuracy of algorithms, with error rates in NISQ phase quantum devices ranging from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$, which substantially impacts the accuracy of the algorithm [7]. To mitigate these effects, robustness factors can be introduced to stabilize estimation by incorporating additional information, thereby counteracting the impact of noise and improving reliability [8]. Furthermore, noise injection techniques can be used to corrupt data with several realizations of noise, which increases the number of available data and enhances the network’s robustness to small variations [6].

In the context of measurement models, cost minimization techniques may be used for value calculation, but model-driven performance is typically measured based on output comparison with a baseline via an error metric with a well-established measurement technique [5]. Distortion is generally defined as a dissimilarity, such as Mean Squared Error (MSE), between the original and reconstructed signals [9]. To reduce such distortion, additional distortion losses, including $L_2$, LPIPS, and Identity preservation ArcFace, can be added to the optimization process [9]. However, the limitation of these approaches remains that results are reliable only when the correct model for the non-linear relationship has been established [2].

For complex signal processing tasks, non-linear features can be incorporated into linear regression frameworks by replacing the input variable with a non-linear function, such as $\phi(x)$ [6]. Similarly, non-linear functions like the sigmoid function $\sigma(.)$ can modify outputs to lie within a specific range, such as [0,1], in probabilistic models [6]. In machine learning-based localization, public-domain channel simulators allow for the imposition of geometric structure and spatial consistency, which is crucial for testing these non-linear models [6]. Experimental results have shown that constrained, block-structured neural models can achieve an order of magnitude reduction in open-loop simulation mean squared error compared to traditional unstructured models [10].

Despite these advancements, robustness against environmental effects in sensing pipelines is often limited, such as in ego-motion estimation [5]. In specific applications like millimeter-wave sensing, methods like DDBR compute differentials of signal points at different time steps to obtain a background-canceled signal point, which helps in isolating the signal of interest [5]. However, the training error on real data can increase significantly with certain parameters, such as $\alpha \to \infty$ in mixup augmentation, indicating that generalization is not guaranteed [11]. Ultimately, while various metrics including prediction error and confidence calibration are used to evaluate these systems, the core challenge remains the accurate modeling of non-linear distortions and phase noise that invalidate simple linear EVM assumptions [12][2].

sections.title: Practical Measurement Considerations and Standards
sections.text:
The quality of the connection in modern telecommunications systems can be estimated by the value of the error vector, where EVM serves as a measure of the difference between ideal transmitter symbols and measured receiver symbols [1]. In the context of model-driven performance evaluation, performance is measured based on output comparison with a baseline, utilizing an error metric with a well-established measurement technique [2]. For specific applications such as millimeter-wave sensing, measurement models may employ a cost minimization technique for value calculation [2]. When estimating data of interest from noisy measurement signals, Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) is a standard approach used to derive accurate parameters [2].

Calibration and measurement precision are critical, as demonstrated by techniques allowing for in situ calibration of control lines in quantum harmonic oscillator systems, which can achieve performance beyond the standard quantum limit [3]. In error-in-variables models, estimating output measurement variances is complicated because true values of inputs may differ when multiple attempts are made to repeat an experiment [4]. To address this, methodologies categorize attempted replicate experiments into true replicates, where uncertain inputs are the same, and pseudo-replicates, where measured inputs are the same but unknown true values differ [4]. Bootstrap methods are proposed to obtain joint-confidence information for the resulting parameter estimates in these scenarios [4].

Averaging methods are frequently employed to enhance measurement stability and accuracy. Averaging multiple received signal strength (RSS) snapshots can reduce the number of beams needed and achieve more than 95% accuracy in both line-of-sight and non-line-of-sight conditions [5]. In localization tasks, the final location is estimated by averaging the location of reference points with their predicted probabilities [6]. While these quantities are usually more stable, they may reduce the granularity of the observations [6]. Model averaging estimation in linear regression models with measurement error constructs a weight choice criterion that is asymptotically equivalent to the unknown model average estimator minimizing the loss function [7].

Compliance with established standards and channel models is essential for realistic system evaluation. The 3GPP channel models, originally designed for 3G cellular communications, have been repeatedly extended and are now used for 4G and 5G cellular systems [6]. However, due to simplifications, channels generated by the 3GPP model might not show the same complexity as real-world measured channels, which can significantly impact localization and other ML-based tasks [6]. In 5G New Radio unlicensed (NR-U) and WiFi coexistence, 3GPP has proposed a fairness criterion, and optimizers can be used to find the optimal 5G NR-U parameters from a pre-decided range to achieve this fairness [8].

Despite the availability of these tools, best practices for certain measurement and detection tasks remain underdeveloped. The settled definitions and best practices required to unify efforts in specific detection tasks are still missing [9]. Similarly, best practices for out-of-domain intent detection have not yet been fully established [10]. In the domain of infrastructure as code, a lack of best practices and comments hampers modifications and complicates deployment [11]. For 5G protocol analysis, all approaches to protocol development and security analysis, such as property extraction and semantic analysis, remain completely manual [12].

evidence.snippet: Abstract-In this paper, we relate the error vector magnitude (EVM) bit error rate (BER) and signal to noise ratio (SNR). evidence.title: Quantum Vector Signal Analyzer
evidence.snippet: A technique that allows a harmonic oscillator to be used as a wideband vector signal analyzer is described and demonstrated using a single trapped 40ca+ ion cooled near its motional ground state. Further, the analyzer is shown to be compatible with both quantum amplification via squeezing and measurement in the Fock basis, allowing performance beyond the standard quantum limit. In addition to providing an attractive platform for quantum sensing of small fields, the technique allows in situ calibration of qubit control lines in systems using quantum harmonic oscillators and transduction of external, non-resonant drives into oscillator motion. This technique is extendable to other quantum harmonic oscillator systems.

sections.title: GNSS PPS Generation Architecture
sections.text:
Current Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) receivers typically incorporate an internal quartz oscillator, such as a Temperature Compensated Crystal Oscillator (TCXO), which is characterized by limited frequency stability and poor accuracy [1]. This inherent instability of the TCXO makes it one of the primary sources of uncertainty in the navigation solution, alongside multipath and ionosphere effects [1]. The use of a TCXO forces the inclusion of a time parameter in navigation algorithms, which can reduce positioning performance under poor satellite constellation conditions [2]. To address these limitations, researchers have proposed replacing the internal TCXO with higher-stability clocks, such as Chip Scale Atomic Clocks (CSACs), to improve navigation solution availability, positioning accuracy, and tracking recovery [1]. A CSAC offers significantly better short-term stability compared to a TCXO, reducing the associated range error from 0.6 meters to 0.075 meters [2].

In systems requiring high-accuracy timing references, such as distributed wireless sensor arrays, the hardware design of GPS-disciplined oscillators remains a critical component [3]. These oscillators are implemented using field-programmable gate array (FPGA) devices to facilitate automatic adaptive drift correction [3]. The performance of such disciplined oscillators is evaluated by measuring the drift in the 1PPS signal, with experimental results indicating that specific FPGA-based designs can achieve drifts of less than 80 ns and 356 ns [3]. Similarly, in the context of multistatic radar systems, the requirement for precise time and frequency synchronization between spatially separated nodes drives the evaluation of GNSS Disciplined Oscillators (GNSSDOs) [4]. The performance of these GNSSDOs is assessed to determine the limitations of one-way GNSS Time and Frequency Transfer, with conclusions suggesting suitability for specific carrier frequencies and waveform bandwidths [4].

The generation of the 1PPS signal is fundamentally tied to the synchronization of the local oscillator with the GNSS-derived time reference. In phasor measurement applications, software-based methods utilize Pulse Per Second (PPS) signals from GPS to synchronize the local oscillator [5]. This synchronization process involves transforming raw data affected by the local oscillator’s instability into calibrated data, effectively emulating an ideal sampling rate [5]. The reliability of this timing source is crucial, as GPS signals can be unstable due to weak satellite signals or spoofing, which degrades sampling performance [6]. To mitigate these risks, alternative timing sources, such as Pulsar-calibrated Timing Sources, have been proposed to ensure continuity of sampling accuracy with a drift error of 1 microsecond within 91 holdover minutes [6]. Furthermore, detecting GNSS misbehavior, such as spoofing attacks, can be achieved by relying on alternative time sources or local precision hardware clock ensembles to detect clock offset discrepancies [7]. These local references, such as chip-scale thermally stable oscillators with extended holdover capabilities, provide a stable reference compatible with existing receiver architectures [7].

The underlying localization principle of GNSS is based on Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) and trilateration using radio frequency signals [8]. This process requires a free line of sight to at least three satellites [8]. The ranging signals utilized in this process are pseudorandom sequences with special correlation properties [8]. In advanced applications, such as space-borne GNSS timing receivers, a disciplined high-performance clock is preferable to meet rigorous positioning and timing requirements [9]. The design of these receivers involves fine-tuned positioning algorithms to handle the movement of the satellite, contrasting with stationary ground-based counterparts [9]. Additionally, the rapid evolution of GNSS technology demands rapid prototyping tools, leading to the development of low-cost System-on-Chip Field-Programmable Gate Array (SoC-FPGA) architectures [10]. These architectures combine the flexibility of software-defined radio techniques with the energy efficiency of FPGAs, enabling the development of compact, multi-constellation receivers for testing novel features [10].
